title: US military says it fired on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman after it attempted to breach blockade
text:
US military says it fired on commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman after it attempted to breach blockade
U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for shipping, including oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.
Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has carried out in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.
Related video above: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
Iranian state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn't immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.
For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.

title: Maine voters cap mobile home rent increases in 8 communities
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Cindy Marquis didn’t want to move again.
She and her partner, Cliff, only moved to Cascade Leisure Park in Farmington a little over a year ago, and she’s happy there. She loves her home, her neighbors and being close to her grandkids.
But Marquis has already seen their monthly lot rent go up by nearly $50.
At the New Hampshire park where the couple previously lived, their rent jumped from $410 to $575 over five years.
As she watched the same pattern emerge in Farmington, Marquis, 63, began to look for a house on land she could own.
“We feel like we keep paying and paying and paying, and they want more and more and more, and we’re not getting anything in return,” she said.
Then, on Tuesday, voters in the western Maine town overwhelmingly passed an ordinance to limit how much park owners can raise the rent each year.
Marquis now feels like they can stay where they are. “We want to make sure we can still pay the mortgage and our rent and live,” she said.
Similar policies were approved at the polls this week in Augusta, Standish, Oakland, Wells, Jay, Eliot and Wiscasset.
The rules vary across the eight towns, but most tie hikes to a percentage of inflation and are modeled on a state-drafted sample posted this year.
The votes mean that more than 1,700 families across 53 Maine mobile home parks will be protected from lot rent increases that many affordable housing advocates say have become excessive.
PEOPLE ARE ‘STUCK’
Mobile homes are widely considered one of the only remaining “natural” (meaning unsubsidized) forms of affordable housing.
But as these parks have become more attractive to large-scale investors, who buy them and raise the rents, they’re becoming decidedly less so.
Park residents, often low-income families or seniors on a fixed income, own their homes but not the land they sit on, meaning homeowners have to pay to rent their lot (often on top of a monthly home loan payment).
And those payments are getting harder to manage as lot rents keep increasing.
“People are scared. … They’re really stuck in these communities” said Laura Mitchell, executive director of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition.
“This is a pathway that they can take at the local level to take control back,” she said of the ordinances.
In several cases, the support was overwhelming.
In Standish, for example, the ordinance was approved by 75% of voters.
Mitchell said the broad backing of a pretty targeted policy shows that people recognize what a challenge housing affordability has become.
“In a town of any size and in different areas throughout the state, everyone is seeing this and trying to find solutions at all levels,” she said.
‘SOMETHING NEEDS TO BE DONE’
Theresa Kim, who has been working to pass a rent stabilization ordinance in Standish for two years, said she was gratified to see it approved so decisively.
“It is going to help folks stay in their homes,” she said.
Kim’s monthly lot rent has increased 25% since she moved from Portland to Pine Tree Estates in 2022. Meanwhile, the infrastructure and amenities have not improved at a similar rate. The park is owned by RHP Properties, a Michigan-based corporation.
She pays about $672 a month, but said new residents are paying around $1,000.
Many of her neighbors in the 224-lot park are older adults on a fixed income. “They don’t have the option just to go get a job, or find some money somewhere,” when lot rents go up, she said.
Kim never thought she’d be going to town meetings and trying to draft local policy, but she said “a lot of red flags started going up” when rent increases kept coming.
“I kind of just took it upon myself and was like, something needs to be done,” she said.
Kim said Pine Tree Estates is due for another rent increase, so she’s waiting to see what it will be.
“Now it’s just making sure that the ordinance is followed and enforced,” she said. 
The eight communities join several others in Maine that had already adopted rent stabilization rules, including Old Orchard Beach, Sanford, Saco, Waterville, Arundel and Brunswick.
Voters in Norway overwhelming approved a rent stabilization policy at a special town meeting in October, and officials in Gorham are currently exploring what a similar ordinance could look like in their community.
Mitchell, at the Affordable Housing Coalition, noted that rent stabilization can indirectly help move the state closer to meeting its ambitious goal of adding tens of thousands of new units in the next few years.
“Every affordable home that we lose, whether somebody isn’t able to keep it up and it becomes deteriorated, or whether the rent increases are so high that it’s not affordable anymore, that counteracts every new home that we produce,” she said.

title: Hall-Dale boys soccer holds off Fort Kent for 3rd straight Class C title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
LEWISTON — Greyson Cary was frustrated. The Hall-Dale junior had multiple opportunities in the first half of the Class C boys soccer final, but was unable to put one in the net.
A perfect pass and a open look ended that frustration for Carey, who delivered a goal and a third straight state championship for Bulldogs.
Carey scored with 19:44 left in the second half, the only goal in Hall-Dale’s 1-0 victory over Fort Kent on Saturday at Lewiston High School.
“It feels as good as the first and the second (title), but it feels good that we have a group of kids who get to celebrate again today,” said Hall-Dale coach Jesse Rowe. “You set out for these the day after the last (season) finishes, so tomorrow we’ll be preparing for the future. But they’ll enjoy the next 24 hours, for sure.”
Hall-Dale finishes 17-1-0. Fort Kent, the C North champion, ends 10-7-1.
Senior forward Collin McArthur sent an accurate pass to Cary, who promptly knocked it into the low corner to give Hall-Dale the lead.
“You live those moments in your head so often,” said Cary. “You just have to turn off your brain, just do what you’ve been practicing and just finish the goal.”
McArthur added: “We worked (on the play) all through practice, we knew (Fort Kent) was going to play a sweeper. We planned those diagonal runs and try to see where we could find Greyson, or Karter (Eldridge), or me in that slot. (Cary) yelled my name, I saw him, and he took it from there.”
Cary had two near-goal opportunities in the first half, one shot that went wide, another stopped on a diving save by Fort Kent goalie Kyle Paradis.
“It’s been frustrating, a little bit,” Cary said. “But you just have to be patient, recognize the work, and just let the play come to me.”
The first half of the game was a showcase of goalies. Paradis, a junior, made five saves before halftime, including a diving save to his right on Cary’s shot with 8:45 remaining in the half. The Bulldogs had a 6-2 shot advantage in the first half.
Paradis finished with seven saves.
“He’s an incredible (goalie),” Fort Kent coach Kalusha Kotes said of Paradis. “It wasn’t the result we wanted (today), but I’m confident we will be back.”
While less busy, the work was no less dramatic for Hall-Dale keeper Landon Gilbert. He made a jumping save on a 50-yard indirect kick from Fort Kent’s Dominic Cyr. With 5:40 remaining in the first half, Cyr had Gilbert on a one-on-one breakaway situation, but Cyr’s shot went wide to the left.
Gilbert finished with three saves. All three Hall-Dale title wins have been by 1-0 scores. The Bulldogs beat Washington Academy in 2024 and Orono last year.

title: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (AP) — Berkshire Hathaway repurchased $9.6 billion worth of its own shares in the third quarter, but Geico disappointed and its overall profit fell more than 28% as the value of its investments changed.
But the buybacks likely came to a halt recently as Berkshire’s Class A stock price surged past $878,000 and topped where it was before Warren Buffett surprised investors with his plans to retire at the annual meeting in May 2025. He gave up the chairman title in September after relinquishing the CEO job to Greg Abel in January.
Berkshire’s massive cash pile also returned to growing in the third quarter and reached $377.4 billion, up from $365.5 billion at the end of June.
CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert said Geico is in a tough spot right now with insurance premiums declining at the same time the average cost of the claims are increasing. Geico’s underwriting profit fell to $1.35 billion from last year’s $2.37 billion. Competitors like Progressive are handling the pressure better.
Berkshire’s non-insurance businesses that Abel has overseen for years — such as manufacturers like Precision Castparts, the utilities and BNSF railroad — seem to be performing better than its massive insurance unit even with the lack of major hurricanes or other catastrophes this year.
“I think we’re seeing the businesses that play to Greg’s strengths do well. But the question is what about the rest of the franchise,” Seifert said.
Berkshire reported a $22.1 billion profit, or $15,502 per Class A share, on Saturday morning. That’s down from $30.8 billion, or $21,413 in last year’s third quarter, but those bottom-line figures always tend to obscure how the dozens of companies the conglomerate owns are performing.
The company has long recommended that investors pay more attention to operating earnings, which exclude the value of its investments that can vary widely, but those also slipped nearly 6% to $12.7 billion, or $8,907 per Class A share. That’s down from $13.485 billion, or $9,376.15 per Class A share a year ago.
The four analysts surveyed by FactSet Research had predicted Berkshire would report operating earnings of $8,821.84 per Class A share.
Berkshire owns several major insurers, including Geico, a collection of big utilities, BNSF railroad and a varied assortment of manufacturing and retail companies, including Precision Castparts and See’s Candy.

title: Cape Elizabeth girls soccer successfully defends Class B title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BANGOR — The second half of the Class B girls soccer final Saturday began with Haisel McGeachey taking a soccer ball directly into the face, forcing the Cape Elizabeth junior to leave the game with a bloody nose.
What McGeachey and her teammates will remember most about this game years from now will be what she did when she returned.
McGeachey’s goal with 14 minutes remaining lifted Cape Elizabeth to a 2-1 victory over John Bapst in the state championship game at Cameron Stadium. The win gives the Capers back-to-back state titles and 11 Gold Balls overall.
“I think that really put the game to sleep,” said McGeachey, whose goal followed first-half tallies by Cape’s Alexa Mallory and John Bapst’s Naia Studley. “I think we were fighting so hard to get the next goal, and I’m really just so happy that we got the job done.”
Cape Elizabeth looked more dangerous early, swinging in two crosses that were inches from connecting with a player in the first seven minutes. Yet it was John Bapst (16-1-1) that scored first, as Studley took advantage of a defensive lapse and got around Cape keeper Kelsie Law before shooting into an open net.
That goal, which came with 30:09 remaining in the first half, was met with a quick response by Cape Elizabeth (16-1-1). Four minutes later, Mallory collected the ball on the edge of the penalty area and fired home a screamer.
“Our saying is always, ‘We can go down, but then we come right back up,’” Mallory said. “As soon as we went down, we didn’t let our morale drop, and we got one back. Once we get one, we can always get another.”
Five minutes after Mallory’s goal, Studley made another nice run for Bapst before pushing a shot inches wide of the far post. A powerful shot by Mallory with just under 12 minutes to go in the half was the only other prime opportunity in the opening 40 minutes.
Cape Elizabeth mostly controlled the flow early in the second half, though Bapst countered with a couple pushes. Shortly after returning to the field, McGeachey put the Capers in front with 25:51 remaining, as she short-hopped a goal past Crusaders keeper Abby-May Turner.
“She’s a grinder; she’s played in two state finals, and she’s scored both times,” said Cape Elizabeth coach Branden Noltkamper. “She does all the dirty work, and she does all the chores that no one else wants to do. If that means taking one in the face and getting a bloody nose, that’s what she’ll do.”
Cape Elizabeth didn’t produce many scoring chances the rest of the way, but the Capers didn’t let John Bapst generate much, either. The Crusaders’ only serious threat came with just over five minutes to go, as Quinn Bennett found space but ripped a shot wide of net.
Cape Elizabeth’s repeat title win comes a year after the Capers went 18-0, scoring 89 goals and conceding only seven. That team was voted 2025-26 Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Year for all sports, and Noelle Mallory, Alexa’s older sister, was the Varsity Maine Girls Soccer Player of the Year.
After losing the elder Mallory and several other starters to graduation, Cape Elizabeth was expected by some to take a step back in 2025. Instead, the Capers left a cold, drizzly Cameron Stadium carrying another Gold Ball back home.
“It feels so good (to repeat),” Mallory said. “Everyone told us that this was a rebuilding year for us, but we like to prove people wrong. Well, now we did.”

title: Israel’s president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu
text:
Israel’s president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.
Eisenkot, a former military chief who ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is now a step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving premier.
He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond.
Related video above: Israel's Prime Minister Netanyahu suffers a setback in Tuesday's election
In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government, but putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught.
Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority in parliament in last month's elections. But the bloc led by Eisenkot also didn’t win a majority. That left Arab-led parties, which made historic gains, as potential but politically fraught kingmakers.
An Arab party has been part of a governing coalition just once in Israel's history. Forming such an alliance could be especially divisive for Eisenkot after more than three years of war in Gaza.
Netanyahu has been on a campaign to head off any alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties, including unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties “stole” the elections. Shortly before Herzog's announcement, he called for a “national unity government” in a video statement and warned against “hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters” – language he uses to refer to the Arab-led parties.
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security, while Eisenkot has indicated a willingness to partner with them under certain conditions, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu, whose Likud is the single largest party in parliament, could seek to create a broad unity government with major Jewish parties. However, the men have deep differences over many issues that will be difficult to bridge. That includes Netanyahu's reliance on religious parties that demand draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men, as well as Netanyahu's opposition to a formal investigation into the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attacks.
Eisenkot could also seek to create a “minority” government — shored up by external support from Arab parties that are not formal members of his coalition. However, other members of his bloc have said they would reject such an alliance.
Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister’s video with a statement posted on X and urged members of his party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with “radical parties,” in an apparent reference to the far-right parties in his religious-nationalist base.
The statement argued that Eisenkot would only include parties and parliament members who support its principles.

title: Rent control in Portland has created a problem for realtors
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Linda C. Cohen is association executive of the Greater Portland Board of Realtors.
When buying a home in Maine, families rely upon transparency, clear expectations and a reliable framework of laws and regulations to protect their significant investment. Buyers use property disclosures, real estate professionals and due diligence to understand the conditions, restrictions and opportunities for the property they are purchasing and the financial obligations that may come with it.
Recent events in Portland have made this harder than ever for home buyers. Rent control has created a troubling situation where buyers of rental properties can inherit significant liabilities and potentially astronomical financial penalties resulting from prior owners’ unintentional errors or undiscovered violations, without any clear or standardized process for identifying those liabilities before closing.
Under Portland’s complicated rent control ordinance, a property’s rental history matters. Base rents, allowable annual increases, banked rent, rental registrations, properly drafted tenant notices and prior compliance can all affect what a new owner is legally permitted to charge. However, this can be a complicated patchwork of information to identify and understand.
A single error or omission in any one of these areas can trigger tens of thousands of dollars in financial liability, even years after a property changes hands. These risks extend beyond multi-unit buildings to single-family homes and condominiums, a risk not appreciated by many homeowners.
Consider a recent example: A buyer purchased a condominium intending to make it his home. After living there for a time, he moved out and rented it at market rate, unaware that the property had been rented years earlier, establishing a base rent under Portland’s rent control ordinance. As a result, he was required to roll back the rent to 2021 levels and repay tenants nearly $20,000 for violations he had no part in creating. Unable to absorb the financial burden, he now faces selling the property. This story is far from unique.
In another case, a single-family rental owner who registered the property annually and believed themselves to be fully compliant was audited by the city. The audit uncovered a $20 calculation error made two years earlier that had gone undetected by the city’s own registration system. That $20 mistake resulted in a two-year rent rollback and approximately $14,000 in tenant repayments on a property that cost the buyer $350,000 to purchase. Typically a buyer at that price point does not have the financial resources to incur such a penalty.
These examples illustrate a larger problem: Portland’s rent control system has become so complicated that even property owners making every effort to follow the rules can find themselves facing devastating financial penalties for seemingly minor mistakes. It increasingly resembles a “gotcha” system, where compliance is difficult to establish and errors can be extraordinarily costly.
The problem is that Maine’s existing real estate disclosure framework does not specifically require sellers to provide the comprehensive rent control compliance history necessary to identify these risks. That raises serious questions for buyers and their Realtors who are making sure their clients are informed and protected.
There are no easy methods to verify past years’ rental calculations, notices and registrations. What is the city doing to help purchasers and their Realtors or attorneys uncover violations that may not be apparent in municipal records? What can be done to protect buyers who purchase a home in good faith but later face potentially substantial financial consequences for the prior owner’s undisclosed mistakes?
These are not simply landlord concerns. They are consumer protection issues affecting buyers, sellers, real estate professionals and the integrity of Portland’s housing market. A real estate transaction should not become a guessing game about undisclosed financial liabilities, particularly under an ordinance so complex that even experienced housing providers struggle to navigate it.
Portland’s complex rent control rules and its need to enforce the ordinance also come with the obligation to establish a reliable, transparent process for documenting compliance and identifying potential violations before properties change hands. Sellers should be required to provide meaningful rental histories, and buyers should have a reasonable way to verify the information.
You cannot reasonably expect buyers to assume liabilities they have no practical way to discover. Compounding the problem, even the city is often unable to provide accurate or definitive information, instead advising buyers to consult an attorney.
Portland’s rent control ordinance has already added significant complexity to owning and operating rental housing. Compliance should be achievable, mistakes should be identifiable and buyers should not be left holding the bill for violations they had no way of knowing existed.
Transparency is not too much to ask. It is the foundation of a fair real estate transaction.

title: Maine Mariners halt three-game skid
text:
Antonio Venuto scored twice in the first period, Luke Cavallin made 33 saves, and the Maine Mariners avoided a three-game sweep against the Greensboro Gargoyles by skating to a 2-0 win Saturday night in an ECHL game in Greensboro, North Carolina
Venuto got his third goal of the season at 6:34 of the first period, then added an unassisted goal at 10:58.
The victory snapped a three-game losing streak for Maine, which is 4-4.
The Mariners will host the Wheeling Nailers at 6:30 p.m. Tuesday night.

title: Woman sentenced to life in prison for murder of her 5-week-old daughter
text:
MIDLAND, Texas (KOSA/Gray News) - A woman in Texas has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the death of her 5-week-old daughter.
A jury convicted 24-year-old Sarah Michelle Gilley-Wroe on one count of capital murder of a child under 10 years old.
The infant died May 11, 2022, at Midland Memorial Hospital from severe head trauma.
Investigators said medical evidence showed the girl had two fractures in the back of her skull, and the injuries were consistent with blunt force trauma.
Detectives searched Gilley-Wroe’s phone and found incriminating Google searches. Gilley-Wroe also made incriminating statements while in custody, authorities said.
According to authorities, the 24-year-old told a cellmate that she threw the baby against the wall and struck the girl until she stopped crying.
Gilley-Wroe was the only person alone with the child during the time in which the reported crimes could have occurred.
Medical experts equated the amount of force required to cause the injury to the force of a fall from a two-story building. Gilley-Wroe claimed the injuries could have been caused by her aunt, the baby’s father, or her dog.

title: Officials: 1 dead, 20 injured in crash with cyclists
text:
WAKE COUNTY, N.C. (WRAL) - At least one person is dead after an elderly driver crashed into a group of cyclists, officials said.
The crash happened Saturday in Wake County, North Carolina.
Fire officials said at least 20 others were injured, including seven who were taken to trauma centers.
Officials said the 76-year-old driver crossed the center line, collided with the cyclists, and then ran off the road and into a ditch.
The driver is in custody, with impairment listed as a possible factor in the crash.

title: Congress enters lame duck session following midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Congress has a list of unfinished work during the lame duck session, the period between the election of a new Congress and the start of its term, including a Dec. 11 government funding deadline.
The session follows the 2026 midterm elections, which came to a head on Election Day, Nov. 3.
Top of the agenda: the stopgap funding bill passed earlier this year to keep the government open through Election Day, which expires Dec. 11. A government shutdown is possible before the holidays if lawmakers cannot agree on a spending package.
The agenda also includes the remaining fiscal year 2027 spending bills, the National Defense Authorization Act and the Farm Bill. Both stalled ahead of the midterms.
In the final weeks of the year, Republican leaders will also attempt to carry out President Donald Trump’s top directives before the majority of both chambers flips. Democrats are unlikely to cooperate knowing they will be in charge in 2027, which gives them an edge in negotiations.
During the session, both parties are expected to start planning for the 120th Congress, including new policy pushes and messaging following the midterm elections.
Meanwhile, Trump is threatening to veto anything that does not fit his agenda.
The 120th Congress will be seated in the first few days of January 2027. Current lawmakers will return to the Hill Nov. 9.
Copyright 2026 Gray DC. All rights reserved.

title: Argument over Wi-Fi leads to murder of mother and son, police say
text:
LUFKIN, Texas (KTRE/Gray News) - An arrest has been made in the murder of a mother and son in Texas.
Jeremiah McGee was arrested Friday and charged with capital murder in the shooting deaths of Maria Davalos, 62, and her son, Ariel Arellano Jr., in their home.
“They determined Mr. McGee to be the main suspect and continued to work the information until they had enough to gain a warrant for his arrest and a second search warrant of his home,” Police Chief Travis Brazil said.
McGee, 47, was arrested at his home, and police said they found what they believed to be the weapon used in the murders.
Authorities said a homicide investigation was launched on Oct. 23 when officers responded to a 911 call and found Davalos and Arellano fatally wounded by gunfire.
The man who called 911 was the son and brother of the victims, police said.
Investigators noted that multiple people they interviewed, including McGee, told them that there had been disputes over Wi-Fi.
McGee and the victims lived side-by-side in a duplex on Third Street.

title: Man on probation for child pornography sentenced to life in prison
text:
AMARILLO, Texas (KFDA/Gray News) - A Texas man who was on probation for possessing child pornography will now spend the rest of his life in prison.
Michael Lee Green, 43, appeared before Judge Dee Johnson of Randall County’s 47th District Court on Friday.
Texas authorities said an investigation started in November 2024 when Amarillo Police Department’s Special Victims Unit received a tip from Oklahoma Predator Prevention, an advocacy group that targets online predators.
The tip involved the online activities of Green.
Police investigated the tip, and a department investigator had a forensic examination conducted on Green’s cellphone.
The examination revealed that Green possessed illegal child sexual abuse material involving minors.
Authorities said Green admitted during several interviews with investigators that he received and viewed the material.
He was booked into Randall County Jail on 10 counts of possessing child pornography involving more than 50 depictions or videos of minors.
In March 2025, Green was placed on deferred adjudication for a term of 10 years.
Court records showed that Green was then booked into Randall County Jail again in July on a felony charge of unauthorized absence from a community correction facility.
The offense was related to an incident where he did not report to a court-ordered supervision facility.
At his Friday hearing, Judge Johnson heard evidence from both sides on revocation and punishment.
After hearing the evidence, the judge revoked Green’s probation and sentenced him to life in prison on each of the 10 counts.
Green additionally entered a plea in his other open felony case.
Copyright 2026 KFDA via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: 'He saved my life': Woman rescued from van sinking in floodwaters by police officer
text:
'He saved my life': Police officer rescues woman from van stuck in floodwaters
A Florida police officer rescued two people trapped in a sinking van after floodwaters pushed their van into a canal Monday morning.
Maria Andrade, the woman who was rescued, told Hearst sister station WPBF 25 News she was in the back of the van on her way home from a doctor's appointment when floodwaters pushed the van into a canal.
The driver was able to call 911 and ask for help.
The police officer's body camera footage shows him arriving less than two minutes after the call and immediately entering the water.
The officer first pulled the driver out of the van and, with the help of firefighters, rescued Andrade, who was trapped inside.
Andrade, who only speaks Spanish, explained through her son, Raul Morales, that the floodwaters had gotten so bad, it was hard to tell where the road was.
"She says it was raining really, really hard," Morales said. "She couldn't even see the road. It was just water."
Andrade said the van began sinking and filling up with water.
"She could hear the water just gushing in there, and she was like, 'That's what pretty much told me, uh-oh. I'm in trouble,'" Morales said.
Maria said she couldn’t unlatch her seat belt and was trapped inside the van.
But she also said she didn’t have time to be scared because the officer arrived so quickly.
The van's driver told police the only way to get Maria out was through the back.
One person entered the van and pushed while others pulled her out.
"She wants to thank the first responders for being really, really on top of it. She realized how quick they were about it and made her feel better about her situation," Morales said. "Thank you for helping her out and for being there for her. It’s just ... there's no words for it."

title: Father accused of leaving daughter sleeping outside Target to hold spot for Pokémon cards, police say
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A man in South Carolina is accused of leaving his 6-year-old daughter sleeping in line outside a Target store to hold his place for a Pokémon card release.
John-Michael Dooley, 35, is charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.
Charleston officers responded to the West Ashley store around 2:30 a.m. Friday after receiving a report of an unattended child.
Customers had gathered outside overnight for the release of a new Pokémon trading card set.
Witnesses told police that sometime after 1 a.m., Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and blanket before leaving her asleep in line.
After he had been gone for about an hour, concerned customers called police.
When Dooley returned to the store, witnesses identified him, and he was arrested.
Dooley allegedly told detectives he had gone home and left his daughter at the store to maintain his place in line.
The girl was unharmed and placed in emergency protective custody with the South Carolina Department of Social Services.
Copyright 2026 WCSC via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Lawyer who represented defendant in Tupac Shakur murder case found dead
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — The defense attorney who represented Duane “Keffe D” Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial has died.
Michael Sanft was reported dead Thursday night in Las Vegas. The Clark County coroner’s office confirmed the 55-year-old’s death.
The cause and manner of death remain pending. Details surrounding his death were limited, with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department referring all inquiries to the coroner’s office.
Sanft was the lead trial attorney at SOS Injury Lawyers, where he tried more than 150 cases to jury verdict and argued before the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
According to his website, he moved to San Diego at 12 and later attended BYU-Hawaii.
Sanft represented Davis pro bono during his Las Vegas trial. A jury later found Davis guilty in August.
In an interview with FOX5, Sanft said he would not have done anything differently.
“We had the best team possible in this case, from the motion practice work on this appeal to our investigator to our firm here at SOS Injury. We all did our part. I don’t see what I could’ve done differently,” Sanft said.
After the verdict, Sanft also mentioned sitting down with Davis.
“We were just sitting there taking in the moment,” Sanft said. “He had reminded me this is phase one. Because I was upset with the verdict, I was very disappointed in the jury. Mr. Davis was the one who said, ‘Don’t worry about it, man, this is the first phase,’ and I said, ‘I understand; I hate to lose.’”
Attorney Mike Troiano said Sanft was an honest, humble and good human being.
“I’m in total shock by this news, as is the legal community as a whole. An extremely talented trial lawyer who jurors and his peers loved,” Troiano continued.
Davis’ defense team stated they had planned to appeal the conviction. A notice of the appeal was filed Oct. 30.

title: Two men accused of handing out psychedelic gummies to nearly 15 kids on Halloween, police say
text:
SAN DIEGO (Gray News) - Two men in California are accused of giving psilocybin-infused gummies to young trick-or-treaters on Halloween night, according to authorities.
Police arrested Michael Goff, 80, and Shawn Michael Foster, 45, a press release said.
On November 4, officers recovered suspected psilocybin gummies, cannabis, methamphetamine, firearms, ammunition, and drug sales at the home.
Police said nearly 15 children took packages of the gummies that had been left on the home’s porch on Halloween. Parents noticed the unusual packaging, intervened and contacted police.
Frank Cary, one of the parents, told NBC 7 San Diego he took a package from his 2-year-old after noticing a design featuring a giraffe and melting text.
The label listed a 5-gram dosage and included the words “psilocybin mushrooms.”
Parents confronted a resident before filing a police report and giving the packages to officers.
Testing later confirmed the presence of psilocybin.

title: Maine’s most popular game bird is declining in other states. Why is it thriving here?
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
I’d rather be in the North Maine Woods than virtually anywhere else on the planet. However, I tend to avoid it during upland game bird hunting season. Too crowded.
I don’t mind. There’s plenty of room for everyone to enjoy the woods any way they please. Ruffed grouse are Maine’s most popular game bird, by far. Up to 500,000 grouse are bagged each year.
The ruffed grouse is Pennsylvania’s official state bird, yet its population has declined so dramatically that the bird may disappear altogether. Several states have banned hunting them. Others have listed the birds as threatened or endangered. Yet Maine’s population remains in good shape. Why?
Ruffed grouse require young forests, preferably with lots of aspens and birches. The buds and catkins of those trees, supplemented by berries from young shrubs, help the birds survive the winter. In spring, the chicks need plenty of insects for the protein that supports their rapid growth.
That ideal habitat precisely describes Maine’s working forest. We have young trees and abundant bugs.
By the end of summer, there are more ruffed grouse in Maine than people. Admittedly, the grouse are doing most of the work. They survive by making a lot of babies. Hens lay up to 14 eggs. The precocial chicks can follow Mom a quarter mile through the forest within four days of hatching. They can fly short distances within five.
Despite all the hunters prowling the woods these days, humans are a minor threat compared with the foxes, bobcats, hawks and owls that prey on grouse. Raccoons and skunks devour the eggs in every nest they find. Up to a third of nests are destroyed before the eggs ever hatch. Cold, wet weather can be an even bigger threat, leading to forest-wide nest failures. As every hunter knows, grouse numbers vary considerably from year to year.
Maine does not keep track of how many grouse are taken annually. It’s pretty easy to survey the population, if necessary. Males drum loudly in the spring, and counting the birds heard along a survey route provides a useful estimate of breeding numbers.
A dozen years ago, I joined a University of Maine graduate student on a drive along the Stud Mill Road, east of Milford. We stopped every half-mile along the seven-mile route and heard grouse drumming at a third of those stops.
An adult male’s territory is small, roughly 10 acres. All he needs is food, water, thick cover and a favorite drumming log. If the surrounding habitat provides those basic requirements, he may never travel more than 800 feet from his log for the rest of his life.
Adult females occupy a bigger territory, perhaps 30 acres. They have sole responsibility for raising the chicks and need more room to feed their large families. Young grouse may range up to 100 acres in winter to find enough food.
Let’s address why ruffed grouse are popularly called partridge, especially by hunters and foresters. The ruffed grouse resembles a European game bird species, so early American colonists called them partridge — and the moniker stuck. Grouse and partridge are in the same family as turkeys and quail, but the similarity ends there. Ruffed grouse are forest birds. European partridges prefer open fields and grasslands.
Grouse have a way of surprising people. Every Mainer has been startled by an unseen grouse suddenly thundering away in flight. Some Mainers have been astonished by encounters with unusually friendly grouse. Popular lore is full of stories about a ruffed grouse wandering into a yard and keeping company with people and pets.
It’s odd behavior from a bird that has been hunted by humans since the last Ice Age. Many of these encounters may not represent friendliness at all. During breeding season, grouse can become aggressive and challenge people who enter their perceived territories.
Nonetheless, it’s my opinion that some grouse enjoy human companionship. A territorial bird would typically strut, ruffle its feathers and perhaps chase. But many of the tales involve birds that did none of those things. Two years ago, I had a grouse walk into my campsite and sit beside me, occasionally cooing quietly.
Perhaps that’s the clue. Grouse can become habituated to people. They live deep in the Maine woods, but also in settled areas. I encounter them regularly in Bangor City Forest and Essex Woods. Historical accounts suggest they were always rather tame. The only reason they avoid us now is because we think they’re tasty.

title: Melania Trump and LSU are set to announce a scholarship program for students who were in foster care
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Melania Trump was headed to Louisiana on Saturday to announce a partnership between Louisiana State University and her “Fostering the Future” program to provide scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system.
The first lady also planned to attend the LSU-Alabama football game in the afternoon.
The foster care program will be featured across the LSU campus in Baton Rouge as well as on the field at Tiger Stadium just before kickoff, the White House said.
Trump and LSU secured $5 million to create an endowment fund for the scholarships, the White House said. It provided no details on the source of the money.
The first lady started working on foster care issues after President Donald Trump’s first term ended in 2021, and created “Fostering the Future” to provide resources and support, including scholarships. LSU is among more than 20 colleges and universities nationwide that participate in the program.
Earlier this year, Melania Trump was on Capitol Hill to push Congress to pass a legislative package that would broaden access to services for young people in foster care by updating a decades-old program. The measures cleared the House and are pending in the Senate.
During the appearance, she told members of the House Ways and Means Committee that young people in foster care face barriers to housing, transportation and other challenges outside of the classroom that affect their performance in school along with their future financial independence.
“We can close this gap,” she said in April. “New legislation for the foster care community is a moral imperative.”
Last November, the first lady spearheaded an executive order signed by the Republican president linking the federal government, colleges and universities, the private sector and charitable groups to create educational and employment opportunities for those in foster care.
She also created “Fostering the Future Together,” a global version of the program with more than 45 participating countries.
Alabama and LSU, meanwhile, are historical regional rivals and both teams entered the week in contention for a College Football Playoff berth.
Donald Trump has attended two prior LSU games as president: one at Alabama in 2019 and one in New Orleans in January 2020, when LSU defeated Clemson for the national championship. Melania Trump accompanied him to the second game.
The president was not scheduled to attend Saturday’s game.
___
AP Sports Writer Brett Martel in Baton Rouge, La., contributed to this report.

title: 2 skydivers die midair after their parachutes become entangled
text:
LAKE ELSINORE, Calif. (AP) — Two experienced skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in Southern California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.
The Riverside County Sheriff’s Office on Saturday identified the two who died as Georgia Jean, 56, of Box Elder, South Dakota, and Levi Pimentel, 29, of Aurora, Illinois.
Jean founded the company Circle Evolution, which “is the collaboration between conscious channel Georgia Jean and the non-physical collective The Circle of Light,” according to the company’s website. Jean said in a bio that she started skydiving in 2015 and had more than 1,700 jumps.
Pimentel was listed on LinkedIn as a lead instructor at iFLY Naperville, an indoor skydiving company.
The accident occurred at about noon Friday at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement, and both were licensed skydivers.
The Riverside County Fire Department said the two suffered traumatic injuries and were taken to a local hospital in critical condition.
Skydive Elsinore said the free fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet (about 46 meters) above the ground.
“The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground,” Skydive Elsinore said in a statement. They were pronounced dead at the hospital.
The Federal Aviation Administration was notified, the sheriff’s office said. It will collect the skydivers’ parachutes and conduct an investigation.
The U.S. Parachute Association reports that in 2025, members made 3.47 million skydives and there were 16 fatalities. The organization said 5.6% of members reported suffering an injury that required medical treatment, with the most common being ankle injuries during landings.

title: Brunswick boys soccer claims 8th Class A crown
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
KENNEBUNK — Led by standout midfielder Liam Rapoza, Brunswick seemed in control of the Class A boys soccer championship game for most of the first 68 minutes, except on the scoreboard.
Then the Dragons seized their championship. Lyle Sokoloff scored with 12:10 to play and Rapoza struck six minutes later as Brunswick beat first-time state finalist Thornton Academy 2-0 at Kennebunk High School.
Rapoza said Brunswick (17-1) knew little about Thornton (14-2-2) until watching film after the Golden Trojans blitzed Falmouth, 5-1, in the South final.
The Dragons could see that Thornton had strength across the field.
“Everything was solid, their midfield, their back line, their attack. We just shut it down, honestly,” Rapoza said. “We knew coming in (that) the midfield had to be solid and we had to step it up, big time. And we did.”
Brunswick had a 6-0 edge in first-half corner kicks (9-0 for the contest). The game was still scoreless, though, and remained that way in the second half after near misses by the Dragons on loose balls deep in Thornton’s defensive end.
“Ten minutes in, I just knew our seniors were not going to lose this game,” said Brunswick coach Mark Roma.
The Dragons finally got on the board after Rapoza drew a foul near the Brunswick sideline. Brendan Quinn’s free kick was knocked from the far post to the near side, and Sokoloff was in the right spot.
“It came off Asher (Foushee) and right to me, and I knew just to head it in. Yeah, a simple goal,” Sokoloff said. “That just gave us so much momentum for the rest of the game.”
Rapoza made it 2-0 with 6:19 to play. He used two slick dribbling moves to work around defenders before unleashing a left-footed laser from 20 yards that Thornton goalie Lucas Stolf could only watch whistle into the back twine.
“Going on the dribble, seeing it go in the net, it was so surreal,” Rapoza said. “I almost felt like I wasn’t even there. I almost felt like I was floating.”
Brunswick, the unanimous No. 1 in the Varsity Maine poll, won its eighth Class A title in its 16th state final, and its second championship in the past five seasons under Roma, who took over the program in 2012. The Dragons lost to Marshwood in the 2021 state final, beat Scarborough in 2022, and lost to Scarborough in 2025.
“This is my second championship. I’ve been on the other side as well. This side is better,” Roma said.
Brunswick had critical contributions across its lineup. Quinn, Foshee and Jacob Fallis were stellar in the midfield along with Rapoza. The back line held up well against Thornton attackers. Left back Simon Stadnicki defused multiple rushes up the wing. Joelson Malongo’s strength on the opposite side complemented the center back duo of Oscar Gartside and Ethan Stern-Hayes.
Backup keeper William Danahy came in cold when starter Declan Thebarge (three saves) was given a yellow card for a collision with Moyemade. Danahy made a diving save on Andres de Haro’s well-struck direct kick from 20 yards.
Prior to this season, Thornton had never even played in a regional final. The lack of big-game experience perhaps showed, especially with the Trojans getting two bench misconduct yellow cards in the final 10 minutes.
“It was a good battle overall and they took their chances. And that second goal was unbelievable,” said Thornton coach George Sherry. “It was unfortunate, but to get to this game was huge for the program.”

title: US military says it fired on commercial vessel after it attempted to breach blockade on Iran
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for global shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.
Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.
Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
The Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the tankers’ flags or destinations.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.
For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, which were held on Nov. 3. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
The more than 8-month-old war has rattled global markets and diplomacy to end it has stalled. October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.
___
Associated Press writer Konstantin Toropin contributed from Washington.

title: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
text:
Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
Related video above: Russian missile strikes on former Ukrainian school
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It’s very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren’t sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. “I’m old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?”
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems."
Zelenskyy slams Russian attacks ahead of trilateral negotiations
In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by “launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.”
Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression,” he wrote in an online post.
The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.
The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.
“When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone,” Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said Saturday’s missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Death toll rises to 55 after the strike on aid center in Komyshuvakha
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills 1 person
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged “civilian infrastructure” and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia’s Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol’s Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

title: Pope Leo 'proud to be an American' and vote in US midterms
text:
Pope Leo ‘proud to be an American’ and vote in US midterms
Pope Leo XIV has said he was proud to exercise his right to vote as an American in the recent U.S. midterm elections.
Video above: Oncologist reacts to 'good news' about Pope Leo one day after surgery
Speaking on board the papal plane to South America, the first U.S.-born pope responded to a question from CNN about the significance of him voting. The pope's decision to cast a mail-in ballot is likely the first time a pope has voted in secular, democratic elections.
"I am proud to be an American, and exercise the right [to vote]," Leo XIV said.
The pope did not give any reaction to the US midterm election results while on board and said "no comment" when asked about the outcome in Texas, which saw the traditionally Republican state elect Democrat Sen. James Talarico. Leo made his remarks as he both addressed and personally greeted journalists traveling with him from Rome to Montevideo on Friday.
On Oct. 30, the Vatican confirmed that Pope Leo had voted in the midterm elections, adding that he had always sought to vote when possible. The pope also referred to that statement when on board.
Records show that, before his election as pontiff, Leo, whose baptismal name is Robert Prevost, had in the past voted in both Republican and Democrat primaries in Illinois. He also cast a vote in the 2024 election. While it is not known how Leo XIV voted, the Chicago-born pontiff has publicly disagreed with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration over issues such as the war in Iran and migration.
Video below: Pope Leo XIV leads Sunday prayers as he recovers from lung surgery
The pope is embarking on the most significant visit of his papacy a little over three weeks after lung cancer surgery. Despite the intense schedule of the visit, the pope told reporters he had always been confident the trip would go ahead and praised his "wonderful" medical team.
His 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru is very intense and will see him covering 19,000 miles, give 36 speeches, participate in around 50 events. He will visit Cusco, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath.
"I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place," the pope told reporters. "I confess that from the first day I had no doubt, and was convinced, that this trip had to go forward."
He added that he was in "fairly good shape," telling another reporter that he relies on "trust in God, good doctors and a healthy lifestyle."
According to the Vatican, doctors have said that Leo XIV's cancer was detected at an early stage during routine checks, that the surgery successfully removed the cancer and that he needs no further treatment.
The pope, speaking to a journalist from The New York Times, said that following his time in hospital he wanted to underline "how healthcare should be a right of all people."
He added that he felt "close to those who are sick."
Leo XIV, who likes to stay active and enjoys sports, said he planned to get back to playing tennis and told another reporter for the Catholic outlet Our Sunday Visitor that those who are facing a cancer diagnosis should not be afraid. He added that "early detection is obviously the best way to go" and that "regular checks are a blessing."
Addressing journalists collectively, the pope pointed out that the longest part of the visit was to Peru, the country he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades. Leo added that he was "very happy to be going back there."
The pope also shared some jokes on board. A Reuters journalist asked the pope, given his recent meeting with Bob Dylan, if Leo could arrange for Bruce Springsteen to have a concert for Vatican journalists.
"Some things are above my pay grade," the pope said, jokingly.

title: Argument over Wi-Fi leads to murder of mother and son, police say
text:
LUFKIN, Texas (KTRE/Gray News) - An arrest has been made in the murder of a mother and son in Texas.
Jeremiah McGee was arrested Friday and charged with capital murder in the shooting deaths of Maria Davalos, 62, and her son, Ariel Arellano Jr., in their home.
“They determined Mr. McGee to be the main suspect and continued to work the information until they had enough to gain a warrant for his arrest and a second search warrant of his home,” Police Chief Travis Brazil said.
McGee, 47, was arrested at his home, and police said they found what they believed to be the weapon used in the murders.
Authorities said a homicide investigation was launched on Oct. 23 when officers responded to a 911 call and found Davalos and Arellano fatally wounded by gunfire.
The man who called 911 was the son and brother of the victims, police said.
Investigators noted that multiple people they interviewed, including McGee, told them that there had been disputes over Wi-Fi.
McGee and the victims lived side-by-side in a duplex on Third Street.

title: Monmouth Academy boys soccer shuts out Madawaska to claim Class D title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
OAKLAND — Monmouth Academy’s journey back to the Class D state championship game began on the way home from Hermon High School last year.
“I think (losing to Fort Fairfield in the state final) certainly left a sour taste in our mouths, and we just had a mission from mid-August to Nov. 7,” said Jake Harmon. “That was our goal.”
On Saturday, that goal came to fruition, as the Mustangs dominated Madawaska on the way to an 8-0 mercy-rule win at Messalonskee High.
“I think that loss last year really fueled us all year, brought us together, and we just worked hard all year, drove for this,” Noah Schultz said.
Monmouth won its fourth state title, and second in four seasons. Schultz and Harmon were freshmen on the 2023 championship team.
“Full-circle moment,” Harmon said. “Winning it as freshmen … lost on PKs (in the South final) sophomore year, lost in the state final last year, and then to win your last game, there’s nothing like it.”
It didn’t take long for Monmouth (18-0) to separate itself from Madawaska (15-3), both on the scoreboard and in level of play. The Mustangs were up 3-0 by the 12th minute after Schultz, Bryce Fletcher and Zane Foyt all found the back of the net.
Fletcher scored twice more before halftime.
All four postseason wins for Monmouth were via the mercy rule, which goes into effect when a team leads by eight goals in the second half.
“We came into the game thinking ‘let’s make sure we come out aggressive and try to get a quick one to put them on their heels, and we certainly did that,’” Monmouth coach Joe Fletcher said. “I’ve been using the word relentless a lot, and the proof is in the pudding. Four playoff games …scoring eight or more goals.”
In the second half, Bryce Fletcher and Tyler Day scored to extend Monmouth’s lead to 7-0. With four and a half minutes to go, a goal by Wade Givens ended the game.
“I think we just wanted to play at a fast pace and that was our goal coming into this game, and we did it very well today and it showed,” Bryce Fletcher said.
Madawaska, which shut out all three of its opponents in the North regional — Maine School of Science and Math, Hodgdon and Fort Fairfield — couldn’t stop the Mustangs.
The Owls had a few chances to get on the scoreboard, perhaps their best coming with under 15 minutes to play when a free kick from Josh Querze hit the crossbar. For the bulk of the game, however, they were unable to match Monmouth’s level.
“That’s an amazing team that we just played,” Madawaska coach Ben Gagnon said. “First time we faced anything like that this season. We had a good run. Had a big group of seniors that worked hard the whole season, pushed their teammates hard and left everything out on the field.”
Monmouth will graduate six seniors in the spring, including two of its leaders in Schultz and Harmon. Fletcher and Foyt are both juniors, however, and will be back for the Mustangs’ title defense in 2027.

title: Northern finches are moving into Maine for winter
text:
The sounds of winter are in the air, as the classic “zzzips,” “tews,”and “piicks” call out from above. These are the call notes of various finches that are coming south and are likely to spend the winter around your backyard bird feeders.
While most of our neotropic migrants, like the warblers and vireos that bred here during the summer, have departed until next spring, there are a handful of northern finches that are moving into Maine for the winter. Each year, a report known as the “Winter Finch Forecast” is published, most recently by Tyler Hoar of Ontario for the Finch Research Network (FiRN), which looks at wild bird food availability (cones and fruit) across southern Canada to make predictions about what birds might move this winter. Here’s a summary of the report and some related recent observations to help you make sense of it all.
First, the phenomenon that we are discussing with these bird movements is called an irruption (different from an eruption). This is when a species that typically migrates from point A (breeding grounds) to point B (wintering grounds), but might not have enough resources (typically food) in one place, needs to temporarily move to point C (in this case, Maine) to survive. Most birds will return to that point A to point B movement after an irruptive year. Snowy owls are perhaps the best known example of this, and it is much more localized in finches, but it’s the same driver nonetheless.
The most obvious finch showing up lately has been the pine siskin. These small finches resemble a heavily striped American goldfinch, with more yellows in the flight feathers, and they often mix with goldfinches. Over the last month, they’ve been moving through in variable flocks, often 10 to 20 at a time, but with some reports of hundreds in a single group. Siskins love cedar and hemlock seeds, and the Winter Finch Forecast reports “Southeastern Canada, the Great Lakes region, and the northeastern United States have a very good northern white cedar crop (some areas have a good eastern hemlock crop as well).” So we have plenty of food for siskins coming here, and this abundance of naturally-occurring seeds may mean you won’t see as many at your bird feeder.
One fun measure to compare across years is looking at “frequency” on eBird.org, a citizen science project by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology where people report what birds they see, where, and with how much effort. That effort portion is important because we can then compare across all lists and calculate measures like frequency, which is the percentage of all checklists that a species is reported on. Looking at pine siskins over the last few years, their frequency in late October was 3.5% in 2025 and 3.15% in 2024, but this year it is at 12.6%. Interestingly, in 2023 we also saw a minor irruption, with frequency hitting 10% in late October, but it dwindled as birds continued moving south, presumably because they weren’t finding enough seeds here.
The forecast also mentions siskins having a good nesting season thanks to the ongoing spruce budworm outbreak (spruce budworm is a native moth that feeds on needles, buds, and flowers of spruce and fir trees, and its cyclical population outbreaks can devastate large areas of spruce and fir forests). In recent years we’ve seen large flights of evening grosbeaks in Maine thanks to this outbreak, but so far that doesn’t appear to be shaping up this year. Looking at frequency over the same time period, evening grosbeaks were reported on 3% of lists during irruptions in 2022 and 2025, but are only on 0.48% of lists this season. The lack of movement this year is likely due to the abundance of mountain-ash in Canada forests, as reported in the Winter Finch Forecast.
Purple finches are the other finch we are seeing move south right now. As the report says, purple finches will move to “take advantage of the good spruce and great eastern white pine and mountain-ash crops,” and we’ve definitely seen an increase, with handfuls showing up on our weekly bird walks at Gilsland Farm.
I highly recommend reading the full Winter Finch Forecast at finchnetwork.org, where you can see the coverage of other birds like crossbills and redpolls. And join us for a walk at Gilsland Farm or around the state to see how these finchy flights shape up this winter.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth. Walks move to an 8 am start in December.

title: Yarmouth boys soccer beats John Bapst again in Class B final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BANGOR — There was plenty of space for the Yarmouth boys soccer team to operate throughout a rainy Class B state championship game.
It was only a matter of time before the Clippers would score, and one section of the net in particular became a frequent target.
Yarmouth put three goals into the bottom-left corner Saturday to claim a 3-0 victory over John Bapst at Cameron Stadium. The win marked the 10th state title in the last 12 seasons for the Clippers, who now boast a state-record 18 overall, including one in Class C.
It was also Yarmouth’s third victory over John Bapst in the state championship game since 2022.
“We always emphasize, ‘Finish low and hard because that’s the hardest ball to get to,’” said Yarmouth coach Justin Morrill. “We have great creativity up top to just feint those runs, run over balls and allow space to open up, and it’s really nice to see our kids focusing on finding a spot instead of just hammering it.”
Senior midfielder Lucas Hayner scored the first two goals in a brilliant display. Cael Woelflein added the third goal and the Clippers dominated possession, producing 10 shots on goal to John Bapst’s one.
“We’ve been working on finishing a lot this week in practice,” Woelflein said. “It feels really good, especially my senior season. It feels good to have our last game be a win, especially in this weather and on this stage.”
After a decent spell of play from John Bapst (16-1-1) in the first couple of minutes, Yarmouth (16-1-1) took control. The Clippers forced a tough save out of Crusaders goalkeeper Bode Phillips less than four minutes in, after which Hayner sent two shots just wide of the net.
With 15:27 left in the first half, Hayner found the breakthrough. The senior midfielder received a pass in the middle of the box, and slotted a shot past Phillips.
Yarmouth came close three more times in the first half and also nearly scored in the opening minute of the second. Four minutes later, the Clippers got their second goal, as Hayner again collected the ball in the box and scored from a tight angle.
“Slotting it was a big thing we’ve been talking about and focusing on the whole season, and (we) did it today,” said Hayner, who finished his senior season with 20 goals and 19 assists. “All props to my teammates for setting me up and putting me into the positions I was able to get in. All I had to really do was shoot.”
Yarmouth kept pushing, forcing Phillips into two more nice saves. Then, with 14:48 left, Woelflein removed any doubt over the result, connecting from slightly further out toward the edge of the box.
Besides scoring twice, Hayner was the midfield maestro for everything Yarmouth did. His ball control helped the Clippers dominate possession, and his runs and passing helped his team produce countless scoring opportunities.
“I’m probably a little biased, but even though there’s probably more kids who have scored more goals, I’d like to find a kid who’s had a more collective season,” Morrill said when asked if Hayner was the state’s best player. “That, singlehandedly, is a huge accomplishment for him.”
The win was the performance Yarmouth craved after eeking out a victory on penalty kicks in the Class B South final against a Cape Elizabeth team it had beaten 4-1 and 4-0 in the regular season. Morrill said his team produced two of its best practices of the season in preparation for the state final.
“We needed to get our focus back and get back to playing the way we want to play,” Morrill said. We wanted to make life difficult for them and control the run of play on the field, and I thought we did a really, really good job of that today.”
