title: Young voters overwhelmingly backed Democrats this year. The question is whether they'll stay
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Andy Soma, 24, doesn’t identify with either political party, and he’s been skipping elections since he became old enough to vote. But this year, disappointed with the economy and President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, he cast his midterm ballot for Roy Cooper, the North Carolina Democrat now headed to the Senate.
“I would describe it as the first time that I’ve truly felt the need to vote,” said Soma, who is pursuing a Ph.D. in mathematics at North Carolina State University. He said he wanted to “kind of take a stand, if you will.”
Young voters overwhelmingly turned their backs on Republicans on Tuesday, erasing the gains Trump had made in the 2024 presidential election. Voters under age 30 moved left by double digits in nearly all the major Senate races compared with two years earlier.
It was a similar story in House campaigns across the country. The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, showed that about three-quarters of voters under 30 supported their local Democratic candidate, while about one-quarter voted for the Republican.
The support for Democrats outpaces even 2018, when Trump’s Republican Party suffered midterm losses during his first term, and is a dramatic shift from 2024, when young voters were roughly split between Trump and Democrat Kamala Harris, according to AP VoteCast, a survey of more than 120,000 voters that year.
For Soma, the tipping point was Trump’s broken pledge that he would keep the U.S. out of Middle East conflicts, a sentiment that student after student echoed in interviews on the university’s Raleigh campus the day after the election.
Other young voters who broke for Democrats this year said their choices were motivated by personal experiences, including working multiple jobs to get by and watching artificial intelligence data center projects advance into their communities.
“I’m trying to save money and buy a house and all that, but it’s difficult right now,” said Corey Herzog, 28, an independent-turned-Democrat in the traditionally conservative town of Celina, Ohio. Herzog works at Walmart during the day and bartends at night, all while building out a small side business selling house plants.
John Della Volpe, a pollster who regularly surveys U.S. youth for the Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics, said the whiplash over the past two elections suggests that young voters aren’t a generation of Democrats or Republicans.
“They’re up for grabs,” he said. “Especially given the state of the economy and their concerns about the future.”
In 2024, Trump won over young men. This year, many sat out or backed Democrats
To win back the presidency two years ago, Trump courted young men who felt disillusioned by economic stagnation, interventionist foreign policy and the government’s focus on diversity, equity and inclusion. He attended football games and UFC matches and appeared on podcasts with comedians who rebuffed “cancel culture.”
More than half of male voters under 30 supported him in 2024, according to AP VoteCast.
But once in office, Trump started the war with Iran and rammed through tariff policies that continued to drive up inflation. He also resisted releasing documents about convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and launched an immigration crackdown that faced widespread criticism.
“This was the perfect cocktail for disaster,” said Charlie Sabgir, director of the Washington-based Young Men Research Project.
Young voters’ unhappiness on every major issue in the midterm election was palpable. Voters under 30 were more likely than older age groups to say the cost of living was crucial for their vote for Congress, and to say the U.S. was wrong to take military action against Iran.
About half of young voters said they were angry about the way things were going in the U.S. today, compared with only about one-third of voters 65 and older.
The anti-Trump backlash was particularly strong among young voters
Even in a year when anti-Trump backlash was one of the major themes, young voters stood out.
Only about one-quarter of voters under 30 said Trump is a strong leader or has the mental capacity to serve effectively as president, according to The AP Voter Poll. That’s a sharp contrast with 2024, when about half of voters under 30 felt Trump was a strong leader and mentally fit. The decline was larger than in any other age group.
“This cultural coalition and cultural cache that Trump had behind him going into 2024 — they’ve clearly soured on him,” Sabgir said.
About 6 in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their House vote was to express opposition to Trump.
A national consortium of college Republican groups put out a statement making their dissatisfaction clear, writing that young Republicans “were not given what they were promised.”
“In the wake of last night’s election results, the College Republican Patriot Coalition unequivocally lays the blame for the greatest Republican defeat by Democrats since 1974 at the feet of the Trump administration and the Republican Party,” the group said in a statement.
Kidus Girma, campaigns director for the left-leaning Sunrise Movement, said that while he was knocking on doors in Michigan, he met young men who may not typically turn out in a midterm election but did this time because they were disappointed by Trump.
He recalled one person who complained that he was struggling to find a job even though Trump was insisting the economy is going great.
“It’s like this deep disillusionment with the statements the president makes versus the material impacts people are facing in their everyday lives,” Girma said.
Gen Z voters get their ‘millennial optimism’ moment. But to keep them, Democrats must deliver
Sarah Stull, an 18-year-old student at the University of Texas at Austin, thought it was funny that so many of her classmates spent Halloween dressed up as “millennial optimism,” wearing skinny jeans and infinity scarves with grins on their faces to satirize the elder generation for being unabashedly hopeful.
Stull got the joke. Like others her age, she described herself as “very sarcastic, very jaded — and do sometimes expect the worst.”
But Tuesday night, sitting in a dorm room with friends watching election results stream in, that all went out the window.
“We were freaking out, all of us were crying,” said the young Democrat, who voted for James Talarico for Senate and Gina Hinojosa for governor. “I just felt this sense of community that I had never felt before.”
She posted a video of herself and friends on TikTok, literally jumping for joy outside the Texas Capitol, captioning it “millennial optimism cause texas went blue.”
Young adults like Stull — who was 7 when Trump rode down the escalator in New York’s Trump Tower in 2015 to announce his first presidential campaign — have only ever known “the Trumpification of politics,” said Katherine Haenschen, a political science and communication professor at Northeastern University. Now that era seems to be coming to a close, bringing hope for the first time to left-leaning young people.
But it’s a fragile moment.
Dakota Hall, executive director of the progressive youth political organization Alliance for Youth Action, said he thinks young voters could shift to the right again if Democrats leading Congress don’t do enough to lower the cost of living, regulate AI and address government corruption.
“Young people have a very short leash,” Hall said. “If you do not deliver, ’28 will be a rough road ahead.”
___
Rankin reported from Raleigh, N.C.

title: Penobscot Valley girls soccer edges Monmouth Academy to win Class D title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
OAKLAND — McKenna Ireland earned playing time as an eighth-grader late last season in Penobscot Valley’s state title run.
A year later in the Class D state championship game, Ireland scored the Gold Ball-clinching goal.
Ireland’s goal Saturday gave Penobscot Valley a 1-0 win over Monmouth Academy in the Class D state championship game at Messalonskee High School.
“(Ireland) came in clutch for us last year as an eighth-grader … and I think that benefited her in a big way this year to come in and not be as nervous,” said coach Lana Cummings. “And she can hold her own out there, for sure.”
The Howlers capped another successful playoff run by beating the Mustangs, who made their first state final appearance in 26 years.
“It’s crazy,” Penobscot Valley keeper Brooklynn Raymond said. “Everybody doubted us. They said we weren’t going to be the same team, that we were rebuilding. And we knew we just had to believe in each other and we had a coaching staff that believed in us and pushed us every day, and it’s amazing just to know we could make it here again.”
Monmouth (10-7) didn’t make it easy on three-time defending champion Penobscot Valley (11-3-4). The Mustangs took nine shots on goal to the Howlers’ one in the first half, and both teams had four apiece in the second half.
Penobscot Valley broke through when Ireland scored on a breakaway four and a half minutes into the second half.
“It was just all so fast,” Ireland said. “I was just so grateful that my team could set me up for that goal. I wasn’t the reason why we won, it was my whole team working together and setting everybody up to win.”
Monmouth nearly scored on several occasions, including a deflection of a cross that went just wide with under 10 seconds to play.
“We were real close,” co-Monmouth coach Haley Fletcher-Springer said. “We had a lot of opportunities and we unfortunately just couldn’t finish those opportunities. And (the Howlers) capitalized on their opportunities, so props to them. Stinks to go out this way, for sure, but really proud of our team.”
Raymond was a force all game, finishing with 13 saves. A senior, she was a state champion every year of her career.
“I looked at Coach after the game, I said, ‘I maxed out my career and it still doesn’t feel like it was enough,’” Raymond said. “So just being a part of something this special has been amazing, and it’s tough. It’s going to be hard not coming back next year.”

title: Letter: Democrats need to focus on the economy to stay in power
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Certainly the incompetence of Donald Trump and his narcissism of insisting he was on the ballot was a big factor in the mid-term election disaster for Republicans. But so was affordability — so many voters not sure if they could pay the bills next month or who are swamped by debt.
Democrats don’t need to point to Trump’s lies, corruption (himself and his cronies) and bumbling mistakes; he takes care of that himself. But, to get elected or re-elected in 2028, I believe Democrats need to address the U.S. economy by making sure every person in it has enough and no one has too much.
There are many ways to do that. Here are a few I suggest: Raise the minimum wage and make sure every worker is paid a living wage. Tax wealthy (top 5%) people at a much higher rate, especially for capital gains. Stop building data centers and using AI to eliminate jobs that real people need. Start treating the environment and climate as an ally, not an opponent. Most importantly, gear the economy to the needs of the worker, not to the investor or the corporation. Make the economy human-centered, not just about GDP, stock prices, and corporate profits.
Good luck, Democrats, and any (elected) official who cares about affordability. The economy should be for the wellbeing of everyone.
Larry Dansinger
Bangor

title: Officials: 1 dead, 20 injured in crash with cyclists
text:
WAKE COUNTY, N.C. (WRAL) - At least one person is dead after an elderly driver crashed into a group of cyclists, officials said.
The crash happened Saturday in Wake County, North Carolina.
Fire officials said at least 20 others were injured, including seven who were taken to trauma centers.
Officials said the 76-year-old driver crossed the center line, collided with the cyclists, and then ran off the road and into a ditch.
The driver is in custody, with impairment listed as a possible factor in the crash.

title: Bayside should not keep shouldering Portland’s social problems
text:
Thomas Blackburn lives in Portland.
I have lived in Portland’s Bayside neighborhood for 25 years. I have watched this neighborhood change dramatically — some changes welcome, some difficult and some that have fundamentally altered what it means to live here.
That is why the city of Portland’s plan to place another winter warming center in Bayside deserves more scrutiny than simply asking whether people need a warm place to sleep. Of course they do.
The question is not whether Portland should care for people experiencing homelessness. We should. The question is whether it is equitable to continue placing that responsibility so heavily on one small neighborhood.
The proposed warming center would be located at 252 Oxford St., in the basement of Preble Street’s Elena’s Way. If funding and approvals move forward, it is planned to operate nightly from November through April.
For Bayside residents, this is not an isolated or temporary decision. It is another chapter
in a decades-long pattern.
In 2012, when Portland’s Homelessness Prevention Task Force presented its recommendations, Bayside residents were already telling the city that social services and homelessness-related facilities had become too concentrated in our neighborhood. One resident put it plainly: “You can’t ask one neighborhood to bear the brunt of a lot of issues.”
Nearly a decade later, the City Council acknowledged the same problem. In 2021, the council enacted a moratorium on new emergency shelters in Bayside, citing concerns about concentrating shelters in an already overburdened neighborhood and the resulting demands on police, fire and other services. Those concerns were not theoretical.
Bayside occupies only about 1% of Portland’s land area and has roughly 5% of the city’s population. Yet historical police data showed the neighborhood accounting for about 20% of police calls for service. In 2024, nearly 30% of citywide arrests and summonses occurred in Bayside even though the neighborhood represented only about 5% of Portland’s population.
These numbers don’t tell us why every individual call or arrest occurred, and they should not be used to stigmatize people experiencing homelessness. They do, however, tell us something important about the concentration of public-service demands in a very small area.
And Bayside is not an empty industrial district. It is a residential neighborhood. Families live here. Children walk these streets. Seniors live here. Small businesses operate here. Homeowners and renters pay Portland property taxes here.
And Bayside is one of the most culturally and ethnically diverse parts of Maine, with immigrant families and new Mainers making up an important part of the community. That diversity matters to this conversation.
Many living in Bayside are themselves working families and recent arrivals to Portland. They should not be expected to absorb an ever-growing concentration of social problems simply because their neighborhood happens to be close to the agencies providing services.
There is another uncomfortable reality that longtime Bayside residents know well. Daily, residents encounter discarded needles, people passed out on sidewalks and other visible consequences of untreated addiction and serious behavioral health problems. We should not pretend that adding another service for a highly vulnerable population into an already concentrated service district has no effect on the surrounding neighborhood.
The city itself has acknowledged that shelter operations can create neighborhood impacts. The current proposal is being accompanied by discussions about additional security staffing and cleanup support.
That should prompt a larger question: Why does the solution to Portland’s homelessness crisis repeatedly begin and end in Bayside?
Portland has spent years talking about equity. Equity cannot mean distributing resources according to which neighborhood has been most willing or able to absorb them. Equity must mean looking honestly at the cumulative burden.
We are asking for the same consideration that any other Portland neighborhood would reasonably expect: look at the whole picture.
How many shelters and service facilities does Bayside already carry? How many police, fire and EMS resources are directed here? What are the cumulative effects on residents and businesses? What alternatives were seriously evaluated outside of Bayside?
Those are not questions of compassion versus indifference. They are questions of planning, fairness and shared civic responsibility.
People experiencing homelessness deserve warmth, safety, dignity and a path toward
permanent housing. The people who live in Bayside deserve those things too. Both can be true.

title: Judge wants former US attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital during President Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.
Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.
The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events.” An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.
Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government’s conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.
As the city’s chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job.
Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP.
David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial’s participants “can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.”
Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.”
Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on.
The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real.

title: Democrats should forget about retribution and focus on America
text:
While it’s understandable for Democrats to want to go after many of the abuses that have occurred in the past two years of this Trump presidency, one would caution that retribution is not what they were elected to do. With a party favorability rating of just 29%, the Democrats should be looking at how they can bring in universal healthcare, affordable housing and childcare services into reality.
When it comes to the 2028 presidential election, voters are going to look at not how many corrupt officials were put in jail but how many folks were put safely into housing.
Yes, those elected should work to root out corruption, trading in office, etc. But they should keep their focus on what working-class Americans elected them for. Perhaps the Democrats may even bring people back around to the “big tent” that is the party.
Jake Hawkins
Arundel

title: Camden Hills girls soccer tops Scarborough in overtime to win Class A title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
KENNEBUNK — The Camden Hills girls soccer team had not been seriously challenged all season.
That changed Saturday in the Class A championship game against Scarborough, which went to double overtime. That’s when Molly Williams scored her school-record 51st goal of the season to give the Windjammers a 1-0 victory.
“It feels so good. This was our goal coming into the season,” Williams said. “It’s been my goal since freshman year, and we finally did it.”
Camden Hills finishes 18-0. Coach Meredith Messer is now 5-0 in state championship games, having directed the Windjammers to four straight Class A titles from 2016-19.
Williams set the school record for goals with her 50th (and fourth of the game) in a 5-1 win against Mt. Ararat in the North final. The previous record of 49 goals was set in 2019 by then-senior Kristina Kelly, the 2019 national player of the year.
Scarborough (16-1-1) suffered its first loss of the season and lost in the championship game for the third year in a row. While Camden Hills had outscored its opponents by a whopping margin of 127-4, Scarborough had battled against tougher competition in Class A South. The Red Storm reached the state final with a 46-8 scoring margin and seven one-goal wins, including a 2-1 overtime decision in the regional semifinals against South Portland.
Camden Hills was the aggressor throughout the first overtime, sparked by sophomore midfielder Liv Domareki, who frequently won contested balls and pushed forward while imploring her teammates to keep up the pace. Eve Domareki nearly got her toe on a well-placed Williams cross. A few minutes later, Williams fired a tight-angle shot that was deflected wide by Scarborough keeper Vera DiSotto (three saves).
“I think these girls all year long wanted to have this accomplishment, to be able to say, ‘On any given day, we can go out and compete,'” Messer said. “We practice against ourselves, so in a lot of ways, our defense has to defend our offense and we get a lot of good practice.”
Throughout the contest, Camden Hills looked to either thread passes to Williams, or she would come back to her midfielders to receive a pass and try to turn. The Scarborough defense was intent on stopping her. Center backs Josie Duncan and Wren Bodah often double-teamed Williams, and midfielder Jill Morris marked her all over the field for long stretches in the second half.
But with two minutes gone in the second overtime, Thea Laukka — one of just two seniors for Camden Hills — heard Williams call for the ball.
“She made that run and I could hear her, she was communicating,” Laukka said. “We’ve gone over that many times on plays like that this season, and we connected and it worked out.”
Laukka got the ball to Williams, and DiSotto had to come off her mark. Williams, who has committed to play at Boston College, showed why she’s a premier scorer, sliding the ball past DiSotta’s lunge and then taking her time to set herself and hit a clean right-footed shot into the goal.

title: Maine Lobstermen's Association welcomes change in federal whale policy
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Lobstermen's Association welcomes change in federal whale policy
The MLA says the shift comes after a 2023 court win over right whale protections.
Maine Lobstermen's Association welcomes change in federal whale policy
The MLA says the shift comes after a 2023 court win over right whale protections.
The Maine Lobstermen's Association says the federal government has changed its whale policy. It says the change comes after a court win over the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) regarding protections for the endangered North American right whale.
In June 2023, an appeals court sided with lobstermen, who argued that the NMFS acted arbitrarily by failing to rely on the best available scientific information and by failing to account for the positive impact of conservation measures already adopted by the Maine lobster fishery. The ruling overturned an earlier ruling in favor of the federal government, which the Maine Lobstermen's Association appealed in 2022.
On Nov. 5, the NMFS announced new scientific analysis showed U.S. fisheries may be meeting the federal standard for protecting right whales.
"This is what we fought for. MLA took the federal government to court and won because its claims about our fishery weren't supported by the science or the law," said Patrice McCarron, the executive director of the Maine Lobstermen's Association. "That court victory forced NMFS to change course. Now the government's own analysis is beginning to confirm what Maine lobstermen have been saying for years."

title: Two men accused of handing out psychedelic gummies to nearly 15 kids on Halloween, police say
text:
SAN DIEGO (Gray News) - Two men in California are accused of giving psilocybin-infused gummies to young trick-or-treaters on Halloween night, according to authorities.
Police arrested Michael Goff, 80, and Shawn Michael Foster, 45, a press release said.
On November 4, officers recovered suspected psilocybin gummies, cannabis, methamphetamine, firearms, ammunition, and drug sales at the home.
Police said nearly 15 children took packages of the gummies that had been left on the home’s porch on Halloween. Parents noticed the unusual packaging, intervened and contacted police.
Frank Cary, one of the parents, told NBC 7 San Diego he took a package from his 2-year-old after noticing a design featuring a giraffe and melting text.
The label listed a 5-gram dosage and included the words “psilocybin mushrooms.”
Parents confronted a resident before filing a police report and giving the packages to officers.
Testing later confirmed the presence of psilocybin.

title: What could happen next in razor-thin rejection of moving the Penobscot County Jail
text:
Penobscot County residents may not know for weeks if the county jail can move out of Bangor after the measure initially failed by 60 votes.
County officials have hinged their plans for a new $70 million to $80 million jail on moving the facility out of Bangor. If the certified result confirms the measure failed, they will have to restart their planning.
The results of the jail ballot question will be certified along with those of the state’s other races, according to the Maine Department of the Secretary of State. State law gives the secretary of state 20 days after the election, or until Nov. 23, to send certified results to the governor.
“The Secretary of State provides proclamation of the winners of county referendum questions when certified election results for federal, state and county offices are provided to the Governor,” said Jana Spaulding, a spokesperson for the department.
The county sees it differently. In a statement Friday, County Administrator Blair Tinkham said certifying a county referendum is the responsibility of the local governing authority. The county is seeking legal advice on how to accept and certify the results, and commissioners “will determine the appropriate action consistent with state law and established election procedures,” his statement said.
Tinkham did not answer questions about the discrepancy in who will certify these results.
Once the vote is certified, Penobscot County officials will have the opportunity to conduct a recount if they choose to pursue one, Spaulding said. County Commissioner David Marshall and Tinkham did not respond to questions asking about the county’s plans to hold a recount.
It’s not clear how long a recount would take. The same ballots are already undergoing a ranked-choice tabulation for the race between Congressional candidates Matt Dunlap and Paul LePage.
The county’s vote tabulation shared by Tinkham also differs from the Bangor Daily News’ results collection. By the county’s count, the measure failed by 136 votes, which is more than double the 60-vote difference tabulated by the BDN.
County Commissioner Andre Cushing did not share how the county obtained that figure when asked by phone Friday.

title: In Madrid, Maine, large-scale Crucifixion sculpture takes shape
text:
In 2013, John Boyko got an idea for a sculpture project in a field at his 40-acre property in Madrid. “I just felt like building a cross,” he said.
Now 88, Boyko is still working on the large-scale depiction of the Crucifixion of Jesus. The cross, which is 800 feet long and 335 feet wide, is comprised of pine and fir trees that are cut short in height, and the face of Jesus is made of stones stacked like a wall and of smaller colored stones depicting his hair and beard. The crown of thorns is made from quarter-inch-thick stainless steel abstract shapes cut by Boyko himself.
In recent years, Boyko has focused on constructing memorial stands that are made from stainless steel, plastic and fiber optic cable that light up at night, and he has converted an old chicken coop into a visitor center where people who stop by can learn more about his project.
“I have a lot more work to do,” Boyko said. “Maybe two more summers’ worth.”

title: Monmouth Academy boys soccer shuts out Madawaska to claim Class D title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
OAKLAND — Monmouth Academy’s journey back to the Class D state championship game began on the way home from Hermon High School last year.
“I think (losing to Fort Fairfield in the state final) certainly left a sour taste in our mouths, and we just had a mission from mid-August to Nov. 7,” said Jake Harmon. “That was our goal.”
On Saturday, that goal came to fruition, as the Mustangs dominated Madawaska on the way to an 8-0 mercy-rule win at Messalonskee High.
“I think that loss last year really fueled us all year, brought us together, and we just worked hard all year, drove for this,” Noah Schultz said.
Monmouth won its fourth state title, and second in four seasons. Schultz and Harmon were freshmen on the 2023 championship team.
“Full-circle moment,” Harmon said. “Winning it as freshmen … lost on PKs (in the South final) sophomore year, lost in the state final last year, and then to win your last game, there’s nothing like it.”
It didn’t take long for Monmouth (18-0) to separate itself from Madawaska (15-3), both on the scoreboard and in level of play. The Mustangs were up 3-0 by the 12th minute after Schultz, Bryce Fletcher and Zane Foyt all found the back of the net.
Fletcher scored twice more before halftime.
All four postseason wins for Monmouth were via the mercy rule, which goes into effect when a team leads by eight goals in the second half.
“We came into the game thinking ‘let’s make sure we come out aggressive and try to get a quick one to put them on their heels, and we certainly did that,’” Monmouth coach Joe Fletcher said. “I’ve been using the word relentless a lot, and the proof is in the pudding. Four playoff games …scoring eight or more goals.”
In the second half, Bryce Fletcher and Tyler Day scored to extend Monmouth’s lead to 7-0. With four and a half minutes to go, a goal by Wade Givens ended the game.
“I think we just wanted to play at a fast pace and that was our goal coming into this game, and we did it very well today and it showed,” Bryce Fletcher said.
Madawaska, which shut out all three of its opponents in the North regional — Maine School of Science and Math, Hodgdon and Fort Fairfield — couldn’t stop the Mustangs.
The Owls had a few chances to get on the scoreboard, perhaps their best coming with under 15 minutes to play when a free kick from Josh Querze hit the crossbar. For the bulk of the game, however, they were unable to match Monmouth’s level.
“That’s an amazing team that we just played,” Madawaska coach Ben Gagnon said. “First time we faced anything like that this season. We had a good run. Had a big group of seniors that worked hard the whole season, pushed their teammates hard and left everything out on the field.”
Monmouth will graduate six seniors in the spring, including two of its leaders in Schultz and Harmon. Fletcher and Foyt are both juniors, however, and will be back for the Mustangs’ title defense in 2027.

title: Cape Elizabeth girls soccer successfully defends Class B title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BANGOR — The second half of the Class B girls soccer final Saturday began with Haisel McGeachey taking a soccer ball directly into the face, forcing the Cape Elizabeth junior to leave the game with a bloody nose.
What McGeachey and her teammates will remember most about this game years from now will be what she did when she returned.
McGeachey’s goal with 14 minutes remaining lifted Cape Elizabeth to a 2-1 victory over John Bapst in the state championship game at Cameron Stadium. The win gives the Capers back-to-back state titles and 11 Gold Balls overall.
“I think that really put the game to sleep,” said McGeachey, whose goal followed first-half tallies by Cape’s Alexa Mallory and John Bapst’s Naia Studley. “I think we were fighting so hard to get the next goal, and I’m really just so happy that we got the job done.”
Cape Elizabeth looked more dangerous early, swinging in two crosses that were inches from connecting with a player in the first seven minutes. Yet it was John Bapst (16-1-1) that scored first, as Studley took advantage of a defensive lapse and got around Cape keeper Kelsie Law before shooting into an open net.
That goal, which came with 30:09 remaining in the first half, was met with a quick response by Cape Elizabeth (16-1-1). Four minutes later, Mallory collected the ball on the edge of the penalty area and fired home a screamer.
“Our saying is always, ‘We can go down, but then we come right back up,’” Mallory said. “As soon as we went down, we didn’t let our morale drop, and we got one back. Once we get one, we can always get another.”
Five minutes after Mallory’s goal, Studley made another nice run for Bapst before pushing a shot inches wide of the far post. A powerful shot by Mallory with just under 12 minutes to go in the half was the only other prime opportunity in the opening 40 minutes.
Cape Elizabeth mostly controlled the flow early in the second half, though Bapst countered with a couple pushes. Shortly after returning to the field, McGeachey put the Capers in front with 25:51 remaining, as she short-hopped a goal past Crusaders keeper Abby-May Turner.
“She’s a grinder; she’s played in two state finals, and she’s scored both times,” said Cape Elizabeth coach Branden Noltkamper. “She does all the dirty work, and she does all the chores that no one else wants to do. If that means taking one in the face and getting a bloody nose, that’s what she’ll do.”
Cape Elizabeth didn’t produce many scoring chances the rest of the way, but the Capers didn’t let John Bapst generate much, either. The Crusaders’ only serious threat came with just over five minutes to go, as Quinn Bennett found space but ripped a shot wide of net.
Cape Elizabeth’s repeat title win comes a year after the Capers went 18-0, scoring 89 goals and conceding only seven. That team was voted 2025-26 Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Year for all sports, and Noelle Mallory, Alexa’s older sister, was the Varsity Maine Girls Soccer Player of the Year.
After losing the elder Mallory and several other starters to graduation, Cape Elizabeth was expected by some to take a step back in 2025. Instead, the Capers left a cold, drizzly Cameron Stadium carrying another Gold Ball back home.
“It feels so good (to repeat),” Mallory said. “Everyone told us that this was a rebuilding year for us, but we like to prove people wrong. Well, now we did.”

title: Nithya Raman to take charge in LA amid homeless crisis and political division
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — In her bid for Los Angeles mayor, Nithya Raman ran as an outsider. The democratic socialist didn’t win a single endorsement from her 14 colleagues on the city council. The police union opposed her, she had friction with the Jewish community and the Democratic establishment lined up squarely behind the incumbent, Karen Bass.
She now has to show she can lead.
As mayor-elect following a stunning upset, Raman will need to navigate political rifts in balkanized City Hall while taking on an array of problems that have defied her predecessors, including a long-running homeless crisis, an exodus of Hollywood jobs and boundless miles of crumbling streets and sidewalks — all with a strained budget.
Appearing before reporters Thursday for the first time as mayor-elect, Raman was succinct about her agenda.
“Homelessness, housing costs and public safety,” she said. “These will have to be the priorities that I take on in the city.”
Even after the campaign, the millennial, India-born Raman will be a new face to many Angelenos in a city that tends to shrug at local politics. But how she governs the nation’s second most populous city will be closely watched nationally, especially as she prepares to welcome the world to LA for the 2028 Olympics.
Raman joins a new crop of democratic socialist mayors
When she takes office in mid-December, Raman will join the vanguard of democratic socialists in municipal government that includes Zohran Mamdani in New York and Katie Wilson in Seattle. Janeese Lewis George was elected Tuesday as mayor of Washington, D.C.
While she is expected to steer the city to the political left, she has been outspoken about her willingness to break from the Democratic Socialists of America when she believes their agenda conflicts with interests of the city. “My independence will always be paramount,” Raman said at a candidate forum in September.
At a time when the Democratic Party has been deeply divided over the war in Gaza and aid to Israel, Raman has faced questions about her interview with progressive commentator Hasan Piker last spring in which she responded “I do, yes,” when asked if she believed Israel had committed genocide. At a forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, she said she recognized genocide is “a deeply painful word” but said she was compelled to speak out after seeing images of “the targeting of hospitals, the deaths of children,” prompting murmurs in the audience.
At the same time, she faced pushback from within the DSA, where some believed her positions on Israel was not sufficiently tough.
After her surprise win, the federation called on Raman to “rebuild trust with Jewish Angelenos that was strained during the campaign.”
A win for democratic socialists without Mamdani star power
To Occidental College political scientist Caroline Heldman, Raman needs to propose concrete solutions to address the day-to-day headaches that frame life in LA, whether potholes or thousands of broken streetlights or clearing homeless encampments.
“She didn’t win the election by positioning herself as being really ideologically distinct from Karen Bass,” Heldman said. “She positioned herself as the pothole politician, very similar to Zohran Mamdani. I see her taking a page out of his playbook.”
Raman, however, never had the star power known as a Mamdani trademark. The contest in LA was relatively low key and overshadowed by turmoil in Washington and the fight for control of Congress.
Mike Bonin, a former LA city council member and executive director of the Pat Brown Institute for Public Affairs at California State University, Los Angeles, described Raman as philosophically progressive but temperamentally moderate.
“She got painted in this campaign as a crazy socialist idealogue or a flip-flopper with no core values,” said Bonin, who served with Raman from December 2020 to 2022. But, he said, “she wanted to work with people. She is very focused on results.”
Raman is just starting to assemble her City Hall team
She has not delivered a financially detailed plan on how she will take on some of the city’s persistent maladies.
There are few issues in LA — birthplace of the car culture, where driving is part of everyday life for most residents — that prompt more grumbling than traffic and potholes. In 2013, former Mayor Eric Garcetti, campaigned on a “back to basics” platform to deal with street paving, yet little happened.
Under Bass, the city began focusing on filling potholes rather than resurfacing streets. Raman has said she will recast that policy, but how much money will go toward streets — and how quickly they can be repaved — is not yet known.
In remarks on election night, before she was declared the winner, Raman depicted a city in statis and broadly sketched her vision for what Los Angeles could be.
“LA stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things,” she said. Raman added that she wanted to revive “that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles.”
On the city council, the reaction to her election was somewhat muted. Council member Traci Park, who voted for Bass and said she had “concerns about the leadership and effectiveness” of both candidates, said in a statement she looked forward to working with Raman in a city with “great challenges.”
Raman won against a wounded incumbent
Raising 10-year-old twins with her TV writer and producer husband in the Silver Lake neighborhood, her unlikely rise to the mayoralty came at least in part because she was running against a wounded incumbent at a time when voters nationwide were eager for change. Bass was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared.
An urban planner, educated at Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Raman’s background includes founding a homelessness outreach nonprofit in LA.
Mayors in LA don’t have the clout of their counterparts in New York and Chicago — power is shared with the city council. Bonin described it as an accordion, which can expand or contract depending on who holds the office.
He said former Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, known for his chatty personality and charm, “swung for the fences.” Bass, by nature a compromiser, was different. Raman will set her own course.
“I can’t think of a mayor who had to take office with so many problems,” Bonin said. “Everybody leaves unpopular. … It’s not a job that makes you well loved.”

title: Westport Island Remembers Longtime Select Board Member’s Dedication
text:
Nearly 300 guests gathered at the town hall in Westport Island to celebrate the life of George D. Richardson Jr. on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Richardson dedicated his life to his town and has left an indelible mark on generations of family, neighbors, friends, and even foes. The family held a graveside burial service on Oct. 23 at the Richardson-Jewett Cemetery, a private cemetery that sits on a hill overlooking the Richardson’s home on Route 144, near Jewett Cove.
The burial service was opened with military honors by representatives from the U.S. Navy. The service included the playing of taps, the formal folding of the American flag that draped the casket, and the presentation of the flag to his wife of 67 years, Marcia Richardson.
Although dealing with her grief, Marcia Richardson officiated the funeral service for her husband, having served as a deacon at St. Philip’s Episcopal Church in Wiscasset for over 25 years.
The family and friends gathered at the service were what she said gave her the strength to complete the task.
“My mother’s faith gives her the strength,” said Gary Richardson, the couple’s son.
During the service, Marcia Richardson read from a 1989 New Zealand prayer book that was given to her by a friend in the Episcopal Church.
“Today we will pray for the soul of George Richardson,” Marcia Richardson said. “Also for ourselves to experience God’s healing and loving care, now and forever.”
An opportunity was given to share memories of George Richardson at the gravesite.
“When word got out in heaven George had passed, they said ‘Hold onto your hats, boys, here comes George,’” Gary Richardson said.
George Richardson’s grandson, Caleb, said his grandfather did a “lot more good than he did bad.”
“They say a person dies twice, once when your heart stops beating and the second time when the last person living that knew you dies,” Caleb Richardson said. “If that is the case, my grandfather will live for a long time, because he is known by a lot of people.”
Corinne Richardson, also shared memories of her father.
The graveside service concluded with the singing of “Amazing Grace,” a song written in 1772 by John Newton, a clergyman and sea captain. George Richardson and his three sons were all captains of their own boats.
At George Richardson’s celebration of life, there were no formal speakers. Instead, it was a conversational gathering with guests mingling, sharing stories, and remembering him.
Marcia Richardson spoke briefly to welcome the guests, inviting them to visit the memory table and board displayed in the front of the room with photos and memorabilia. She also encouraged the guests to enjoy the food and drink tables.
Gary Richardson shared that when he and his two brothers, Chuck and Lincoln, were captains of their own boats, they would follow their father out in the morning for a day of fishing, often referring to him as the “mother ship.” Their father, in turn, would call his three sons the “ducklings.”
Throughout the years, George Richardson enjoyed his coffee club meetings on Wednesday mornings, the group visiting different restaurants for coffee and conversation. Members from the club, Richard Grondin and Park Pino, remembered their times with George Richardson, sharing that their lives will not be the same without him.
The widow of the late E. Davies Allan, Nancy Shaul, was also in attendance. E. Davies was an adversary of George Richardson on many issues in town. Both men did not hesitate to share their differences and Shaul said they always “worked it out for the good of the town.”
Westport Island resident William Hopkins, who also sometimes disagreed with George Richardson, was also in attendance
“George loved this town and cared deeply for the people in it,” Hopkins said.
Over the years, George Richardson was called many things, including selectman, captain, “mayor of Westport Island,” and sometimes a character. Many of the guests at his celebration of life referred to him as a man to reckon with. He was a man who got results, gained respect, and was dependable, influential, and stood firm on what he believed to be good for the town.
During his 90 years of life, he served his country in the U.S. Navy, his state while on the Maine Municipal Association’s legislative policy committee, his county while on the Lincoln County Advisory Budget Committee, and to his town through a life long history of community. He leaves behind a legacy that will never be forgotten.
George Richardson lived on Westport Island all of his life except for two years in the Navy and while he attended Maine Maritime Academy in Castine.
He made it very clear he loved his town the way it was and not want change. If change were to come, he believed it should come slowly.
George Richardson served on the select board for 32 years, 25 of those years as chair. He made himself available to the residents, spending almost every day at the town office.
Among his legacies is the construction of the town office on Fowles Point Road, the development of the Wright Landing, the town public landing at the old Ferry Landing, and the Westport Island History Center.
George Richardson previously spoke to The Lincoln County News in 2012 about his near-death experiences on the water and his life on the island.
“Looking into the future, when we aren’t here anymore and the island is more populated, there will be public access to the water,” George Richardson said in the article.
That public access is due in part by the dedication and determination of a man who did not give up on something so important to the town. There is no doubt he will be missed and never forgotten by the residents of his island.

title: Soaking rain continues overnight into Sunday before clearing late
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Rain will continue on and off throughout much of the evening and into tomorrow as a weak low pressure system continues to meander off our coast. While sun won’t be the dominant story as it has been for much of the last two weeks we are in serious need of the rain so I think most of us will trade a sunny weekend for a rainy one considering the drought conditions. While it won’t be an overwhelming amount of rain it certainly will do some damage to the drought. Once it clears later Sunday, the weeks ahead looks calm with much more seasonable (cooler) temps.
Tonight: Rain continues for most with some breaks
The rain will continue for a good percentage of everyone overnight as showery activity associated with the slow moving low pressure system continues to inch northeastward. It will likely be heavier along the coast with the possibility to pick up to an inch or so along the coast with a few places inland cashing in to an extent as well depending on where heavier rain may set up. Lows will likely only drop a few degrees in the lower 40s. Breeziness will continue with gusts up to 20-25 mph.
Sunday: Some rain early, then clearing and cooler in the afternoon
The rain will continue in the morning with the chance for some wintry mix across colder spots in the west and the far north on Sunday but will begin to move east as the day goes on. The showers should be out of the state by 4 or 5 pm except for maybe extreme eastern Washington county. Temps will be cool once again with highs only reaching the mid to upper 40s for most.
Sunday night: Rain finally fully departs
After a soggy few days things settle down and a seasonably cool night arrives with some lingering cloudiness. Temps will be in the upper 30s for most.
Monday and beyond: A dry day and a more settled week
Things dry out and Monday looks to be a somewhat cloudy day but otherwise typical November weather with highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. After last week was more active this week looks quieter with few chances of active weather besides the weekend.
We are watching a system for late in the week towards next weekend that could provide some early season snow especially for inland and northern regions. It’s a long way off and there are lots of details to work out but it is something we are watching.
Today: Rainy and cooler. Highs in the 50s. Winds NE at 10-20 mph.
Tonight: Scattered showers otherwise overcast. Lows in the 40s. Winds NE 10-15 mph.
Sunday: Showers early, clearing late. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds NE at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: Rain ends clouds stick around. Lows in the upper 30s and low 40s. Winds NE 5-10 mph then going calm.
Monday: Mostly cloudy but dry. Highs in the upper 40s and low 50s. Winds W 5-10 mph.
Monday night: Still mainly cloudy. Lows in the 30s. Light wind.

title: House Democrats will start their majority focused on boosting healthcare and ending the Iran war
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leaders are placing an early emphasis on healthcare as they discuss their immediate priorities upon the swearing-in of the new Congress on Jan. 3.
Early votes in the House next year are expected to focus on boosting Medicaid and restoring an enhanced tax subsidy that is designed to lower the cost of Affordable Care Act health plans for millions of enrollees.
Democrats are also promising swift action on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump’strade tariffs.
“We’re going to get out of the gate fast,” said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who is in line to become the next House speaker.
The legislative flurry carries enormous stakes for Democrats as they seek to translate their sweeping victories in the midterms — their numbers will exceed 250 in the 435-member House — into achievements that deliver on their promises to lower the cost of living.
Obstacles abound for the Democratic agenda
Passing those bills should not be a problem with such a large Democratic House majority. Getting them signed into law most certainly could be.
A 60-vote threshold in the Senate looms for the legislation, as does a potential presidential veto. Trump on election night posted a photo on his social media site of a red hat with a simple message on it: “VETO”.
Following those early votes, Jeffries said five working groups are developing plans to put forward bills that would lower costs in areas such as housing, energy, groceries and caregiving.
Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., said Democrats will at some point take up legislation dealing with artificial intelligence and data centers. He is part of a group of lawmakers working on a document that will lay out some of the priorities for Jeffries to consider.
“House Republicans last year made a conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild, and that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy,” Lieu said. “Two things will change next term. We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI, and specifically data centers.”
New Congress will return to past political fights
Democrats are trying to reverse Medicaid changes that are expected to cut more than $900 billion from the program over a decade. The Republican-approved cuts helped offset some of the costs of Trump’s big tax and spending cut bill that was signed into law last year. The Medicaid changes in the bill imposed new administrative requirements and added conditions for eligibility, including work requirements.
Some of the most substantial changes have yet to take effect. Still, enrollment in Medicaid has dropped by about 5 million, or about 7% since July 2025, when the bill was signed into law, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization.
Reversing those cuts would likely require Trump and the Republicans to abandon the hard-fought changes they made to cut entitlement spending in their signature tax bill. It’s an unlikely proposition.
The effort to extend enhanced tax subsidies for certain enrollees in ACA plans has also been debated and voted on in the current Congress. The measure passed the House with some Republican support but stalled in the Senate.
There also have been numerous war powers votes regarding Iran — 14 in the Senate and six in the House.
Gridlock may be on the horizon
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said going into the election that a Democratic majority in the next Congress would amount to “two years of paralysis.”
“I don’t think that’s good for anybody,” Thune said.
But Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York is insisting that Democrats will push their agenda with or without the Republican president’s help.
“If he vetoes it, it will show the divisions. As much as we didn’t want to shut down, when we shut down the government for a month over healthcare, people knew we were on their side,” Schumer said in an interview with The New York Times’ podcast “The Daily.”
Schumer said he believes Democrats can gain some Republican votes on restoring the enhanced subsidies for ACA plans. When asked if he was hearing from Republicans expressing a willingness to work with him on legislation, he replied: “They’re never so definitive but, yes, I am getting initial signs that way on certain issues, not on every issue.”
While the prospects for getting any of the early priority bills over the finish line are uncertain, the votes in Congress will help frame the choices voters will face during a presidential election in 2028.
Tensions exist within the new Democratic majority
Progressive groups call the agenda outlined by Jeffries a good early start, but they have much greater expectations for Democrats this Congress.
“It’s perfectly fine if the Senate and the House are unified and Donald Trump is standing in the way because that sets up another tidal wave election in 2028,” said Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a Democratic-aligned group that backs progressive candidates and policies.
At the same time, he said Schumer cannot be content to let bills die in the Senate because of the 60-vote threshold.
“It will require the Democrats to get rid of the filibuster,” Green said. “There’s no doubt about it.”
He said there’s a disparity because Republicans’ top priorities — tax cuts and Supreme Court justices — can get through with simple majorities. But the Democratic Party’s top priorities require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.
“The only question is will the American public trust Democrats enough to keep giving us more power or will this week’s gains whittle away because we do nothing? That’s why the filibuster is a threshold question,” Green said.
Schumer in an interview with The Associated Press this week would not say whether he would try and eliminate the filibuster.
“The focus has got to be on getting things done,” Schumer said. “That’s all I am saying.”
In a memo to fellow members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said Democrats also need to target what he called “powerful forces outside of government.” Examples he cited were corporations using Americans’ private data to adjust their pricing based on a consumer’s personal data and AI companies that he says are putting jobs and lives at risk.
“By focusing not just on the Trump administration but also on big corporations and billionaires, we will show the American people we are not just anti-Trump but also pro-worker and pro-consumer,” Casar said.
___
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

title: Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Want to fly to the moon and help build a permanent lunar base? NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class that will help grow the Artemis program.
Officials announced the news Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration as well as advances in aviation and technology.
NASA’s last call for new astronauts was two years ago. More than 8,000 applied, with 10 making the final cut in September 2025.
With only 32 active astronauts, the space agency needs more recruits as it looks to expand humanity’s presence beyond low-Earth orbit as quickly as possible. April’s lunar flyaround by the Artemis II crew kicked off the lunar campaign.
“We have far more work than we have astronauts,” Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told The Associated Press on Saturday.
Aspiring astronauts have between now and Dec. 3 to submit their applications. NASA expects to make its final selection by late 2027, with the new candidates beginning their training by early 2028 — the same year that NASA intends to return astronauts to the lunar surface after an absence of more than half a century.
By then “we’re going to have people on the moon — so don’t delay,” Bresnik urged potential candidates.
Bresnik and his three crewmates will blast into orbit next summer to practice docking their capsule with a pair of lunar landers, one built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the other by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. Their mission will stick close to Earth — no lunar flyby — and serve as a dress rehearsal for the following year’s Artemis IV mission that will attempt to land two astronauts near the lunar south pole.
The moon base will materialize as more rovers, robots, structures and power grids are launched.
Patience is essential for becoming an astronaut, noted Artemis III’s Frank Rubio, whose 371 consecutive days in space is a U.S. endurance record. Candidates must also be U.S. citizens with college degrees and professional work experience.
The two years of mandatory training can be grueling, and it could take another several years on top of that before finally rocketing into space.
“It’s important for them to realize most of that work is not going to the moon, right?” Rubio told the AP. “That will be about 1% of your experience. What you’re doing is contributing to the mission of going to the moon.”
This will be NASA’s 25th astronaut class since the original Mercury Seven in 1959.

title: Brunswick boys soccer claims 8th Class A crown
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
KENNEBUNK — Led by standout midfielder Liam Rapoza, Brunswick seemed in control of the Class A boys soccer championship game for most of the first 68 minutes, except on the scoreboard.
Then the Dragons seized their championship. Lyle Sokoloff scored with 12:10 to play and Rapoza struck six minutes later as Brunswick beat first-time state finalist Thornton Academy 2-0 at Kennebunk High School.
Rapoza said Brunswick (17-1) knew little about Thornton (14-2-2) until watching film after the Golden Trojans blitzed Falmouth, 5-1, in the South final.
The Dragons could see that Thornton had strength across the field.
“Everything was solid, their midfield, their back line, their attack. We just shut it down, honestly,” Rapoza said. “We knew coming in (that) the midfield had to be solid and we had to step it up, big time. And we did.”
Brunswick had a 6-0 edge in first-half corner kicks (9-0 for the contest). The game was still scoreless, though, and remained that way in the second half after near misses by the Dragons on loose balls deep in Thornton’s defensive end.
“Ten minutes in, I just knew our seniors were not going to lose this game,” said Brunswick coach Mark Roma.
The Dragons finally got on the board after Rapoza drew a foul near the Brunswick sideline. Brendan Quinn’s free kick was knocked from the far post to the near side, and Sokoloff was in the right spot.
“It came off Asher (Foushee) and right to me, and I knew just to head it in. Yeah, a simple goal,” Sokoloff said. “That just gave us so much momentum for the rest of the game.”
Rapoza made it 2-0 with 6:19 to play. He used two slick dribbling moves to work around defenders before unleashing a left-footed laser from 20 yards that Thornton goalie Lucas Stolf could only watch whistle into the back twine.
“Going on the dribble, seeing it go in the net, it was so surreal,” Rapoza said. “I almost felt like I wasn’t even there. I almost felt like I was floating.”
Brunswick, the unanimous No. 1 in the Varsity Maine poll, won its eighth Class A title in its 16th state final, and its second championship in the past five seasons under Roma, who took over the program in 2012. The Dragons lost to Marshwood in the 2021 state final, beat Scarborough in 2022, and lost to Scarborough in 2025.
“This is my second championship. I’ve been on the other side as well. This side is better,” Roma said.
Brunswick had critical contributions across its lineup. Quinn, Foshee and Jacob Fallis were stellar in the midfield along with Rapoza. The back line held up well against Thornton attackers. Left back Simon Stadnicki defused multiple rushes up the wing. Joelson Malongo’s strength on the opposite side complemented the center back duo of Oscar Gartside and Ethan Stern-Hayes.
Backup keeper William Danahy came in cold when starter Declan Thebarge (three saves) was given a yellow card for a collision with Moyemade. Danahy made a diving save on Andres de Haro’s well-struck direct kick from 20 yards.
Prior to this season, Thornton had never even played in a regional final. The lack of big-game experience perhaps showed, especially with the Trojans getting two bench misconduct yellow cards in the final 10 minutes.
“It was a good battle overall and they took their chances. And that second goal was unbelievable,” said Thornton coach George Sherry. “It was unfortunate, but to get to this game was huge for the program.”

title: Northern finches are moving into Maine for winter
text:
The sounds of winter are in the air, as the classic “zzzips,” “tews,”and “piicks” call out from above. These are the call notes of various finches that are coming south and are likely to spend the winter around your backyard bird feeders.
While most of our neotropic migrants, like the warblers and vireos that bred here during the summer, have departed until next spring, there are a handful of northern finches that are moving into Maine for the winter. Each year, a report known as the “Winter Finch Forecast” is published, most recently by Tyler Hoar of Ontario for the Finch Research Network (FiRN), which looks at wild bird food availability (cones and fruit) across southern Canada to make predictions about what birds might move this winter. Here’s a summary of the report and some related recent observations to help you make sense of it all.
First, the phenomenon that we are discussing with these bird movements is called an irruption (different from an eruption). This is when a species that typically migrates from point A (breeding grounds) to point B (wintering grounds), but might not have enough resources (typically food) in one place, needs to temporarily move to point C (in this case, Maine) to survive. Most birds will return to that point A to point B movement after an irruptive year. Snowy owls are perhaps the best known example of this, and it is much more localized in finches, but it’s the same driver nonetheless.
The most obvious finch showing up lately has been the pine siskin. These small finches resemble a heavily striped American goldfinch, with more yellows in the flight feathers, and they often mix with goldfinches. Over the last month, they’ve been moving through in variable flocks, often 10 to 20 at a time, but with some reports of hundreds in a single group. Siskins love cedar and hemlock seeds, and the Winter Finch Forecast reports “Southeastern Canada, the Great Lakes region, and the northeastern United States have a very good northern white cedar crop (some areas have a good eastern hemlock crop as well).” So we have plenty of food for siskins coming here, and this abundance of naturally-occurring seeds may mean you won’t see as many at your bird feeder.
One fun measure to compare across years is looking at “frequency” on eBird.org, a citizen science project by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology where people report what birds they see, where, and with how much effort. That effort portion is important because we can then compare across all lists and calculate measures like frequency, which is the percentage of all checklists that a species is reported on. Looking at pine siskins over the last few years, their frequency in late October was 3.5% in 2025 and 3.15% in 2024, but this year it is at 12.6%. Interestingly, in 2023 we also saw a minor irruption, with frequency hitting 10% in late October, but it dwindled as birds continued moving south, presumably because they weren’t finding enough seeds here.
The forecast also mentions siskins having a good nesting season thanks to the ongoing spruce budworm outbreak (spruce budworm is a native moth that feeds on needles, buds, and flowers of spruce and fir trees, and its cyclical population outbreaks can devastate large areas of spruce and fir forests). In recent years we’ve seen large flights of evening grosbeaks in Maine thanks to this outbreak, but so far that doesn’t appear to be shaping up this year. Looking at frequency over the same time period, evening grosbeaks were reported on 3% of lists during irruptions in 2022 and 2025, but are only on 0.48% of lists this season. The lack of movement this year is likely due to the abundance of mountain-ash in Canada forests, as reported in the Winter Finch Forecast.
Purple finches are the other finch we are seeing move south right now. As the report says, purple finches will move to “take advantage of the good spruce and great eastern white pine and mountain-ash crops,” and we’ve definitely seen an increase, with handfuls showing up on our weekly bird walks at Gilsland Farm.
I highly recommend reading the full Winter Finch Forecast at finchnetwork.org, where you can see the coverage of other birds like crossbills and redpolls. And join us for a walk at Gilsland Farm or around the state to see how these finchy flights shape up this winter.
Have you got a nature or wildlife question of your own? It doesn’t have to be about birds! Email questions to [email protected] and visit www.maineaudubon.org to learn more about birding, native plants, and programs and events focusing on Maine wildlife and habitat. Maine Audubon Staff Naturalist Doug Hitchcox and other naturalists lead free bird walks on Thursday mornings starting at 7 am, at Maine Audubon’s Gilsland Farm Audubon Sanctuary in Falmouth. Walks move to an 8 am start in December.

title: Rockland man charged in connection with Damariscotta hit-and-run
text:
The Damariscotta Police Department arrested a person in connection with a hit-and-run crash that seriously injured a 65-year-old female bicyclist at the intersection of Main Street and Biscay Road in Damariscotta on the morning of Wednesday, Nov. 4.
In a Thursday, Nov. 5 press release, Damariscotta Police Chief Erik Josephson identified John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, as the driver. Barczak was arrested without incident at approximately 4 p.m. on Nov. 4 and transported to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset.
Barczak was charged with elevated aggravated assault, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, and leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury.
The vehicle, later found at a local business, was identified as a red Toyota Tacoma by Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith using physical evidence, surveillance footage, and vehicle-related information. Smith then identified Barczak as the driver.
According to a Nov. 4 Facebook post from the Damariscotta Police Department, a 911 call was made to the Lincoln County Communications Center at approximately 5:26 a.m. advising that a woman on a bicycle had been struck by a vehicle, which had then fled the scene by the time emergency responders arrived.
The woman was transported by Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta for treatment. Due to the severity of her injuries, she was later transported Maine Medical Center in Portland for further treatment.
The Damariscotta Police Department was assisted by the Damariscotta Fire Department, Lincoln County District Attorney’s Office, and Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office responded to the scene.
This is an ongoing story and will be updated as more information is provided.

title: Cheverus field hockey captures 4th straight Class A championship
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — Once again, it was close. And once again, with a championship on the line, it went the Cheverus field hockey team’s way.
Avery Tinker and Sydney Brunelle scored first-half goals, and the Stags returned to the state summit with a 2-1 victory over fellow unbeaten Mt. Ararat in the Class A final at Edward Little High School.
Update the numbers. State title No. 4 in a row — and their fifth in six years — ups the Stags’ winning streak to 35 games and their unbeaten streak to 72, dating back to a loss to Skowhegan in the 2022 final.
“It’s so special. It’s so nice to go 4 for 4, and that is not due to just the seniors, just me. It’s due to the entire team,” said Brunelle, a Miss Maine Field Hockey finalist. “I’m just so grateful to be a part of this and end my career on the highest note possible.”
Mt. Ararat (17-1-0), making its first appearance in a state final, erased a 2-0 deficit against Skowhegan in the A North final, and the Eagles generated hope they could do it again when Krystah Coen’s goal early in the third quarter trimmed the deficit to one.
The Stags (18-0-0), however, didn’t let them get any closer, burying the Eagles with waves of pressure that resulted in 10 corners over the final 28 minutes. It was Cheverus’ seventh one-goal win of the season, and third one-goal win in a state final in four years.
“We had this as a goal, to play all 18 games, and we got here. And so this is the next step,” said Mt. Ararat coach Krista Chase said. “We punched through. That’s what we said last year. We got to the door last year, we kicked through the door this year.”
The Eagles seized control quickly, with three corners in the first five minutes of the game. But Cheverus took over, tilted play to the other end, and it paid off when freshman Avery Tinker scored off a Brooke Brunelle assist on a corner with 7:26 left in the second.
“Coming out of that first quarter, we were like, ‘Why are we letting them kind of have control of this game right now?'” senior midfielder and captain Ava Martin said. “We needed to take control, and that’s what we did. We had that momentum and that fire.”
Seconds after returning to the field after being carded, Sydney Brunelle made it 2-0 with 1:39 to go in the first half. Cheverus coach Andrea Musante said she knew that goal would be needed, which proved prophetic when Coen finished a Leah Lachance assist with 13:07 left in the third.
The Stags, though, weren’t about to let their latest title slip away.
“We knew Mt. Ararat wasn’t going to go down without a fight. That’s just who they are,” Musante said. “But we started getting into our rhythm, so we were able to hang on.”

title: Memory card with uncounted ballots found, launching investigation
text:
SEMINOLE COUNTY, Ga. (WCTV/ANF/Gray News) — A memory card from election night has been discovered containing uncounted ballots from Seminole County, Georgia, voters.
According to a release from the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office, a post-election check revealed: “approximately 388 more voters recorded as having checked in at polling places on Election Day than the number of ballots reported as cast.”
The release detailed that the Secretary of State’s office caught the discrepancy and notified Seminole County’s Board of Elections.
This discovery may prove critical in the still-uncalled State House District 154 race, in which Democrat challenger Harry James led by 58 votes. With these new votes, incumbent Republican Gerald Greene has taken the lead by 262 votes. The Secretary of State’s office says the county has until Monday to certify its election results.
Brad Raffensperger’s office is investigating to find out “how the memory card was overlooked, whether required election procedures were followed, and what corrective measures are necessary to prevent similar incidents in future elections,” according to the release.
WCTV, Atlanta News First’s sister station in Tallahassee, has reached out to the Seminole County Board of Elections Friday afternoon for comment, but no one was available for comment.
