Tuesday will be partly sunny, with highs in the mid-50s. Tuesday night will be partly cloudy during the evening before skies clear. Overnight lows will be in the lower 30s.
Veterans Day will be partly sunny, with highs in the mid-50s. Wednesday night will be partly cloudy, with lows in the upper 20s.
Thursday will be partly sunny, with highs around 50 degrees. Thursday night will be partly cloudy, with lows in the mid-20s.
Friday will be partly sunny, with a chance of rain in the afternoon. Highs will reach the upper 40s, with a 40 percent chance of rain.
Maine’s Total Weather is keeping an eye on a potential storm that could move into New England late next week or next weekend, around November 13 or 14.
So, could we be looking at our first taste of winter weather? It’s possible, but a lot will depend on where the storm tracks. If it moves too far north, warmer air could move in, bringing mostly rain and possibly some ice. If it tracks just south of Maine, we could see a better chance of snow. However, if it stays too far south, we may miss out on most of the precipitation.
There is still plenty of uncertainty this far out, so we aren't ready to make any calls just yet. We'll be watching the forecast closely as things come into better focus next week. Stay tuned for updates!

title: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White press secretary job
text:
(Gray News) - President Donald Trump offered UFC president and CEO Dana White the job of press secretary on Saturday.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.”
The president also said the offer extended to White’s assistants, “even though some are not from our Country.”
“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote. “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”
In response to Trump, White posted a photo on Instagram Stories of himself standing behind the press secretary’s lectern in the White House, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”
It was unclear whether White has accepted the position or is simply acknowledging the president’s request in jest.
In October, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia left the position just five days after her stint as Karoline Leavitt’s replacement began.
The president told reporters he suggested Zacharia quit after her first and only press briefing.
The president’s appeal to White follows Friday’s announcement that Trump’s deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, would be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

title: Trump says he's asked UFC's Dana White to be his press secretary
text:
Trump says he's asked UFC's Dana White to be his press secretary
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president and one that nobody in the White House immediately confirmed.
Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior” to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.
Related video above: Zacharia makes first statement on departure as White House Press Secretary
Trump said he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as “assistants,” adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”
The White House did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.
White was in London on Saturday for a boxing event. A spokesperson for UFC did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
The UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words “On to the next chapter.”
Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.
The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.
The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.
Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.
He brought White and the sport to the White House’s South Lawn in June for the celebration of America’s 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.
“It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one,” said White afterward.
White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

title: Defense attorney for man convicted in Tupac murder trial found dead in Las Vegas
text:
Defense attorney for man convicted in Tupac murder trial dies
The defense attorney who represented Duane "Keffe D" Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial has died.
Michael Sanft, 55, was found dead in Las Vegas on Friday, Nov. 6, a spokesperson for the Clark County Office of the Coroner confirmed, according to USA Today.
His cause and manner of death are currently pending.
Sanft was a Nevada-based attorney most widely known for defending Davis in his murder trial for the 1996 shooting of rapper and actor Tupac Shakur.
In August, Davis was found guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon for facilitating the shooting. He was sentenced in October to 40 years to life in prison. He is the only person to be charged in the case.
At the time of sentencing, Sanft said he would appeal the conviction. Court records indicate he filed a notice of appeal on Oct. 30.
Sanft spoke to a Las Vegas news outlet after the sentencing.
"We had the best team possible in this case, from the motion practice work on this appeal to our investigator to our firm here at SOS Injury. We all did our part. I don't see what I could've done differently," he said. "He had reminded me this is phase one. Because I was upset with the verdict, I was very disappointed in the jury. Mr. Davis was the one who said, 'Don't worry about it, man, this is the first phase,' and I said, 'I understand, I hate to lose.'"
According to his law firm's website, Sanft grew up on the island of Tonga before moving with his family to San Diego when he was 12 years old. He would go on to serve a mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and attend BYU-Hawaii.
The site describes him as "one of the most respected and effective trial attorneys in America," with decades of experience trying more than 150 cases, crediting his "relentless work ethic, natural ability to connect with people, and desire to help society's most vulnerable individuals."

title: Nokomis field hockey tops Freeport for first title in 13 years
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — A state championship seemed like a longshot for the Nokomis field hockey team back in August. The Warriors were just looking for a coach.
They quickly got one of those. And on Saturday, they got the championship.
Nokomis won its first Class B title in since 2013, defeating Freeport 1-0 in the state final at Edward Little High School.
The Warriors, who have now won three state titles, finish the season 17-1. Freeport, which was playing in the final for the fourth time in five years despite replacing eight starters, finishes 14-4.
“We all have wanted this win for so long,” said MaKenzie Watson, an impact player both offensively and defensively Saturday. “We were like, when’s it going to be our chance? When’s it going to be our time? And finally, that was today.”
Nokomis was without a head coach until Aug. 17 following Shaunessy Saucier’s departure to coach at Husson University.
“We were panicking about that,” Watson said.
But Lauren Neal, a Nokomis alum, took over the role, and the Warriors began proving themselves the team to beat. On Saturday, that continued.
“It’s crazy, I don’t even know how I feel about it yet,” Neal said. “It was a stressful game, but defense showed up entirely. I’m just super proud of them.”
Nokomis took the lead in the opening minutes. Watson took a soft shot from the left side, just hoping to find the stick of a teammate up close. The ball instead found a path through the Freeport defense and eluded the stick of a diving defender, making it 1-0 with 11:21 left in the first.
“That was my plan. My plan is always to send it in and see what happens,” Watson said. “I was so excited when it went in. … It took me a second to realize it.”
While Nokomis continued to bring pressure — sophomore Maeve Rush just missed connecting with an open Annie Nyce late in the second quarter — the Warriors’ defense became the story of the second half. The Falcons buzzed around the cage and had seven corners, but a defense led by Watson, Ella Toulouse, Kaylee Paradis and Ava Burke time and again kept shots away from the net.
A final stand decided the game. Freeport had a corner in the final minute and whipped a hard shot on net, but Toulouse made a final block. Seconds later, the celebration was on.
“We’ve been working so hard all season towards this,” Rush said. “I wouldn’t rather do it with anyone else.”
The Falcons had good looks, especially early. Briella Boudreau hit the post shortly after Watson’s goal, and Nokomis goalie Anna Russell made a good kick save on an Ava Emmons shot late in the second.
“No one thought we were going to get past that regional (final vs. Yarmouth),” Falcons coach Marcia Wood said. “We felt zero pressure. … We’re here, and no one expected it. That’s what I said to them. You’re one of the last teams playing, and no one expected you to be doing that.”

title: Plane hits, kills woman on runway
text:
WILMINGTON, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) - One woman is dead after an accident involving a plane in upstate New York.
It happened around 3:45 p.m. Friday.
State police said a single-engine, two-seat plane landed at Catalano Airfield and was making its way to the hangar when it struck a person on the runway.
Police said 67-year-old Pamela Haselton was on the runway taking photos of the plane with a camera on a tripod.
They said when the plane was approaching, Haselton tried to move the tripod out of the way, and the pilot didn’t see her.
New York State Police are working with the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board to investigate the incident.

title: Uplifting sign at Red Barn in Augusta leads to misconception over political message
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Trever Benedict, co-owner of The Red Barn in Augusta, came in to work Wednesday, the first thing he did was place a new roadside sign in front of his business. He switches the sign to display a new uplifting message every couple of weeks, he said, and this change was overdue.
This sign, reading “Sorry to spoil the ending for you, but everything is gonna end up okay,” was especially meaningful to Benedict because his dad has suffered two strokes this year as his mother’s health also declines. He thought of them as he put it up, he added, thinking nothing else was out of the ordinary.
But when he posted a picture of the sign on Facebook, it was met with hundreds of angry comments, direct messages and later some phone calls from people who thought he was celebrating the overwhelming victory of Democrats in Maine and across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Some people said they would boycott The Red Barn, according to Benedict.
“Naturally it was taken entirely out of context, and it basically created this uproar that we’re in the midst of now,” Benedict said Saturday morning. “For it to come back as this backlash, name-calling from the community, it’s really disheartening, it’s infuriating, and it’s ridiculous, frankly.”
Benedict posted an update on Facebook Thursday that clarified the intent behind the sign, but turned the comments off to avoid negativity. He said people continued to message him directly.
The Red Barn has stirred some controversy in the past under previous owner Laura Benedict, Trever Benedict’s aunt. Laura lashed out at Augusta city officials in 2017 after mistakenly believing that she had been fined for not having a mass gathering permit for a fundraising event, and she publicly removed an employee from the restaurant’s work schedule after he made racists remarks on Instagram.
Trever Benedict said there has never been anything political about the signs the restaurant posts, and that people sometimes stop in just to thank them for how the message improved their day.
“I hope that people can just strive to see the good and not scrutinize everything to the point where they look so hard to find the negative in everything,” Benedict said. “We have never been more divided than we are right now, and this whole example of this sign is exhibit A.”

text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org.

title: Obituary: Daniel J. MacGillivary
text:
GEORGETOWN – Daniel J. MacGillivary of Old Schoolhouse Road, died Monday Oct. 26, 2026 after a short visit at Maine Health Midcoast Hospital of Brunswick, Maine at the age of 93.
He was born in the family home on Oct. 9, 1933 the son of Percy S. and Alice M. Pinkham MacGillivary, where he lived for 40 years taking care of his parents until he married Linda Swanson.
He worked various jobs starting as a young man. He drove trucks for the State of Maine, worked with his dad on the road and bridge for Reid State Park, Dave’s Texaco in Woolwich until going to BIW where he worked for 30 years and retiring at the age of 70.
Surviving is his wife, Linda of Five Islands of 52 years; and his four stepchildren, Brian Swanson (Theetra), Rhonda Haase, Sherry Stewart and Bruce (Jennifer) Swanson; a brother Andrew (Karen) MacGillivary and a sister Karen (Barry) Fake; along with many nieces and nephews.
He was predeceased by his parents Percy S. and Alice M. MacGillivary; four brothers, John H., Bruce A., Keith C., and Wayne L. MacGillivary, four sisters, Ida M. Olson, Claire E. Reynolds, Dorothy L. McDorr and Marilyn A. Tardif.
There will be a private memorial service later.

title: Former doctor photographed patients’ genitals during medical procedures, lawsuit alleges
text:
TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG/Gray News) - A Toledo doctor who has been indicted for possession of child sexual abuse material also photographed his patients’ genitals during medical procedures, according to a newly filed lawsuit.
Bryan Sack, former doctor and chief of pediatric urology at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Toledo, was arrested earlier this year for allegedly having tens of thousands of explicit images of children.
According to a statement from Nationwide Children’s at the time of Sack’s arrest in February, the charges were not related to his work at the hospital.
The surgical photos in question were disclosed in an FBI affidavit in May, according to Flood Law, the firm representing the families.
A lawsuit has now been filed Nov. 4 on behalf of 13 children and their families, alleging that Sack’s Dropbox account had more than 27,000 files of children.
The lawsuit also states that 1,200 files of child sexual abuse material were found, along with close-up images of children’s genitals, including images Sack is accused of taking with his cellphone during examinations.
The lawsuit named Sack, Nationwide Children’s Hospital - Toledo, Nationwide Children’s Hospital and Mercy Health St. Vincent Medical Center as defendants.
Nationwide Children’s in Toledo operates on the Mercy Health Toledo campus.
The lawsuit claims invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence, negligent supervision, negligent hiring, credentialing and retention against both hospitals, and fraudulent concealment against Nationwide Children’s.
In addition to financial compensation, the families want the hospitals to notify every patient Sack treated, audit the images he accessed, and require Sack to identify and hand over any patient image in his possession before evidence can be destroyed through federal forfeiture.
They also want counseling for affected children and their families to be paid for.
Sack was arrested after an investigation prompted by a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. A search warrant was executed at his residence, where digital evidence was seized, authorities said.
According to Nationwide Children’s Hospital, Sack was terminated from his position following the reported charges.

title: Charlie Woods, son of Tiger Woods, commits to Florida State University
text:
Charlie Woods, son of Tiger Woods, commits to Florida State University
Charlie Woods, a Florida state champion golfer and the son of legendary golfer Tiger Woods, will play at Florida State University.
The young athlete made it official at The Benjamin School's national signing day event with a dozen of his fellow student-athletes.
Woods celebrated with loved ones, including his father, who donned a Florida State Seminoles shirt for the occasion.
The young golfer will look to win a third state championship with his golf team from The Benjamin School — a private college prep school in Palm Beach County, Florida — later this month.
The student-athletes in attendance said the day was about celebrating their hard work and community.
"It's definitely a dream come true. All the kids put in the hard work throughout the years," said Jack Kelleher, a lacrosse player who will play at Yale.
"I'm super excited. I'm proud of everyone and myself for getting here and excited for the future for not only myself but everyone here," said Phoebe Apple, who will play soccer at the University of Georgia.
"I think this school has prepared us well both academically and athletically and taught us to be a community and good teammates," said swimmer Rachel Nussbaum, who will compete for Johns Hopkins.

title: Prosecutors seek mental health evaluation of Standish woman charged with murder
text:
Prosecutors seek mental health evaluation of Standish woman charged with murder
A hearing is scheduled for November 19 in the murder case against Lynn Perkins, who is accused of fatally shooting Matthew Hamilton in 2025
Prosecutors seek mental health evaluation of Standish woman charged with murder
A hearing is scheduled for November 19 in the murder case against Lynn Perkins, who is accused of fatally shooting Matthew Hamilton in 2025
Maine prosecutors are asking a judge to order a forensic mental health evaluation of a Standish woman accused of killing a man she had previously been in a relationship with.
Lynn Perkins is charged with murder in the October 2025 shooting death of 49-year-old Matthew Hamilton, who was found dead inside a home on River Road in Standish.
In a motion filed on September 28, the Maine Attorney General's Office requested that Perkins undergo an evaluation to examine her mental condition, including issues related to criminal responsibility and her state of mind at the time of the shooting.
According to the filing, Perkins' defense attorney previously presented two experts who argued that she believed her use of deadly force was justified because of mental conditions associated with battered woman syndrome.
Prosecutors also stated that law enforcement officers who responded to calls involving Perkins observed what appeared to be a deterioration in her mental condition in the weeks leading up to the shooting.
The filing says that Perkins' attorney, David Bobrow, opposes the state's request for an evaluation.
A hearing is scheduled for November 19. According to the Maine Attorney General's Office, the court is also expected to discuss scheduling the trial and a defense request to allow jurors to view the crime scene.
The Attorney General's Office clarified that Perkins' competency to stand trial has not been raised as an issue.
Perkins previously pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.

title: Troy Jackson inherits Susan Collins’ seat but not her federal funding clout
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson heads to Washington in early January with the enthusiasm of a party that swept control of Congress but without the clout of Sen. Susan Collins, the outgoing head of the Appropriations Committee.
The five-term Republican made bringing home federal dollars a centerpiece of her campaign, often touting the $1.5 billion she brought to Maine over the past five years. But Collins fell victim to a nationwide and statewide push for change at a time of deep anger and economic uncertainty under the second administration of President Donald Trump.
That change is certain to come with a cost when it comes to federal earmarks, based on similar dynamics in other states that lost a senior appropriator. After a handful of states lost appropriators, earmarks dried up by as much as half in a flow that gradually reverses after the lawmaker departs, according to a Journal of Political Economy study from 2012.
The problem shows itself even more when the incoming senator doesn’t get on the Appropriations Committee, a rarity for a freshman. Jackson has expressed interest in a spot on the panel currently chaired by Collins.
“The Senate is so seniority driven,” Larry Persily, an Alaska newspaper publisher and former federal and state government official who served as an aide to former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, said in an interview. “By losing [the late Republican Sen.] Ted Stevens and his position in the Senate, of course Alaska lost clout in getting money.”
Collins helped drive almost $425 million, fourth-most among senators, to Maine this fiscal year. The entire congressional delegation’s earmarks totaled about $460 million, or $328 per resident, a per-capita rate second only to Alaska, according to The Maine Monitor.
The Jackson campaign and Collins’ office did not respond to requests for comment. Federal staffers and experts said Thursday that it’s too early to delve into committee assignments in the new Congress for either Jackson or independent Sen. Angus King, who will be Maine’s senior senator but does not sit on Appropriations.
Jackson still arrives on Capitol Hill without some of the advantages of other freshmen who previously replaced prominent drivers of earmarks. Several said that while Jackson faces challenges on earmarks, Democrats and Maine’s congressional delegation are likely to work together to keep the state front and center as appropriators craft budgets.
“They’ll be aware of his needs to produce,” Persily said of Democrats and Jackson.
When former Sen. Richard Shelby of Alabama was the appropriations chair, he helped secure more than $548 million in home-state projects in fiscal year 2022, the second-most in the country. That jumped to $656 million the following year, his final year in office.
When Republican Sen. Katie Britt took over in 2023, Alabama’s total fell to less than half of that. But Britt was assigned to appropriations, so she secured $232 million for ninth-most among senators. She was previously Shelby’s chief of staff, coming into office knowing the committee and its processes.
“We’ve been fortunate to have federal officials who are focused on growing the Alabama Port Authority,” Jason Johnson, a spokesman for the agency, said in a Thursday email. “Senator Britt has done a remarkable job picking up where Senator Shelby left off, and we’re incredibly fortunate that her leadership on the Appropriations Committee has already brought hundreds of millions of dollars back to Alabama to invest in our state’s future.”
The potential dropoff in federal dollars could be mitigated by King, who has also been among the top senators bringing earmarks home in recent years. His office noted Thursday that he has a strong alliance with Sen. Patty Murray, D-Washington, the likely new appropriations chair.
He also has a healthy relationship with Sen. Lisa Murkowski, the centrist Alaska Republican and Collins ally who is likely to step into the top GOP role on the panel in the wake of the Maine senator’s defeat. King has often been in the same room with Murkowski during bipartisan conversations and negotiations over budgets and policy.
On the House side, where former Gov. Paul LePage just won in the 2nd Congressional District over state Auditor Matt Dunlap, Rep. Chellie Pingree sits on the chamber’s Appropriations Committee.
Persily said he would tell any incoming senator hoping to get on the Appropriations Committee to “have a backup plan, buddy.” He noted the government may be “mostly immobilized” over the next two years given the divides between the lame-duck Trump and a Democratic-led Congress. But Jackson and Maine as a whole could be poised for long-term success, Persily said.
“If the Democrats take White House in 2028, there will be even more consideration for making sure the first-term Maine senator can campaign for reelection with success stories,” he said.

title: Father accused of leaving daughter sleeping outside Target to hold spot for Pokémon cards, police say
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - A man in South Carolina is accused of leaving his 6-year-old daughter sleeping in line outside a Target store to hold his place for a Pokémon card release.
John-Michael Dooley, 35, is charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.
Charleston officers responded to the West Ashley store around 2:30 a.m. Friday after receiving a report of an unattended child.
Customers had gathered outside overnight for the release of a new Pokémon trading card set.
Witnesses told police that sometime after 1 a.m., Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and blanket before leaving her asleep in line.
After he had been gone for about an hour, concerned customers called police.
When Dooley returned to the store, witnesses identified him, and he was arrested.
Dooley allegedly told detectives he had gone home and left his daughter at the store to maintain his place in line.
The girl was unharmed and placed in emergency protective custody with the South Carolina Department of Social Services.

title: US military says it fired on commercial vessel after it attempted to breach blockade on Iran
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial strategic waterway for global shipping, including of oil. The last confirmed U.S. strike on a cargo vessel was nearly a month ago in the Gulf of Oman.
Saturday’s disclosure comes in the wake of at least two instances in which U.S. Central Command did not announce military strikes it has taken in the region and officials at the command declined to confirm strikes when asked about local reports of explosions.
Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask. It wasn’t immediately clear what the cause of the explosions was and the U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
The Iranian military said late Saturday that two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire. It did not identify the tankers’ flags or destinations.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. military had carried out new limited strikes against Iran, targeting an Iranian air defense system. Trump described the military action to reporters as “minor.” U.S. Central Command ultimately didn’t comment on the action even after the strikes were confirmed by Trump.
For weeks now, Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, which were held on Nov. 3. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months.
The more than 8-month-old war has rattled global markets and diplomacy to end it has stalled. October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.

text:
Hallowell police chief recommends denying Quarry Tap Room liquor license
The police chief cited at least 15 incidents involving the business over the past three and a half months.
Hallowell police chief recommends denying Quarry Tap Room liquor license
The police chief cited at least 15 incidents involving the business over the past three and a half months.
Hallowell's police chief is recommending that the City Council deny a liquor license renewal for the Quarry Tap Room, citing at least 15 incidents involving the business over the past three and a half months.
The chief said the incidents included several arrests for operating under the influence and that problems typically occur during busy Friday and Saturday nights. He said he has spoken with staff and security several times but has not seen improvements, and that he wants significant safety changes before approving the license.
The taproom's ownership said Friday that it had a productive phone call with the chief after learning of his recommendation. In a news release, the owners said they plan to meet with him for a walkthrough Monday before the public hearing. The chief's letter said an earlier attempt to arrange a visit went unanswered and that no one was present when he arrived for a walkthrough, according to the release.
The owners said they, their employees and customers will address other statements in the chief's letter at the hearing. They said the taproom is committed to providing a safe and comfortable environment.
The City Council is scheduled to discuss the license at its next meeting Monday.

title: Grieving father of Florida Learjet co-pilot defends his daughter's reputation after crash
text:
Grieving father of Florida Learjet co-pilot defends his daughter's reputation after crash
The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot killed alongside eight others in a Florida Learjet crash said Friday he has repeatedly listened to her final radio transmissions, searching for answers and finding pride in how she handled the crisis.
Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras to fly, said he marveled at how “she's tough” even as the plane plunged straight toward the ground Sunday.
“I wanted to be by her side. Inside the plane, to help,” he said at a news conference, often holding back tears.
Related video above: 911 calls reveal shock, confusion in aftermath of deadly Learjet crash
“She showed me what it is to be a hero,” he said, “because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting.”
Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly telling air traffic control about ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm. Turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters), but the situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. “Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!” she said.
Her father and aviation safety experts have praised her composure as she called out updates while knowing the plane's fate was sealed. The captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls.
“For the family — it’s like having the heart torn from my chest,” Allan Filgueiras said in Spanish. “I have to find a way to go on living.”
Young co-pilot's family and instructor say she earned her job on merit
The family has challenged online criticism questioning whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot’s license and Learjet certification.
Her father's attorney, Stuart Grossman, said the news conference aimed to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation.”
“She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,” Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans for any lawsuit.
The National Transportation Safety Board has not yet determined what caused the crash. The Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits as it fell, and pieces of its tail were found miles away from the crash site, which is a deep crater on the edge of a road. Investigators were still searching the area Friday after finding part of an engine a day earlier. The cockpit recorder remains missing.
Allan Filgueiras said he helped teach her how to fly after taking her aloft for the first time at age 12. Once she got a job as a pilot, she told him she couldn’t believe she was getting paid to do something she loved.
“It was her happiest moment, to fly,” he said.
Mentor says her professionalism showed in final calls
Her mentor and instructor, Chris Kirk, said she earned her position through dedication and perseverance by putting in hard work and long hours.
During her Learjet 60 check ride in March, the examiner was so impressed he thought she had more than 5,000 hours of experience — nearly four times the amount of flight time she had logged.
Kirk said her professionalism was evident in those final radio transmissions, which gave the NTSB important information. Many members of the military special forces who Kirk worked with probably couldn't keep their wits in a similar situation.
“This was an incredible human being,” Kirk said, “who did a job that very few people would have been able to do under duress that’s unimaginable.”
Retired airline pilot John Cox said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Nathalia Filgueiras', as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she had done well to earn a Learjet co-pilot's seat.
“To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that’s a good ride. I mean, that’s great. I know she loved it,” said Cox, who now runs Safety Operating Systems, an aviation consulting company.
The other crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family’s nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The other two victims were Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, who owned the Arca Boutique Hotel in Honduras.

title: Officials condemn planned boycott of Jewish-owned businesses as antisemitic
text:
Officials condemn planned boycott of Jewish-owned businesses as antisemitic
State and local leaders have strongly condemned a protest planned for this weekend in Philadelphia that targets Jewish-owned businesses, calling it antisemitic and unacceptable.
Several local activist groups promoted the protest, which is expected Sunday as a bicycle “boycott ride” past Jewish-owned restaurants in the city’s Rittenhouse Square neighborhood. The main organizer, Philly Bike On Your Left, describes itself as being “anti-Zionist.”
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday said the boycott on the eve of the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht is “deeply unsettling.” Kristallnacht, or the “Night of Broken Glass,” was a Nazi-organized riot in which synagogues were burned, Jewish-owned businesses and homes were vandalized, and Jews were assaulted, killed and imprisoned in concentration camps in Nazi Germany.
Related video above: Pennsylvania abuse survivors see new hope for lawsuits as Democrats take Senate
“The bike ride, masquerading as a protest to advance the cause of justice, is nothing more than blatant antisemitism designed to intimidate and drive Jewish businesses out of our communities,” according to a statement from Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office. “There is no place for that in our Commonwealth.”
Shapiro’s office said Pennsylvania State Police is “engaged with our local partners to ensure the safety and wellbeing of our neighbors in Philadelphia.”
Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker said everyone has the right to protest peacefully, “But singling out businesses because their owners are Jewish is unacceptable and has no place in our city,” according to a statement posted on social media.
The planned bike-ride-boycott organizers name six restaurants that officials and local Jewish organizations say are run by Jewish owners.
“Ride around Rittenhouse with us as we show these Zionist business owners that we see them for the disgusting humans they are,” reads a post from Philly Bike On Your Left, the main organizer of the protest. “We’ll flag as many bikes as we can and show our solidarity with the Palestinian community and oppressed (folks) everywhere.”
Philly Bike On Your Left still planned to host its ride in spite of what it described as being “grossly misrepresented,” according to a statement sent to CNN and posted on its Instagram early Saturday morning.
Calling itself a “non-violent social cycling page,” the group said it was “firmly against racism and oppression of all forms, including fascism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, and colonialism.”
“Let us be clear: the reason we are calling for a boycott of these businesses is because of their support for Israel,” the group’s statement said.
The group also addressed the timing of the protest, which is set for a day before the anniversary of Kristallnacht, on the night of November 9. The statement said the group plans rides around people’s schedules.
“Palestinians need our support now,” the statement said. “Any suggestions about the timing of our ride are simply false.”
Philly Bike On Your Left earlier shared a post from another activist group, arguing criticism of the demonstration was “disingenuously conflating Zionism with Judaism” and invoking Kristallnacht is “a cynical take.”
Some businesses named in the group’s flyer have been protested before.
In 2023, protesters gathered outside Goldie, a falafel shop near Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia. It is co-owned by Israeli-born chef Michael Solomonov, who grew up in Pittsburgh and co-owns CookNSolo Restaurants, which operates several area restaurants.
The gathering was one part of a larger protest organized by a different group who said they “demand a complete end to the siege on Gaza and an end to the U.S. complicity with Israel.” Protesters at the time waved Palestinian flags and chanted, “We charge you with genocide.”
That demonstration also drew swift condemnation from the Biden administration and state and local officials.
CookNSolo declined to comment on this weekend’s planned protest.
Local pro-Palestinian groups issued a joint statement late Friday supporting the planned boycott bike ride by a “group of bicyclists.”
Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt called the planned protest “absolutely vile.”
“This is antisemitism disguised as activism. It is Jew-hatred, plain and simple, and it should outrage every person of conscience,” he said in a social media post.
Attorney General Sunday said the boycott “is not simply a protest directed at the policies of Israel, rather it singles out our fellow Pennsylvanians based on their Jewish identity, targeting them for policies they have nothing to do with and no ability to affect because of their faith.”
The mayor said the Philadelphia Police Department will be on hand to “maintain safety and order” during the demonstration, adding, “Anyone who engages in threats, intimidation, or unlawful conduct will be held accountable.”
One of the city’s largest Jewish congregations in the region encouraged congregants to stay away from the Rittenhouse crowds and instead gather for a Kristallnacht commemoration at the Horwitz-Wasserman Holocaust Memorial Plaza on Monday.
“As a small, fringe, antisemitic group plans to demonstrate on Sunday with a bicycle ride to boycott Jewish businesses, I want to offer us a way to respond that does not give the antisemites the attention they crave, that reduces risk of violent confrontation, that supports peace for the Jewish businesses, and that allows us to stand tall as Jews against the haters,” Rabbi Jill Maderer of Congregation Rodeph Shalom wrote on social media.

title: Yarmouth boys soccer wins another state title
text:
BANGOR – The Yarmouth High School Clippers have been one of the state’s best boys soccer teams for a long time and they added to their crowded trophy case at a rainy Cameron Stadium on Saturday morning.
Senior striker/midfielder Lucas Hayner scored a pair of goals and assisted on the other as the Clippers shut out John Bapst High of Bangor 3-0 for their 18th state championship.
Senior back/midfielder Cael Woelflein had a goal and an assist and senior goalkeeper Gabriel Janczuk made a crucial second-half save off a breakaway.
It was John Bapst’s only shot on goal in the contest. The Crusaders had three shot attempts.
John Bapst senior goalie Bode Phillips turned in an exceptional performance, stopping seven shots. Yarmouth had 23 attempts in claiming its second straight B title.
Both teams wound up 16-1-1.
“It was one of our best games of the season. We knew that’s what we needed to do to win this game,” said Hayner, an All-American a year ago who will play for Gettysburg College (PA) next season. “We worked hard. We did stuff we stressed all season: finding passes, moving, dynamic, building out of the back.”
“We really came together today. We played as one,” added Hayner, who opened the scoring with 15:21 left in the first half.
He took a pass from Woelflein with his back to the goal, spun and slipped a perfectly-place shot inside the post to the right of Phillips.
“Cael made a great pass to me. I took a touch around a defender and my momentum was already going to the right so I thought I would cut it back because [Philllips] would be on his toes to the right side.”
It was 1-0 at the half, but Hayner expanded the lead early in the second half.
A Cole MacVane cross went to Tate MacVane and it glanced off his foot into the path of Hayner.
“I don’t know if [Tate MacVane] meant to set me up on purpose but it rolled perfectly to my feet, I was running across it and swung through it,” said Hayner, who steered it past Phillips’s right hand side with the inside of his right foot for his 20th goal of the season.
The Clippers were completely controlling play but, with 18:18 left, the Crusaders had a golden opportunity to cut the lead in half when Josh Pangburn sent a long pass upfield to Kasper Hansen, who had gotten behind the defense and broke in alone on Janczuk.
Janczuk raced off his line and smothered Hansen’s shot with his chest.
“The goalie made a great play to come out and give Kasper no time,” said John Bapst coach Jason Pangburn.
“That was a really important save,” said Hayner. “It doesn’t seem like it on the scoreboard but if they score that and it goes to 2-1, it’s a whole different game.”
Woelflein pointed out that Janczuk hadn’t played soccer since eighth grade. He had been on the golf team and they talked him into coming out for soccer.
“He’s a wonderful goalie,” said Woelflein, who sewed up the win a few minutes later when he took a Hayner pass off his chest and then volleyed his shot past Phillips.
“They were the best team we played all year,” said John Bapst midfielder and Penobscot Valley Conference Class B Player of the Year Rafa Rentosa, one of the captains.
Coach Pangburn said he was “super proud” of his team.
“We competed well against a machine,” said Pangburn. “They are a super talented team at every position and coming off the bench.”
“We kept playing. We never backed down,” said Rentosa.

title: More than blue wave swept away Susan Collins
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Susan Young is the Bangor Daily News opinion editor.
Susan Collins blamed her loss in Tuesday’s election on voter disdain for President Donald Trump. Voters, she complained, wanted angry rhetoric, not the results she had so long delivered.
She was partly right. Voters across the country swept Republicans out of power, from the U.S. Senate to governor’s offices to state legislatures. Voters were fed up with high prices, a confusing and costly war in Iran and a president who seems more intent on burnishing his image and enriching himself than improving life for average Americans.
Yes, Collins was swept up in that blue wave.
But, there is more to her defeat after 30 years in the U.S. Senate than that simple explanation.
Many journalists harkened back to Collins’ reelection victory in 2020, noting that polls predicted a loss to former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon, yet Collins won that election by nearly 9 percentage points.
That’s the wrong number to focus on. Collins won 51% of the vote in a four-way race. Progressive independent Lisa Savage won 5%, likely taking many of those votes from Gideon. Erratic independent Max Linn, rest his soul, was less of a factor, earning 1.6% of the vote.
To win a two-way race this year, Collins needed to meet or exceed that result, a tall order at a time when populous parts of Maine had become more Democratic and the Republican president was extremely unpopular.
To make matters worse for Collins, her reputation as a moderate was frayed during Trump’s second term in the White House.
Collins built her reputation as a moderate at a time when there were other reasonable lawmakers, from both parties, to work with in the Senate. She was often a member of the “gangs” who negotiated bipartisan agreements. She did this on judicial nominations, ending government shutdowns, immigration (which Trump torpedoed), and most recently the massive infrastructure and jobs act passed during the Biden administration to help boost the economy during the pandemic.
As Washington, and the country, became more polarized and scoring political victories became more important than passing useful legislation, these opportunities to negotiate compromises became less frequent, and then disappeared. Trump, especially in his second term, had little interest in bipartisan work, and increasingly simply went around Congress.
This was especially true with funding. Collins had worked diligently to become the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, becoming the first Mainer to hold the post in nearly a century. But, almost immediately, Trump usurped her power by refusing to release federal funds that had already been approved by Congress. Federal agencies, which had been funded by Congress, were shuttered and gutted.
Yes, Collins successfully got some funding restored for Maine projects and agencies. But, that felt inadequate to what Trump was doing nationally.
Why, many Mainers wondered, wasn’t the senator who voted to convict Trump for his “abuse of power and betrayal of his oath” on Jan. 6, 2021, doing more to stop him? Instead, she voted for most of his cabinet nominees, supported his voter suppression legislation and voted for more money for ICE at a time when it was terrorizing communities and detaining immigrants without criminal records, many of whom were in America legally.
To fully understand how the ground shifted — or maybe even fell away — under Collins, consider this. In July 2017, passengers at the Bangor airport cheered Collins as she entered the terminal. They thanked the senator for her vote to save the Affordable Care Act. She was one of three Republicans to vote against a GOP plan to gut the landmark healthcare bill that extended health insurance to millions of Americans.
A year later, Collins and her office were targeted by threatening phone calls and mailings as she considered Trump’s nomination of Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court. She voted in favor of Kavanaugh, despite allegations that he sexually assaulted several women and concerns that he did not support the Roe v. Wade decision that had made abortion a constitutional right.
Women, especially the brave survivors of sexual abuse, who have spoken out felt betrayed by Collins. That only deepened when Kavanaugh joined the conservative majority of the court to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Collins, who put in long hours researching legislation and policy and never missed a vote, often said she approached all presidents and their nominees the same way. She looked at their qualifications and gave presidents deference to make their own personnel decisions.
This standard failed during the Trump years, especially his second administration when he nominated people who had no expertise in, and were often hostile to, the agencies they were tapped to oversee.
Collins was an institutionalist when Trump was tearing down the very institutions of government, sometimes literally as in his destruction of the East Wing of the White House and the Reflecting Pool.
So, yes, Collins was swept away by a blue wave that was propelled by anger at Trump. But, her tenure also ended because the Senate she helped build was torn down by Trump and fellow Republicans.

title: Nokomis field hockey tops Freeport for first title in 13 years
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — A state championship seemed like a longshot for the Nokomis field hockey team back in August. The Warriors were just looking for a coach.
They quickly got one of those. And on Saturday, they got the championship.
Nokomis won its first Class B title in since 2013, defeating Freeport 1-0 in the state final at Edward Little High School.
The Warriors, who have now won three state titles, finish the season 17-1. Freeport, which was playing in the final for the fourth time in five years despite replacing eight starters, finishes 14-4.
“We all have wanted this win for so long,” said MaKenzie Watson, an impact player both offensively and defensively Saturday. “We were like, when’s it going to be our chance? When’s it going to be our time? And finally, that was today.”
Nokomis was without a head coach until Aug. 17 following Shaunessy Saucier’s departure to coach at Husson University.
“We were panicking about that,” Watson said.
But Lauren Neal, a Nokomis alum, took over the role, and the Warriors began proving themselves the team to beat. On Saturday, that continued.
“It’s crazy, I don’t even know how I feel about it yet,” Neal said. “It was a stressful game, but defense showed up entirely. I’m just super proud of them.”
Nokomis took the lead in the opening minutes. Watson took a soft shot from the left side, just hoping to find the stick of a teammate up close. The ball instead found a path through the Freeport defense and eluded the stick of a diving defender, making it 1-0 with 11:21 left in the first.
“That was my plan. My plan is always to send it in and see what happens,” Watson said. “I was so excited when it went in. … It took me a second to realize it.”
While Nokomis continued to bring pressure — sophomore Maeve Rush just missed connecting with an open Annie Nyce late in the second quarter — the Warriors’ defense became the story of the second half. The Falcons buzzed around the cage and had seven corners, but a defense led by Watson, Ella Toulouse, Kaylee Paradis and Ava Burke time and again kept shots away from the net.
A final stand decided the game. Freeport had a corner in the final minute and whipped a hard shot on net, but Toulouse made a final block. Seconds later, the celebration was on.
“We’ve been working so hard all season towards this,” Rush said. “I wouldn’t rather do it with anyone else.”
The Falcons had good looks, especially early. Briella Boudreau hit the post shortly after Watson’s goal, and Nokomis goalie Anna Russell made a good kick save on an Ava Emmons shot late in the second.
“No one thought we were going to get past that regional (final vs. Yarmouth),” Falcons coach Marcia Wood said. “We felt zero pressure. … We’re here, and no one expected it. That’s what I said to them. You’re one of the last teams playing, and no one expected you to be doing that.”

title: UNE football beats Curry for 4th straight win
text:
Nathan Delgado, Damien Jones and Javen Willis combined for 429 rushing yards and five touchdowns, and the University of New England extended its winning streak to four games as it rolled to a 42-7 victory over Curry in a Conference of New England football game Saturday in Biddeford.
A week after setting a school record with 511 yards on the ground, UNE (4-5, 4-2 CNE) finished with 473 rushing yards against the Colonels (4-5, 3-3).
Delgado gained 176 yards on 17 carries, including a 44-yard touchdown run. Jones had 17 carries for 138 yards and three TDs, and Willis recorded 115 yards and a touchdown on just seven carries.
Quarterback Gabe Martin added 48 yards rushing and threw a 58-yard touchdown pass to Dante Howard.
HUSSON 42, NICHOLS 14: Brett Davis rushed for 159 yards and two touchdowns and also caught a scoring pass as the Eagles (4-5, 4-2 CNE) rolled to a win over the Bison (2-7, 2-4) in Bangor.
Daniel Ruiz Cantu added 60 yards rushing and scored a touchdown, while Anthony Santacroce rushed 12 times for 69 yards. Brody Gibson threw a pair of touchdown passes.
WESTERN NEW ENGLAND 70, MAINE MARITIME 7: Cody Jackson completed 7 of 8 passes for 123 yards and three touchdowns, and the Golden Bears (5-4, 4-2 CNE) easily beat the Mariners (0-9, 0-6) in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Marcus Crawford rushed for 125 yards and two touchdowns for Western New England. Christian Delgado had a rushing and a receiving touchdown.

title: Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
text:
US Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside disputed ballots
The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified.
The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.
The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.
The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with multiple immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump's direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state's Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones."
"The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary," the motion said.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after election day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized.
Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to "safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election."
"We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later," he said outside of court the week before the election.
California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections.
The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

title: Human remains found inside burning car at neighborhood park
text:
PRINCE GEORGE’S COUNTY, Md. (WJLA) — An investigation is underway after human remains were found inside a burning vehicle at Whitfield Chapel Park in Prince George’s County on Thursday night.
Maryland-National Capital Park Police said someone passing the park a little before 10:30 p.m. saw flames. The Prince George’s County Fire Department said it put out the fire. Firefighters then found human remains inside the burned vehicle, according to the department.
Investigation
Prince George’s County police were leading the investigation. Homicide detectives were working with fire investigators on the case.
It remained unclear whether the death was a homicide or a suicide. Police have not released the name or gender of the victim.
Residents react
Maya Wilson, an Upper Marlboro resident, said she was walking in the park Friday with another woman.
“That is crazy that that happened one hundred feet away from us right now,” Wilson said.
Wilson and the other woman said it is nerve-wracking not knowing what led to the incident.
Janiya Prescott, a nearby resident, said she has been coming to the park since she was a child.
“I’ve been here since I was a kid, so it’s like, do I want to come here again?” Prescott said.
Nearby residents described the community and the park as normally quiet.
“A lot of people come here; they play kickball, they play baseball,” Prescott said.
“It’s always been pleasant out here. No problems at all,” said Jerry Blue, a nearby resident.

Gov. Mills promises seamless transition of power as Gov.-Elect Pingree prepares to take the reins
Just days after Hannah Pingree was elected to be the next governor of Maine, her former boss, Gov. Janet Mills, directed her team to work with Pingree's.
In two months, Hannah Pingree will be sworn in as Maine's 76th chief executive. In a press conference on Friday, Gov. Janet Mills invited Pingree and her team into the cabinet room for a press conference to promise a seamless transition of power.
"I formally directed every executive branch, department and agency to fully support the governor-elect and her transition team as they prepare to assume office," Mills said.
Mills and Pingree were first elected to the legislature the same year, in 2002, along with U.S. Senator-Elect Troy Jackson.
Pingree remained in the legislature, rising to Speaker of the House, while Mills was elected by the Legislature to be Attorney General and Jackson went over to the Maine Senate.
Pingree was the Director of the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future in the Mills Administration. Now, it's Pingree's turn to lead the state.
"I want to be clear. I am focused on building the best possible team to lead state government," Pingree said.
Pingree was asked about some of her first tasks when sworn in like presenting a state budget and who she will nominate for cabinet positions.
On the budget, which is facing a $1.3 billion shortfall, Pingree says the state needs to make up the funding that it will lose due to cuts to Medicare at the federal level.
"I am hopeful, whether it's in the lame duck or the new Congress, that they come to their senses and realize just how devastating this will be for health care for people all across the country," Pingree said. "But no matter what, we have to plan for where we'll be in January. And that does mean planning for these cuts. And I know the governor has been working on that as well."
She added that she will be accepting resumes and interviewing cabinet members, including those who are currently working in the Mills Administration and outside candidates.
Not only is the Blaine House remaining blue for the next four years, but both chambers of the legislature are remaining blue, and Democrats picked up seats in both chambers.

title: French Immersion Weekend brings language and culture to life in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - From novice to native speakers, Augusta was the place to be this weekend for anyone looking to practice their French.
From Friday to Saturday, the University of Maine at Augusta campus hosted about 80 people for French Immersion Weekend.
“This is an event that’s going on in Maine for 30 years,” explained Chelsea Ray, a French and humanities professor at UMA. “We invite high school, college, university, students, community members, heritage speakers, like Franco-American speakers, and native speakers, as well as French teachers. So it’s, I think, one of the most diverse campus activities in the country.”
Organized by the university and the Maine chapter of the American Association of Teachers of French, the weekend featured volunteer-led workshops on French literature, language and culture, even offering a taste of French-inspired foods like Congolese beignets.
The weekend encouraged participants to speak only in French, with activities ranging from beginner to advanced levels.
“I learned from immersion that it means more if you’re actually there doing the thing, meeting people. It’s not the textbooks, not the grammar anymore. It’s like, I’m doing this because I’m learning a different way to think, a different way to live, different values, and you really, you immerse yourself not only in the language but the culture,” Ray described.
Louis Fontaine, a second-year volunteer who gave a presentation on Franco-American history, said the weekend has helped him brush up on his native language.
“I actually grew up speaking French here in Augusta. It was my first language. I didn’t speak English until I started school. And then gradually through my teenage years and adult years, I didn’t speak as much, so I lost. And so now, after retirement, I’ve been trying to regain it,” Fontaine detailed. “I think it’s very important as far as strengthening the heritage of Maine people.”
Ray said Maine is the only state in New England seeing a growing number of French speakers, as new and native Mainers have French roots.
“In Maine, we’re very fortunate because we have three French-speaking groups of French heritage between the Acadians and the Franco-Americans, descendants of Quebec people, and then now we have a lot of the African people from French-speaking countries in Africa. All those groups are represented today,” said Nathalie Gorey, president of the Maine chapter of the American Association of Teachers of French.
From African dance performances to French exchange students discussing the ongoing protests in Paris, Ray described the event as a merging of French cultures from around the world.
“It’s all about building community and what’s more integrated in language and being human as seeing each other, speaking to each other,” Ray said. “We’re just kind of creating that sort of cultural feel that’s a little intangible, but for us it becomes very real.”
French Immersion Weekend cost $90 a day for students and $120 a day for community members. Scholarships are also available each year.

title: Navy sailor surprises niece at school after returning from monthslong deployment
text:
Navy sailor surprises niece at school after returning from monthslong deployment
A Manchester, N.H., girl recently got a surprise she won't soon forget.
Navy sailor Cameron Bishop, 22, made a last-minute detour Wednesday to Parker Varney Elementary School after returning from an 11-month overseas deployment to see his niece, Meadow.
"I asked the principal or the front office, and they were like, 'Yeah, you can do it,'" Bishop said. "I was like, 'Sweet.'"
The school helped keep the surprise a secret before he walked in wearing his uniform. A video shows Meadow jumping into her uncle's arms.
"It was honestly awesome, to be honest. It felt really good," he said. "I haven't seen my family in so long, so it feels great to connect with my family again."
"It's one of those things you can't not be moved by," Principal Andrew Sims said.
Bishop served on the USS Abraham Lincoln, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier that spent nearly 11 months operating across the Pacific and Middle East.
"Sometimes it doesn't feel real, because you were deployed for so long, but it's great to be back, to be honest," he said.
Meadow got more time to hang out with her Uncle Cam on Thursday, making up for months apart.
"He scared me," Meadow said.
Bishop will be home for 21 days before he heads back.

title: Yarmouth boys soccer beats John Bapst again in Class B final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BANGOR — There was plenty of space for the Yarmouth boys soccer team to operate throughout a rainy Class B state championship game.
It was only a matter of time before the Clippers would score, and one section of the net in particular became a frequent target.
Yarmouth put three goals into the bottom-left corner Saturday to claim a 3-0 victory over John Bapst at Cameron Stadium. The win marked the 10th state title in the last 12 seasons for the Clippers, who now boast a state-record 18 overall, including one in Class C.
It was also Yarmouth’s third victory over John Bapst in the state championship game since 2022.
“We always emphasize, ‘Finish low and hard because that’s the hardest ball to get to,’” said Yarmouth coach Justin Morrill. “We have great creativity up top to just feint those runs, run over balls and allow space to open up, and it’s really nice to see our kids focusing on finding a spot instead of just hammering it.”
Senior midfielder Lucas Hayner scored the first two goals in a brilliant display. Cael Woelflein added the third goal and the Clippers dominated possession, producing 10 shots on goal to John Bapst’s one.
“We’ve been working on finishing a lot this week in practice,” Woelflein said. “It feels really good, especially my senior season. It feels good to have our last game be a win, especially in this weather and on this stage.”
After a decent spell of play from John Bapst (16-1-1) in the first couple of minutes, Yarmouth (16-1-1) took control. The Clippers forced a tough save out of Crusaders goalkeeper Bode Phillips less than four minutes in, after which Hayner sent two shots just wide of the net.
With 15:27 left in the first half, Hayner found the breakthrough. The senior midfielder received a pass in the middle of the box, and slotted a shot past Phillips.
Yarmouth came close three more times in the first half and also nearly scored in the opening minute of the second. Four minutes later, the Clippers got their second goal, as Hayner again collected the ball in the box and scored from a tight angle.
“Slotting it was a big thing we’ve been talking about and focusing on the whole season, and (we) did it today,” said Hayner, who finished his senior season with 20 goals and 19 assists. “All props to my teammates for setting me up and putting me into the positions I was able to get in. All I had to really do was shoot.”
Yarmouth kept pushing, forcing Phillips into two more nice saves. Then, with 14:48 left, Woelflein removed any doubt over the result, connecting from slightly further out toward the edge of the box.
Besides scoring twice, Hayner was the midfield maestro for everything Yarmouth did. His ball control helped the Clippers dominate possession, and his runs and passing helped his team produce countless scoring opportunities.
“I’m probably a little biased, but even though there’s probably more kids who have scored more goals, I’d like to find a kid who’s had a more collective season,” Morrill said when asked if Hayner was the state’s best player. “That, singlehandedly, is a huge accomplishment for him.”
The win was the performance Yarmouth craved after eeking out a victory on penalty kicks in the Class B South final against a Cape Elizabeth team it had beaten 4-1 and 4-0 in the regular season. Morrill said his team produced two of its best practices of the season in preparation for the state final.
“We needed to get our focus back and get back to playing the way we want to play,” Morrill said. We wanted to make life difficult for them and control the run of play on the field, and I thought we did a really, really good job of that today.”

title: Mississippi, Alaska Senate races still too close to call post-midterms
text:
Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still too close to call post-midterms
Several races in the 2026 midterms that have yet to be called could potentially further Democrats' critical majorities in Congress.
Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still too close to call post-midterms
Several races in the 2026 midterms that have yet to be called could potentially further Democrats' critical majorities in Congress.
Days after Democrats achieved historic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, two Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain too close to call, with thousands of votes still to be counted — a stunning twist for two states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Dan Sullivan by over 600 votes, with thousands of ballots uncounted.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,500 votes. Election officials estimate that approximately 30,000 votes remain outstanding, though that number could change due to Mississippi's decentralized vote-counting process. Counties in the state are not required to report their certified results until 10 days after the election, meaning official results may not be available until late next week.
Both campaigns in Mississippi are preparing for a potentially lengthy process.
"We are not backing down. This election is not over," a social media post from Hyde-Smith read. "Our team is working across Mississippi to monitor the remaining ballots and protect the integrity of the process. We will see this through to the very end."
Colom said he is also preparing for a potential legal battle.
"It's not about her, it's not about the Republican Party. It's about the people of Mississippi. It's clear they've chosen to go into a new direction. If they want to litigate, we got an army of lawyers ready to protect the process, protect the integrity of the decision the voters made on Nov. 3," Colom said in an interview. "If she thinks that she has a path to victory, she needs to get in front of a television and explain how she has a path to victory."
