title: Missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and US
text:
Missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."
Zelenskyy slams Russian attacks ahead of trilateral negotiations
In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by "launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine's critical infrastructure."
The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight. The barrage also involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.
"When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone," Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.
It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Death toll rises to 55 after the strike on aid center in Komyshuvakha
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills 1 person
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouses and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.
Dmytro Zhyhinas and Dan Bashakov in Kyiv, Ukraine, Vasilisa Stepanenko in Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, and Katie Marie Davies in Manchester, England, contributed to this report.

title: Uplifting sign at Red Barn in Augusta leads to misconception over political message
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Trever Benedict, co-owner of The Red Barn in Augusta, came in to work Wednesday, the first thing he did was place a new roadside sign in front of his business. He switches the sign to display a new uplifting message every couple of weeks, he said, and this change was overdue.
This sign, reading “Sorry to spoil the ending for you, but everything is gonna end up okay,” was especially meaningful to Benedict because his dad has suffered two strokes this year as his mother’s health also declines. He thought of them as he put it up, he added, thinking nothing else was out of the ordinary.
But when he posted a picture of the sign on Facebook, it was met with hundreds of angry comments, direct messages and later some phone calls from people who thought he was celebrating the overwhelming victory of Democrats in Maine and across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Some people said they would boycott The Red Barn, according to Benedict.
“Naturally it was taken entirely out of context, and it basically created this uproar that we’re in the midst of now,” Benedict said Saturday morning. “For it to come back as this backlash, name-calling from the community, it’s really disheartening, it’s infuriating, and it’s ridiculous, frankly.”
Benedict posted an update on Facebook Thursday that clarified the intent behind the sign, but turned the comments off to avoid negativity. He said people continued to message him directly.
The Red Barn has stirred some controversy in the past under previous owner Laura Benedict, Trever Benedict’s aunt. Laura lashed out at Augusta city officials in 2017 after mistakenly believing that she had been fined for not having a mass gathering permit for a fundraising event, and she publicly removed an employee from the restaurant’s work schedule after he made racists remarks on Instagram.
Trever Benedict said there has never been anything political about the signs the restaurant posts, and that people sometimes stop in just to thank them for how the message improved their day.
“I hope that people can just strive to see the good and not scrutinize everything to the point where they look so hard to find the negative in everything,” Benedict said. “We have never been more divided than we are right now, and this whole example of this sign is exhibit A.”

text:
1 killed, 22 injured after elderly driver suspected to be impaired strikes cyclists
At least one person is dead and 22 others were injured when an elderly driver struck a group of cyclists in Wake County, North Carolina, shortly after 9:30 a.m. Saturday, according to authorities. The vehicle crossed the center line before traveling away from the scene and running off the roadway, colliding with a ditch, the North Carolina State Highway Patrol said.
Seven people were taken to trauma centers, and 15 others were sent to local hospitals with injuries, Chief LeRoy Smith of the Holly Springs Fire Department told CNN.
The driver was identified by the highway patrol as Donald Robert Morris-Jones, 76, of Apex, North Carolina. He is currently in custody, the agency said.
Related video above: Family of cyclist Louisa Gag presses Boston to act on traffic deaths
Morris-Jones faces multiple charges, including eight counts of hit-and-run causing serious injury or death, one count of serious injury by vehicle and one count of driving while impaired, according to Wake County records. He’s set to appear in court on Monday afternoon, court records show.
CNN is working to determine whether he has legal representation.
The State Highway Patrol identified the person who died as Patrick Allen Turner, 63, of Cary, North Carolina.
Video following the collision appears to show it took place in a wooded area on a winding, two-lane road flanked by trees. Law enforcement could be seen inspecting a stack of bikes propped up against a guardrail as some cyclists remained at the scene, one walking around with a phone to his ear, still wearing his helmet.
The crash occurred about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.

title: Camden Hills girls soccer tops Scarborough in overtime to win Class A title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
KENNEBUNK — The Camden Hills girls soccer team had not been seriously challenged all season.
That changed Saturday in the Class A championship game against Scarborough, which went to double overtime. That’s when Molly Williams scored her school-record 51st goal of the season to give the Windjammers a 1-0 victory.
“It feels so good. This was our goal coming into the season,” Williams said. “It’s been my goal since freshman year, and we finally did it.”
Camden Hills finishes 18-0. Coach Meredith Messer is now 5-0 in state championship games, having directed the Windjammers to four straight Class A titles from 2016-19.
Williams set the school record for goals with her 50th (and fourth of the game) in a 5-1 win against Mt. Ararat in the North final. The previous record of 49 goals was set in 2019 by then-senior Kristina Kelly, the 2019 national player of the year.
Scarborough (16-1-1) suffered its first loss of the season and lost in the championship game for the third year in a row. While Camden Hills had outscored its opponents by a whopping margin of 127-4, Scarborough had battled against tougher competition in Class A South. The Red Storm reached the state final with a 46-8 scoring margin and seven one-goal wins, including a 2-1 overtime decision in the regional semifinals against South Portland.
Camden Hills was the aggressor throughout the first overtime, sparked by sophomore midfielder Liv Domareki, who frequently won contested balls and pushed forward while imploring her teammates to keep up the pace. Eve Domareki nearly got her toe on a well-placed Williams cross. A few minutes later, Williams fired a tight-angle shot that was deflected wide by Scarborough keeper Vera DiSotto (three saves).
“I think these girls all year long wanted to have this accomplishment, to be able to say, ‘On any given day, we can go out and compete,'” Messer said. “We practice against ourselves, so in a lot of ways, our defense has to defend our offense and we get a lot of good practice.”
Throughout the contest, Camden Hills looked to either thread passes to Williams, or she would come back to her midfielders to receive a pass and try to turn. The Scarborough defense was intent on stopping her. Center backs Josie Duncan and Wren Bodah often double-teamed Williams, and midfielder Jill Morris marked her all over the field for long stretches in the second half.
But with two minutes gone in the second overtime, Thea Laukka — one of just two seniors for Camden Hills — heard Williams call for the ball.
“She made that run and I could hear her, she was communicating,” Laukka said. “We’ve gone over that many times on plays like that this season, and we connected and it worked out.”
Laukka got the ball to Williams, and DiSotto had to come off her mark. Williams, who has committed to play at Boston College, showed why she’s a premier scorer, sliding the ball past DiSotta’s lunge and then taking her time to set herself and hit a clean right-footed shot into the goal.

title: Amtrak to allow more guns on eligible trains
text:
(CNN) - Amtrak will soon allow more passengers to bring unloaded guns aboard some of its trains.
According to Amtrak, the guns must be carried in a lockbox, and an Amtrak agent would then add an additional lock to it.
The locks will be removed once the passenger arrives at their final destination.
Amtrak said passengers must be at least 18 years old and declare the weapon and ammunition before the trip.
The new policy goes into effect in January and will apply to certain trains, including those in the Northeast Corridor.

title: Foxcroft Academy field hockey wins 2nd straight Class C title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — The Foxcroft Academy field hockey team was leading everywhere. The Ponies were controlling play. They were ahead in corners. They were ahead in shots.
They were ahead everywhere — but the scoreboard. However, as it went into halftime of a scoreless tie, the second-highest scoring team in Maine history figured the goals were coming.
“We knew we were dominating,” sophomore Addie Rayfield said. “(The talk) was, keep shooting, quick shots. They’ll go in at some point.”
Rayfield scored a pair of goals, both assisted by senior Jenna Hartford, and Foxcroft Academy capped another undefeated season with a 2-0 win over Winthrop/Maranacook in the Class C championship game Saturday night at Edward Little High School.
“To be able to do it last year, but also do it again, undefeated as well, is just an even better feeling,” Rayfield said.
The feeling was better, but so were the Ponies (18-0). Foxcroft outscored teams 144-8 this year, and with two goals Saturday passed the 2017 St. Dominic Academy team (143) for second most in state history. Only the 2012 Skowhegan team (155) scored more.
“It’s very special,” Hartford said. “We aimed to try to beat the state record. We got very close.”
Foxcroft had seven corners in the first half and came within feet of getting goals from Kaydiense Nelson and Rayfield, but the Ponies hadn’t broken through on the scoreboard against the Ramblers (16-2). In the second half, that changed.
On the Ponies’ 10th corner, Hartford had a shot that goalie Cyara Harriman saved, but the rebound went to Rayfield and she buried the follow-up with 2:18 to go in the third.
The two players teamed up for the next goal as well. Hartford found Rayfield with a pass through the circle, and the sophomore skipped in a reverse for a 2-0 lead with 9:07 to play.
“We definitely were very nervous, but it wasn’t like a, ‘Oh, are we going to lose?’ (feeling),” Hartford said. “We were just like, ‘We need to up the intensity. We need to keep trying.'”
The two-goal lead was a commanding advantage, as Foxcroft shut down nearly every Winthrop effort to get into its offense. Lilah French and Payson Hall attacked the ball in the infield, and the Ramblers were unable to register a shot on goal.
Rayfield said the Ponies made it a priority to shut down Winthrop’s outlet passes.
“We knew that we had to give it all we got, especially because it’s the last one,” Rayfield said.
Winthrop spent most of the game on defense, but thanks to their backs and Harriman in net, the Ramblers kept it close.
“I can’t say enough about how well we played defensively tonight. We were challenged, just like we knew we would,” Winthrop coach Holly Daigle said. “I am proud of my girls for the effort they gave for the full 60 minutes.”
In her first year after coaching at Cony, Daigle brought the Ramblers back to the state final after they missed it last year following four straight titles.
“We had an extraordinary season,” she said. “I just really wanted it for them. I really did. They deserve to be here.”

title: Judge wants former US attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation’s capital during President Donald Trump’s first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.
Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.
The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events.” An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.
Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government’s conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.
As the city’s chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job.
Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP.
David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial’s participants “can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.”
Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.”
Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on.
The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real.

title: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The overwhelming victory by the Democrats in the midterm elections shook up Wall Street this week.
The biggest tremors were felt in shares of companies tied to the boom in artificial intelligence on concerns that a Democratic Congress will put the brakes on further development of data centers.
Defense and oil companies fell on expectations Democrats would push for an end to the U.S.-Iran war, which would likely lower energy prices.
Meanwhile, hospital shares rose on the possibility that funding for several government programs could be restored or boosted, while liquor companies and others buffeted by tariffs rose on hopes for relief.
Here’s a look at how certain stocks and industries reacted to the result of the midterms.
AI stocks
The frantic construction of data centers to power the AI boom has meant big profits for a wide array of companies — chip makers, power providers, cooling system producers, cloud computing companies and more. Investors hungry for a piece of those profits dove in, pushing some stocks up by double or more. But concerns grew that AI stocks got too pricey. And then the Democrats swept the midterms to take control of Congress.
Nvidia, Lam Research and others tied to the AI boom swung wildly this week on worries that Democratic victories in statehouses across the country could mean a slowdown in further construction, particularly in Texas. Hyperscalers, or those funding the buildout, like Amazon, fared better.
Defense
Defense companies have been volatile throughout the year, rising and falling with the shifts in the U.S. war with Iran. Hopes for an end to the war increased following the Democrats’ sweep in the midterms. An end to the war could mean slimmer business for several big defense companies, though the war has also depleted stockpiles of weapons, which could result in demand for resupplies by the U.S. government.
Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, RTX and General Dynamics fell between 4% and 12% after Tuesday.
Oil and gas
Oil exploration and refining companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the U.S. war with Iran, which has stifled global supplies since February and raised the price of crude oil and gasoline. Several big energy companies lost ground following the midterms because an end to the war would lower oil prices and reduce the companies’ profits.
Companies such as Exxon Mobil and Phillips 66 are still showing solid year-to-date gains.
Elon Musk’s companies
Elon Musk spent more than $445 million in an attempt to help Republicans maintain control of Congress. Not only was his return on investment not very good, but shares of his two publicly traded companies took a drubbing on concerns a Democratic Congress will investigate Musk’s work as Trump’s cost-cutting chief in 2025. SpaceX, which houses Musk’s xAI business, and Tesla, with plans for a fleet of mostly autonomous vehicles, fell 5% and 10.1%, respectively, after the midterms.
Trump Media
The president’s social media company, Trump Media & Technology, lost 33% of its market value in the three days after the election. Trump’s stake in the company was worth nearly $5 billion in March 2025. Now, it’s worth less than $600 million. The company is hoping to improve its fortunes by merging with the nuclear fusion company TAE Technologies. Completion of the deal is pending.
Power companies
Companies focusing on wind, solar and other forms of renewable energy could see sunnier days ahead with a more industry-friendly Congress. Democrats will have overwhelming influence on funding when they take control of Congress in January, raising hopes for a wide range of green energy companies.
Those companies involved in powering the data centers at the hub of the AI buildout didn’t fare as well, however, after a number of data center skeptics got elected to Congress or governorships.
Hospitals
Hospitals gained ground over hopes that funding for several government programs could be restored or boosted, including Medicaid and subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. Medicaid spending was reduced under Trump. Enhanced tax credits for the ACA were allowed to expire without being renewed, resulting in a decline in enrollment for insurance coverage nationally. More funding for those programs would result in an eventual boost to healthcare providers, including hospitals.
HCA Healthcare rose 6.9%, Tenet Healthcare gained 6.2% and Universal Health Services added 10.4% after Tuesday.
Homebuilders and home improvement
The housing sector, including builders, continues to face pressure from historically high home prices and mortgage rates. The shift in power in Congress could mean a greater focus on policies that address affordability, which was a key theme for Democrats. Cutting tariffs and lowering energy costs could lower supply chain costs. That could also help home improvement retailers by relieving pressure on consumers.
Mortgage rates, though, are a trickier issue for the industry. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate again in an effort to cool inflation. That likely means that interest rates on many types of loans, including mortgages, will remain high.
D.R. Horton gained 4.9%, PulteGroup rose 4.4% and Home Depot added 2.9%.
Alcohol
Beer, wine and liquor companies could see relief from tariffs that have hurt sales both in the U.S. and globally with Democrats taking control of Congress. The hope is that they will take action to end the global tariff conflict that has raised prices. S&P 500 members Constellation Brands, which has U.S. import rights for Corona and Modelo beers, and Brown-Forman, which makes Jack Daniel’s and other liquors, both had gains.
Household goods
Makers and sellers of everyday consumer staples gained ground as investors moved out of riskier sectors. They were also helped by hopes that a shift in control of Congress could mean policies that help cool inflation. Eliminating or reducing tariffs could help lower costs for businesses. Ending the U.S. war with Iran could boost global oil supplies, which would lower oil prices and costs for shipping on everything from food to clothing.
After the election, Costco Wholesale added 3.4%, Procter & Gamble rose 2.1% and Dollar General rose 2.5%.

title: Alaska Senate race remains undecided days after Election Day
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Fewer than 700 votes separated the top two candidates in Alaska’s Senate race Friday with 74% of ballots counted. Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan by a slim margin, which had not changed in more than 24 hours.
As polls closed on Election Day and states began to turn blue or red, Mississippi and Alaska were the only two states left without a new senator.
As Americans keep an eye out for updates on the Last Frontier, Peltola reminded supporters that a long count is not new for Alaska.
“The results are not gonna be fast, but Alaskans are patient... It will be weeks. We know this. We know this. This is how it’s always been. This is normal. This is Alaska normal,” Peltola said.
Alaska has a ranked choice voting system, with ballots tallied in rounds. In a general election, a candidate must reach 50% or more of the vote to win.
If no candidate reaches 50% using first-place votes, officials take the last-place finisher and reallocate those ballots to voters’ second and third choices. That tabulation will not happen before Nov. 18.
Ballots also must be flown in or mailed from hard-to-reach areas of Alaska, meaning the process usually is lengthy, though this year is different.
Sullivan was not the only Dan on the ballot. Another Dan Sullivan was listed as a third-party option. The Justice Department and the FBI are now investigating.
“What’s the first order of business when [Peltola is] going to run for the Senate, to put together a secret scheme. To trick Alaskans to throw away their vote and rig the election,” Sullivan said.
The Trump administration sued to stop the election from being certified if Peltola wins. The administration claimed Democrats plotted to add the same-named candidate as a ploy to pull votes.

title: 76-foot Christmas tree arrives at Rockefeller Center
text:
76-foot Christmas tree arrives at Rockefeller Center
A 76-foot Norway spruce arrived at Rockefeller Center on Saturday, marking the start of the holiday season in New York City.
The tree was brought from West Edmeston, New York, and is about 75 years old.
It measures roughly 50 feet in diameter and weighs about 11 tons. Its arrival begins the process of preparing the centerpiece for the season.
The Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree tradition dates to 1931, when construction workers building the complex put up a small tree decorated with handmade garlands.
That first tree was a modest start to a tradition that would grow over the decades. The first formal Tree Lighting Ceremony followed in 1933.
Since then, the tree and its lighting ceremony have become fixtures of the holiday season in New York City.

title: Lawyer who represented defendant in Tupac Shakur murder case found dead
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) — The defense attorney who represented Duane “Keffe D” Davis in the Tupac Shakur murder trial has died.
Michael Sanft was reported dead Thursday night in Las Vegas. The Clark County coroner’s office confirmed the 55-year-old’s death.
The cause and manner of death remain pending. Details surrounding his death were limited, with the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department referring all inquiries to the coroner’s office.
Sanft was the lead trial attorney at SOS Injury Lawyers, where he tried more than 150 cases to jury verdict and argued before the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
According to his website, he moved to San Diego at 12 and later attended BYU-Hawaii.
Sanft represented Davis pro bono during his Las Vegas trial. A jury later found Davis guilty in August.
In an interview with FOX5, Sanft said he would not have done anything differently.
“We had the best team possible in this case, from the motion practice work on this appeal to our investigator to our firm here at SOS Injury. We all did our part. I don’t see what I could’ve done differently,” Sanft said.
After the verdict, Sanft also mentioned sitting down with Davis.
“We were just sitting there taking in the moment,” Sanft said. “He had reminded me this is phase one. Because I was upset with the verdict, I was very disappointed in the jury. Mr. Davis was the one who said, ‘Don’t worry about it, man, this is the first phase,’ and I said, ‘I understand; I hate to lose.’”
Attorney Mike Troiano said Sanft was an honest, humble and good human being.
“I’m in total shock by this news, as is the legal community as a whole. An extremely talented trial lawyer who jurors and his peers loved,” Troiano continued.
Davis’ defense team stated they had planned to appeal the conviction. A notice of the appeal was filed Oct. 30.

title: 2 skydivers die midair after their parachutes become entangled
text:
LAKE ELSINORE, Calif. (AP) — Two experienced skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in Southern California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.
The Riverside County Sheriff’s Office on Saturday identified the two who died as Georgia Jean, 56, of Box Elder, South Dakota, and Levi Pimentel, 29, of Aurora, Illinois.
Jean founded the company Circle Evolution, which “is the collaboration between conscious channel Georgia Jean and the non-physical collective The Circle of Light,” according to the company’s website. Jean said in a bio that she started skydiving in 2015 and had more than 1,700 jumps.
Pimentel was listed on LinkedIn as a lead instructor at iFLY Naperville, an indoor skydiving company.
The accident occurred at about noon Friday at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement, and both were licensed skydivers.
The Riverside County Fire Department said the two suffered traumatic injuries and were taken to a local hospital in critical condition.
Skydive Elsinore said the free fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet (about 46 meters) above the ground.
“The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground,” Skydive Elsinore said in a statement. They were pronounced dead at the hospital.
The Federal Aviation Administration was notified, the sheriff’s office said. It will collect the skydivers’ parachutes and conduct an investigation.
The U.S. Parachute Association reports that in 2025, members made 3.47 million skydives and there were 16 fatalities. The organization said 5.6% of members reported suffering an injury that required medical treatment, with the most common being ankle injuries during landings.

title: Chimp sanctuary delivers an ape's food by drone amid Florida floods
text:
A Florida chimpanzee sanctuary had to deliver food to one of its 200 apes by drone this week because the property was swamped by heavy rain. But the animals stayed safe, and the water finally was receding significantly on Saturday, the organization said.
As rainstorms soaked southeast and central Florida from Sunday through Tuesday, Save the Chimps’ care houses were secure on high ground, CEO Ana Paula Tavares said in a statement. Some veterinarians and other employees stayed overnight on the 150-acre (61-hectare) property near Fort Pierce to ensure the animals’ care.
Canals overflowed and submerged the internal roads that normally are used to deliver 3,000 pounds (1,361 kilograms) of chimp food per day via golf carts, facilities director Mark Yohannan said by phone. A high-clearance swamp buggy helped but soon broke down. And one chimp, a 38-year-old named Kaleb, had remained in an outdoor area that was cut off by water.
The organization bought a delivery drone some time ago for just such an emergency, Yohannan said. Staffers used the device to bring Kaleb food and blankets until he decided on his own to head for somewhere more accessible.
Save the Chimps captured video of Kaleb munching a banana he plucked from a drone-dropped paper bag, and later steadily picking his way across a rope that bridged some standing water.
The organization used trucks, including a maintenance worker’s personal vehicle, and a tractor to deliver meals, medicine and other items to the rest of the apes.
“Chimps are getting all their food, bananas and oranges on time,” Yohannan said. “They’re good. They haven’t missed a beat.”
Nor have the local alligators. A small one turned up by the sanctuary’s kitchen Friday, apparently using the floodwaters to reach terrain where the reptiles don’t usually tread, Yohannan said.
The water level dropped noticeably overnight Friday, and about 20% of the property’s roads were clear Saturday, Yohannan said.
Widespread flooding in the area has made it difficult for employees to get to work to relieve their colleagues. But “everyone’s in excellent spirits, tired as they are,” he said.
The organization is appealing to the public for help fixing damaged buildings and equipment, and one donor has agreed to match such contributions.
Save the Chimps was founded in 1997. To date, it has cared for nearly 350 chimps from research laboratories, the pet trade and the entertainment industry.

title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it’s a cause for joy
text:
It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn’t be happier.
Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston said this week that after analyzing photos and data about right whales, they have determined it was a calf likely born months ago that went unseen during winter surveys for the giant animals.
The discovery puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said. The whales number only about 380 in the world, and their population has fallen since 2010.
The whale was seen with its mother, a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt, scientists said. Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed.
The whales are extensively cataloged with photography by researchers because they are so rare. It’s also rare for the researchers who study the whales to miss a baby, but the discovery was a welcome surprise, said Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center.
“Silt was briefly seen in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, so it’s possible she had the calf there but snuck away before they were documented together. This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” Warren said.
Baby right whale births are closely tracked by scientists because the tiny population needs successful calving years to remain viable. There are only about 70 reproductive-age females left in the population, and scientists have said the whales have reached 20 calves in a season only a few times since 2010.
That was when their numbers started falling, as they lost about 25% between 2010 and 2020. The whales are vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear, and the warming of the ocean has heightened those threats because they have strayed from protected areas, scientists have said. They also suffered a disastrous year in 2018 when no babies were born.
Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, as the whales have gained back some of their population since 2020. But conservationists have decried recent moves by the U.S. government to delay new protections for the whales for a decade in favor of commercial fishing interests.
The baby whale sighted off Quebec was spotted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a nonprofit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region. The whale wasn’t seen by researchers despite boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast all spring and summer, the New England Aquarium said.
Scientists are celebrating the animal’s addition to a successful breeding season for the rare whales, said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.
“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” he said.

title: Congress enters lame duck session following midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Congress has a list of unfinished work during the lame duck session, the period between the election of a new Congress and the start of its term, including a Dec. 11 government funding deadline.
The session follows the 2026 midterm elections, which came to a head on Election Day, Nov. 3.
Top of the agenda: the stopgap funding bill passed earlier this year to keep the government open through Election Day, which expires Dec. 11. A government shutdown is possible before the holidays if lawmakers cannot agree on a spending package.
The agenda also includes the remaining fiscal year 2027 spending bills, the National Defense Authorization Act and the Farm Bill. Both stalled ahead of the midterms.
In the final weeks of the year, Republican leaders will also attempt to carry out President Donald Trump’s top directives before the majority of both chambers flips. Democrats are unlikely to cooperate knowing they will be in charge in 2027, which gives them an edge in negotiations.
During the session, both parties are expected to start planning for the 120th Congress, including new policy pushes and messaging following the midterm elections.
Meanwhile, Trump is threatening to veto anything that does not fit his agenda.
The 120th Congress will be seated in the first few days of January 2027. Current lawmakers will return to the Hill Nov. 9.

title: ‘Remarkable’: Drunk raccoon leads to $250,000 for animal control
text:
HANOVER, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - Nearly a year after a drunk raccoon was captured in a Virginia ABC store, a campaign tied to the animal has raised $250,000 for Hanover County Animal Control.
Donations from the “Trashed Panda” campaign will cover more than half the cost of a new tool for officers to document animal cruelty investigations.
The tool consists of body cameras for animal protection officers. The money is going back into the shelter and its officers, said Jeffrey Parker, chief of animal protection for Hanover County.
The shelter has raised the money by selling shirts tied to the raccoon’s capture. Parker said the campaign has generated approximately $280,000 since it started a year ago.
His first reaction to the amount raised was shock and then gratitude, because the money is going back into helping the animals at the shelter.
“It was just remarkable the amount of feedback that came with it. I think a lot of people can relate to it as well. But it has just been remarkable,” Parker said.
Parker said the department has considered getting body cameras for some years, “but we never really pulled the plug,” Parker said.
Last year, Parker said the department started getting the data it needed to seek funding.
“This raccoon just helped us a little bit faster,” he said.
Parker said he had planned to present the cameras to the county as a budget request but saw the money generated from the campaign as a way to save taxpayer dollars.
Parker said the cameras are for officer safety, transparency and court documentation.
“We could use cameras every day. I think it provides valuable information and evidence for us. We utilize our sheriff’s office for body cams when we need body cam footage on scene ... So now we can do that on our own,” Parker said.
Parker said the cameras will also help him resolve complaints about staff members and keep reports more accurate. “That way we don’t possibly discipline good officers,” he said.
The “Trashed Panda” funding will pay for all of the equipment and this year’s service. Parker said service for years two through five will come from the county’s budget.
Parker said right now his officers will train over the next couple of months to prepare for the body cameras, with the initial start date for officers to wear the cameras on Jan. 4, 2027.
The shelter is using the money for new housing for animals, toys, a temperature-controlled food shed and a community and pet pantry.
Parker said the money will be shared between field operations and shelter operations. The department is gathering more projects for the remaining funds.
“Our goal is to use all the money for the animals in the department,” Parker said.
And if you’re wondering where the infamous raccoon is now?
“No telling where he’s at. Hopefully he’s living a good life, not doing any kind of more breaking and entering businesses and all that, and living a good life, we hope,” Parker said. “A sober one.”

title: Amtrak to allow more guns on eligible trains
text:
(CNN) - Amtrak will soon allow more passengers to bring unloaded guns aboard some of its trains.
According to Amtrak, the guns must be carried in a lockbox, and an Amtrak agent would then add an additional lock to it.
The locks will be removed once the passenger arrives at their final destination.
Amtrak said passengers must be at least 18 years old and declare the weapon and ammunition before the trip.
The new policy goes into effect in January and will apply to certain trains, including those in the Northeast Corridor.

title: Woman sentenced to life in prison for murder of her 5-week-old daughter
text:
MIDLAND, Texas (KOSA/Gray News) - A woman in Texas has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the death of her 5-week-old daughter.
A jury convicted 24-year-old Sarah Michelle Gilley-Wroe on one count of capital murder of a child under 10 years old.
The infant died May 11, 2022, at Midland Memorial Hospital from severe head trauma.
Investigators said medical evidence showed the girl had two fractures in the back of her skull, and the injuries were consistent with blunt force trauma.
Detectives searched Gilley-Wroe’s phone and found incriminating Google searches. Gilley-Wroe also made incriminating statements while in custody, authorities said.
According to authorities, the 24-year-old told a cellmate that she threw the baby against the wall and struck the girl until she stopped crying.
Gilley-Wroe was the only person alone with the child during the time in which the reported crimes could have occurred.
Medical experts equated the amount of force required to cause the injury to the force of a fall from a two-story building. Gilley-Wroe claimed the injuries could have been caused by her aunt, the baby’s father, or her dog.

title: Mother sentenced to life in prison for murdering 4-year-old, abandoning 1-year-old on interstate
text:
LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC/Gray News) - A mother in Louisiana was sentenced to life in prison for killing her 4-year-old child and abandoning her baby near an interstate.
Aaliyah Jack, 28, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for killing her son, Legend, and 15 years for cruelty to juveniles for abandoning her 1-year-old child, Kingtrail.
Legend had been living with his paternal grandmother, Dion Polk, since May 2024. Polk said she dropped him off with Jack’s mother on July 6, 2024, after which Jack ran off with him and Kingtrail.
Legend’s body was found in the water near an interstate welcome center two days later. A truck driver spotted Kingtrail crawling along I-10 just a few miles away the next morning.
Jack was arrested in Mississippi the same day Kingtrail was rescued. She was later charged with second-degree murder and cruelty to a juvenile.
When deputies brought Jack to the Calcasieu Correctional Center on July 20, she told a KPLC reporter that she had killed Legend and abandoned Kingtrail while “under the influence of drugs.”
A Calcasieu Parish jury convicted Jack of second-degree murder and child cruelty in September after seeing Legend’s autopsy photos and hearing from detectives and family members.
While the murder conviction came with a mandatory life sentence, a decision had to be made regarding the cruelty to juveniles charge.
Jack made a statement in court that was hard to follow and repeatedly said she did not know what to say.
During the sentencing, Jack did not apologize and instead talked about spending money for someone’s birthday. It was unclear who she was referring to.
Ultimately, the judge ruled that Jack had shown deliberate cruelty to both victims.
The prosecution says justice was served.
“I am always sorry for the families on both sides. Nobody wins here. I believe that justice was done. I believe that Ms. Jack is going to spend the rest of her life in prison, which is where she belongs, because of the nature of what she did,” first assistant district attorney Jacob Johnson said.

title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy is discharged from hospital after a stroke and goes to rehab facility
text:
Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy is discharged from hospital after a stroke and goes to rehab facility
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut said on Friday that he has been discharged from the hospital after suffering a stroke last weekend and will miss “several weeks” of votes in the Senate as he recovers in a rehabilitation facility.
Murphy, 53, said in a statement that doctors are “very encouraged by the progress I've made so far" and that the stay at the rehabilitation center will get him back to work on the quickest timeline possible.
Murphy said doctors diagnosed him with a small hemorrhagic stroke, which is a bleed in the brain. He said he called 911 on Oct. 31 out of an abundance of caution after feeling that “something was not right” with his body.
Related video above: Doctor explains recovery after Sen. Chris Murphy’s stroke
“This has been a scary experience for me and my family, and I appreciate the continued respect for our privacy,” he said.
The press release updating Murphy's condition included a statement from Dr. Jose Suarez, chief of neurosciences critical care at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. Suarez said the senator has shown tremendous progress and “we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation.”
In the Senate, Murphy serves on the Appropriations Committee and is a leading voice on immigration and gun policy. He is considered a contender for more senior leadership positions in the Senate and among the many Democrats seen as potential 2028 candidates for the White House.
Murphy said that he has been staying engaged with his team and colleagues remotely and that his staff continues to ensure the work of his office continues uninterrupted.
“I want to extend my deepest thanks to the excellent doctors and staff at Johns Hopkins who have treated me and cared for my family,” Murphy said.
Murphy had been traveling the country in support of House and Senate candidates as his party raced for majority control, which it secured in Tuesday’s midterm elections. A day before the stroke, he posted that he had been campaigning in his home state for Gov. Ned Lamont. The week before, he posted from Minnesota campaigning with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for the Senate.
Lamont won re-election Tuesday, and Flanagan won her race, becoming the first Native American female U.S. senator.
The final sprint before Election Day capped Murphy’s whirlwind trip to the Middle East at the start of October for meetings with several leaders, including Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. In early September, Murphy completed his annual “walk across Connecticut,” covering about 70 miles over four days, talking with residents about their concerns along the way.
Three other Senate Democrats have had strokes in recent years.
Sens. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland had strokes in 2022 and have since recovered. Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman had a stroke while campaigning for his seat that year and now uses adaptive technology in the Senate, including live captioning on a phone or tablet that transcribes words as people speak to him and helps him process the conversation.
Fetterman said on social media the day after Murphy's stroke that his family was “rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery.”

title: Memory card with uncounted ballots found, launching investigation
text:
SEMINOLE COUNTY, Ga. (WCTV/ANF/Gray News) — A memory card from election night has been discovered containing uncounted ballots from Seminole County, Georgia, voters.
According to a release from the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office, a post-election check revealed: “approximately 388 more voters recorded as having checked in at polling places on Election Day than the number of ballots reported as cast.”
The release detailed that the Secretary of State’s office caught the discrepancy and notified Seminole County’s Board of Elections.
This discovery may prove critical in the still-uncalled State House District 154 race, in which Democrat challenger Harry James led by 58 votes. With these new votes, incumbent Republican Gerald Greene has taken the lead by 262 votes. The Secretary of State’s office says the county has until Monday to certify its election results.
Brad Raffensperger’s office is investigating to find out “how the memory card was overlooked, whether required election procedures were followed, and what corrective measures are necessary to prevent similar incidents in future elections,” according to the release.
WCTV, Atlanta News First’s sister station in Tallahassee, has reached out to the Seminole County Board of Elections Friday afternoon for comment, but no one was available for comment.

title: Late goal gives Cape Elizabeth girls 2-1 win over John Bapst in B soccer final
text:
BANGOR – On a wet, slippery soccer field, it is never a bad idea to shoot from everywhere.
Cape Elizabeth junior midfielder Haisel McGeachey knew that when she stepped up to take a 35-yard free kick late in the second half of her team’s State Class B soccer championship game against John Bapst High of Bangor at Cameron Stadium on Saturday afternoon.
McGeachy’s well-struck free kick took one hop in front of John Bapst sophomore goalie Abby-May Turner and skipped by her into the short side corner with 14 minutes remaining to break a 1-1 tie and give the defending state champion Capers a hard-fought 2-1 victory.
It was their 11th state championship while the John Bapst girls were playing in their first ever state title game.
Both teams concluded the season with 16-1-1 records.
Sophomore phenom striker Naia Studley had staked the Crusaders to a 1-0 lead 10 minutes into the game with her 42nd goal of the season but sophomore midfielder Alexa Mallory equalized five minutes later with a long, perfectly-placed 28-yarder from the middle of the field.
“I was trying to put it on target and hoping it would slide in because it was very slick,” said McGeachey. “Honestly, I was really surprised when it went in.”
“They have a number of midfielders who can shoot the ball from distance,” said John Bapst third-year head coach Greg Bennett. “That one slipped by the ‘keeper. Unfortunately, things like that happen on days like today.”
Turner had come off her line to try to snare the ball.
“[McGeachy] is our free kick specialist,” said Cape Elizabeth coach Branden Noltkamper, who encouraged his players to shoot from everywhere due to the slick field conditions.
Turner finished with seven saves on 29 shot attempts while Cape Elizabeth goalkeeper Kelsie Law made two saves on eight Crusader attempts.
Studley opened the scoring 9:51 into the game when she used her impressive speed to slip behind the Caper defense and track down a perfect through ball from Ella Williams.
Law sprinted off her line to confront Studley but Studley calmly pushed the ball around the goalie and slotted a left-footed shot into the open net.
Mallory answered with her long shot over the outstretched hands of Turner.
“There was a girl in front of me and I shot it and it went in,” said Mallory.
“That was a very good shot,” said Bennett. “We gave her a little too much space.”
Studley, who gave the Cape Elizabeth back line plenty of angst throughout the game with her skill and explosiveness, nearly restored the lead late in the first half with another major burst, this time down the left channel in the penalty area. But she rolled her shot inches wide of the far post.
“She is one of the best players I’ve seen this year,” said Noltkamper. “I knew she would be a handful but not to that degree.”
“She has a very bright career,” he added.
Despite the disparity in shot attempts, the Crusaders, led by their back three of Reese Monnier, Elza Cahn and Khloe Grass, often succeeded at limiting Cape Elizabeth’s high-percentage chances.
“We did a very good job keeping the ball in front of us and keeping their shots at a distance. We didn’t have any shots from really close by,” said Bennett. “It’s something we’ve worked on.”
“Bapst did a great job, defensively. They are so difficult to break down centrally,” said Noltkamper. “They’re a great team.
“We made some adjustments at halftime and the girls did really well applying those and executing them. It was awesome to see,” said Holtkamper.
He used a number of different backs to try to contain Studley and influential midfielder Quinn Bennett, and he was pleased with their performances.
Azara Govind headlined the defense corps and she was joined by Alice DeGeorge, Phoebe Evans, Amelia Morgese, Eloise Hackett and Finley DiGiovanni.
John Bapst entered the game having scored 95 goals and conceded only 11 while Cape Elizabeth scored 77 goals and surrendered just six.

title: 'Bees are a mission': Beekeeping farm helps veterans find purpose after military service
text:
'Bees are a mission': Beekeeping farm helps veterans find purpose after military service
Veterans are swapping uniforms for bee suits at an Oklahoma farm, where a beekeeping program is helping them refocus after service.
'Bees are a mission': Beekeeping farm helps veterans find purpose after military service
Veterans are swapping uniforms for bee suits at an Oklahoma farm, where a beekeeping program is helping them refocus after service.
For many veterans, leaving the military can mean leaving behind a purpose, but a farm in Oklahoma is helping them find a new one — thanks to bees.
Veterans are trading their military uniforms for bee suits at Warriors to Bees as they learn how to become beekeepers, helping them find purpose after service.
"Most people say, 'That's crazy. Four thousand bees are coming out at you, how could that be peaceful or relaxing?'" said Steve Easom with Easom Farms. "Veterans are mission-oriented, and bees are a mission."
Veterans from across the country come to Easom Farms in Slaughterville, Oklahoma, where they stay for a free nine-month beekeeping program.
They first learn in a classroom before doing it for real.
"We use our land to work with veterans to help them refocus and gain a new purpose," Easom said.
After serving in the U.S. Air Force, Easom made it his mission to help fellow veterans find theirs.
"When you come out, there is a void, and if we don't work hard to figure out how to fill that void," Easom said, "there becomes challenges."
There is a bee therapy house on the farm, and inside, there are two beds with bees directly below them.
Veterans come to lie down and listen to the buzz.
"We have all the hives. Three hives on the right, three on the left, and these hives are mic'd so we can adjust the volume of the buzz," Easom said. "Usually, they will come for about a one-hour session and spend time listening to the frequency of the bees. If you Google research, there is some scientific medical research behind the actual frequency in helping people kind of refocus."
For Easom, success isn't measured in honey. It is measured in the lives touched.
"Since 2018, we have trained 556. This year, we will graduate another 60 through the program Warriors to Bees, and not one has committed suicide. We give all the glory to God, number one. Number two, to the bees, and we just get to be a part of it," Easom said.

title: Rounds of showers through midday Sunday
text:
Rounds of showers through midday Sunday
Rounds of showers through midday Sunday
Intermittent showers continue on Saturday, with the steadiest rain falling on the Midcoast and Downeast Maine, where an additional 1 to 3 inches is possible. Elsewhere, an additional 0.25 to 0.5 inches is possible by midday Sunday.
Some patchy fog is also possible Saturday, and temperatures fall gradually during the afternoon. Northerly winds around 10 mph could gust up to 25 mph.
Overnight, showery weather continues, and the higher summits will likely see a changeover to wet snow late night. Elsewhere, spotty showers continue Sunday morning.
Scattered showers wind down by midday Sunday and will likely end by mid-afternoon. Temperatures will top out in the 40s and low 50s, normal for early November. Clouds break up late in the afternoon, with gradual clearing expected Sunday evening.
On Monday, a few hit-or-miss showers are possible in the afternoon and evening, with highs in the 40s to mid-50s. Next week is generally cool and cloudy, with a cold snap likely by the end of the week.
Maine's Total Weather is watching a potential storm that could arrive next Friday or Saturday (November 13/14). With cold air in place, snow is a possibility, along with rain and gusty winds. If the storm trends farther south, Maine would miss out on the precipitation and get more cold air flowing in.

title: Cheverus field hockey captures 4th straight Class A championship
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUBURN — Once again, it was close. And once again, with a championship on the line, it went the Cheverus field hockey team’s way.
Avery Tinker and Sydney Brunelle scored first-half goals, and the Stags returned to the state summit with a 2-1 victory over fellow unbeaten Mt. Ararat in the Class A final at Edward Little High School.
Update the numbers. State title No. 4 in a row — and their fifth in six years — ups the Stags’ winning streak to 35 games and their unbeaten streak to 72, dating back to a loss to Skowhegan in the 2022 final.
“It’s so special. It’s so nice to go 4 for 4, and that is not due to just the seniors, just me. It’s due to the entire team,” said Brunelle, a Miss Maine Field Hockey finalist. “I’m just so grateful to be a part of this and end my career on the highest note possible.”
Mt. Ararat (17-1-0), making its first appearance in a state final, erased a 2-0 deficit against Skowhegan in the A North final, and the Eagles generated hope they could do it again when Krystah Coen’s goal early in the third quarter trimmed the deficit to one.
The Stags (18-0-0), however, didn’t let them get any closer, burying the Eagles with waves of pressure that resulted in 10 corners over the final 28 minutes. It was Cheverus’ seventh one-goal win of the season, and third one-goal win in a state final in four years.
“We had this as a goal, to play all 18 games, and we got here. And so this is the next step,” said Mt. Ararat coach Krista Chase said. “We punched through. That’s what we said last year. We got to the door last year, we kicked through the door this year.”
The Eagles seized control quickly, with three corners in the first five minutes of the game. But Cheverus took over, tilted play to the other end, and it paid off when freshman Avery Tinker scored off a Brooke Brunelle assist on a corner with 7:26 left in the second.
“Coming out of that first quarter, we were like, ‘Why are we letting them kind of have control of this game right now?'” senior midfielder and captain Ava Martin said. “We needed to take control, and that’s what we did. We had that momentum and that fire.”
Seconds after returning to the field after being carded, Sydney Brunelle made it 2-0 with 1:39 to go in the first half. Cheverus coach Andrea Musante said she knew that goal would be needed, which proved prophetic when Coen finished a Leah Lachance assist with 13:07 left in the third.
The Stags, though, weren’t about to let their latest title slip away.
“We knew Mt. Ararat wasn’t going to go down without a fight. That’s just who they are,” Musante said. “But we started getting into our rhythm, so we were able to hang on.”

title: ‘Remarkable’: Drunk raccoon leads to $250,000 for animal control
text:
HANOVER, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - Nearly a year after a drunk raccoon was captured in a Virginia ABC store, a campaign tied to the animal has raised $250,000 for Hanover County Animal Control.
Donations from the “Trashed Panda” campaign will cover more than half the cost of a new tool for officers to document animal cruelty investigations.
The tool consists of body cameras for animal protection officers. The money is going back into the shelter and its officers, said Jeffrey Parker, chief of animal protection for Hanover County.
The shelter has raised the money by selling shirts tied to the raccoon’s capture. Parker said the campaign has generated approximately $280,000 since it started a year ago.
His first reaction to the amount raised was shock and then gratitude, because the money is going back into helping the animals at the shelter.
“It was just remarkable the amount of feedback that came with it. I think a lot of people can relate to it as well. But it has just been remarkable,” Parker said.
Parker said the department has considered getting body cameras for some years, “but we never really pulled the plug,” Parker said.
Last year, Parker said the department started getting the data it needed to seek funding.
“This raccoon just helped us a little bit faster,” he said.
Parker said he had planned to present the cameras to the county as a budget request but saw the money generated from the campaign as a way to save taxpayer dollars.
Parker said the cameras are for officer safety, transparency and court documentation.
“We could use cameras every day. I think it provides valuable information and evidence for us. We utilize our sheriff’s office for body cams when we need body cam footage on scene ... So now we can do that on our own,” Parker said.
Parker said the cameras will also help him resolve complaints about staff members and keep reports more accurate. “That way we don’t possibly discipline good officers,” he said.
The “Trashed Panda” funding will pay for all of the equipment and this year’s service. Parker said service for years two through five will come from the county’s budget.
Parker said right now his officers will train over the next couple of months to prepare for the body cameras, with the initial start date for officers to wear the cameras on Jan. 4, 2027.
The shelter is using the money for new housing for animals, toys, a temperature-controlled food shed and a community and pet pantry.
Parker said the money will be shared between field operations and shelter operations. The department is gathering more projects for the remaining funds.
“Our goal is to use all the money for the animals in the department,” Parker said.
And if you’re wondering where the infamous raccoon is now?
“No telling where he’s at. Hopefully he’s living a good life, not doing any kind of more breaking and entering businesses and all that, and living a good life, we hope,” Parker said. “A sober one.”

title: High school band member stunned as 'Thunderstruck' performance goes viral
text:
You've been 'Thunderstruck': High school senior's band performance goes viral
A high school senior gained viral fame after a video of her playing "Thunderstruck" by AC/DC on mallet percussion in her marching band last year was reposted on social media last week, amassing millions of views.
"He sent me the link, and it had, like, already 6 million views, and I was like, aw, jeez," said Layla Clark, a senior at Thomas Jefferson High School in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
Clark was excited but showed humility while talking about the viral video. She said that mastering "Thunderstruck" was a lengthy process.
"It took forever to learn the song," she said. "I'm going to be really honest, I don't even have it perfected yet."
The video's popularity has spread far beyond the Pittsburgh area, even reaching a famous football player.
"I just found out getting on the bus today that Taylor Swift's husband (Travis Kelce) reposted my video and was talking about me, so that's exciting," Clark said. "That's the first actual celebrity I've heard talking about my video."
Clark also shared how her classmates have reacted to her newfound fame.
"I've heard people watching my video in the hallways, and they point and go, 'Oh, that's her,'" she said.
During the school's football game Friday night, the band also performed songs from "The Wiz," Elvis Presley's "Viva Las Vegas" and "Party in the USA" by Miley Cyrus.
Clark credited her band family for her success and personal growth.
"I wouldn't be the same without my band. I'd probably still be, like, the super shy, nervous kid," she said. "I couldn't have done any of this without them."
Clark dreams of attending college next fall to become an exotic-animal veterinarian and hopes her future school will also have a band.

title: You can visit some of Maine’s giant boulders
text:
This story was originally published in November 2024.
Deep in the forest near my house, massive boulders lie scattered along a hill, chunks of granite so tall they dwarf surrounding trees.
Walking among them, I navigate a maze filled with dark nooks and crannies, the rough walls embedded with black and white crystals and draped with lichen and ferns.
The wilderness sparks my imagination. When I enter this area of the woods, sometimes I envision the boulders as slumbering giants. Any minute, they might stir and stretch to the sky.
Meanwhile, the part of me that knows a little bit about geology understands that a glacier transported these rocks thousands of years ago, then dropped them off as it retreated.
These types of glacial deposits can be found throughout Maine, and the stick season — the drab period between brilliant fall foliage and winter wonderland — is the perfect time for finding them.
With leaves off the trees, you can see farther into the dense forest to spot the hulking shapes of boulders and other interesting geological features that might be hidden by greenery during the summer and cloaked in snow during the winter.
But you don’t have to go bushwhacking to visit some of Maine’s most impressive boulders. Many parks and preserves feature trails that are designed to visit them.
A few days ago, for example, I passed by a group of boulders while hiking Tunk Mountain in eastern Maine. That’s on the state-owned Donnell Pond Public Land.
Earlier this summer, I hiked past a famous boulder on the edge of Kidney Pond in Baxter State Park. The name? Kidney Stone.
I also visited the Debsconeag Ice Caves, which are small caves formed in the spaces between boulders that are piled on top of each other. The 2-mile round-trip hike is located in the Debsconeag Lakes Wilderness Area, which The Nature Conservancy owns, and it features a number of beautiful, fern-covered boulders.
When the composition of the boulder is different from the bedrock underneath it, it’s called a glacial erratic.
One of the most famous glacial erratics in Maine is Bubble Rock, which is located on the small mountain called South Bubble in Acadia National Park. While not particularly big, Bubble Rock is notable because it sits at the edge of a cliff, balancing as if it could tumble down the mountain at any moment.
While the bedrock of the area is called Cadillac Mountain Granite, Bubble Rock is made up of Lucerne Granite, which formed about 30 miles northwest of where the boulder now lies. A glacier transported it from its original location to where it sits.
And that’s not at all unusual. Daggett Rock — thought to be Maine’s largest glacial erratic at 80 feet long, 30 feet wide and 25 feet high — lies at the end of a short walking path in Phillips. Yet, due to its composition, it’s believed to have originated in the Saddleback Mountain area, several miles away.
It’s estimated to weigh about 8,000 tons. That’s a large piece of glacial debris.
Bass Rock is another famous erratic. Just peeking above the surface of Webb Lake, you can spot it from Webb Beach at Mount Blue State Park. A favorite spot for paddlers to stop, Bass Rock is a metamorphic rock, while the bedrock underlying the lake is igneous rock.
It’s hard to pinpoint exactly where Bass Rock came from, but since glacial ice generally flowed from northwest to southeast, it was probably carried to the lake from the nearby Tumbledown Mountain area, according to the Maine Geological Survey.
Most glacial erratics don’t get named. They’re so common throughout Maine that they blend into the landscape. If you live here, you might see them so often that you don’t think they’re anything special.
Some of my neighbors have boulders in their yards that compete with the size of their houses. And in the nearby lake, submerged erratics lurk just below the surface, threatening to sink boats.
Yet to people visiting Maine from other states or countries, these giant boulders stand out as spectacular landmarks. And if you think about it, they are pretty cool.
I count myself as fortunate to have so many interesting boulders scattered through the forest near my home. And I’m willing to bet that they’ve only been admired by me and a few hunters in the past 50 years or so.
Today, I went out to admire some of them with my dog Juno. My boots crunching in the dry leaves, I wove through bare-branched trees to find boulders larger than my tool shed, covered in rock tripe, a lichen that forms in rubbery sheets of vibrant green and black.
Many of the boulders were topped by rock ferns, which are among the few species of ferns in Maine that will remain green and lively-looking throughout the winter, even when dusted with snow.
I picked my way through the maze of boulders until I found it: the rock I’d been searching for — or two rocks, to be precise. Years ago, I stumbled across a boulder sitting on top of a larger boulder. And there it was, just as I remembered it.
My best guess is that a glacier dropped the boulders off like that, but maybe there’s another explanation. Whatever the case, I think it’s quite special. It reminds me of a cherry on top of an ice cream cone, or a pom-pom on top of a hat.
Perhaps I should name it. Any suggestions?

title: Snow potential brewing for mid-November
text:
Snow potential brewing for mid-November
Snow potential brewing for mid-November
Maine's Total Weather is monitoring the potential for an impactful storm arriving late next week or next weekend. Long-range weather models indicate a storm system moving into New England around November 13th or 14th.
A cooling trend is expected next week, and by Friday, highs are only in the 30s to low 40s. Temperatures aloft will be plummeting as well, allowing for snow formation in the upper levels.
Where the storm's center ends up will have a major impact on what type of precipitation falls across Maine. If positioned too far north, warmer air would flow in, making for more rain and the potential for ice. A track just south of Maine would make snow a high possibility. Too far south, however, we could miss out on the precipitation altogether.
This far out, details are highly uncertain but will be ironed out next week. Check back for updates.

title: Bake royally sweet treats with the new ‘Disney Princess Cookie Party’ cookbook
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Author Sarah Walker Caron returned to the WABI Book Club to discuss her latest cookbook, “Disney Princess Cookie Party.”
About the cookbook
“Be our guest for a princess party like no other as you dine on royally sweet cookie recipes inspired by the magic of the Disney Princesses!
“Capture the wonder of Moana, Rapunzel, Tiana, Belle, and the rest of the Disney Princesses with this whimsical baking book featuring 50+ cookie recipes. Get ready to bring a whole new sweetness to your next princess party, holiday spread, or Friday-night movie, with Princess-approved recipes such as Scottish shortbread from Brave or seashell cookies inspired by the vibrant colors of Ariel’s ocean home. From colorful macarons and cookie bars to simple chocolate chip and sugar cookies, you can get the whole party in on decorating. There are even simple recipes for kid bakers and more involved showstopper recipes to make photo-worthy cookie displays. And with easy-to-follow instructions for chefs of all ages, vibrant full-color photography, and the magic of Disney on every page, each recipe brings you special moments from your favorite heroines all while making baking fun! Jump into a whole new world . . . of delicious treats!”
How the book came together
“This is my fourth book with Insight Editions. They brought the concept to me as my previous Disney Princess cookbook, Disney Princess Tea Parties, had been so well received. From there, I developed a recipe list and other content for the inside, which Disney approved. And then I worked on developing the recipes, which took a lot of testing over about six months,” Caron said.
She said testing the recipes meant baking hundreds of cookies.
Caron’s other books
This is her 11th book overall and ninth cookbook. The “Pizza Planet Cookbook” was released in March 2026, and “Disney Princess Tea Parties,” was released in March 2022.
